News.title: Thomas Markle asked to leave care home after cops launch probe into ‘stash of child sex images’ following Sun expose
News.content:
Next

THOMAS Markle has left the care home he was living in following The Sun’s world exclusive that he is being probed by police over child sex abuse images.

That location, which The Sun has chosen not to reveal, has been described as a luxury rehabilitation centre that resembles a hotel.



A source at the home said last night: “He has been transferred following the news of his alleged crimes as it’s not a good look for us.”

Markle Snr was recovering and learning to walk again following the amputation of his left leg in the Philippines 11 months ago.



He is now in a nursing home in Florida, The Sun can reveal.

The Sun previously reported in a world exclusive how cops in the Philippines are investigating Meghan’s dad over boxes of sick material containing a child abuse video and child sex images.



We reported on the full inventory of surrendered computers, DVDs, mobile phones, video tapes, film negatives, memory data cards, books and pictures.

This included photos allegedly showing Thomas Snr in his 40s or 50s with a young girl in what appears to be a hotel room, and another showing her naked.

Thomas Junior – Meghan’s half-brother – told The Sun how he stumbled upon a child abuse video on a phone among his father’s abandoned possessions and reported it to cops.

Markle Snr denies all of the allegations, and has publicly denied the allegations as “sick lies.”



Thomas Jnr told The Sun he handed over four large boxes of items to cops last week in a world exclusive.

The window fitter became his father’s full-time carer after he suffered a stroke in 2022 and moved to Mexico to support him.

The pair relocated to Cebu City in the Philippines in January 2025 before a life-threatening blood clot led to the amputation of award-winning lighting technician Markle Snr’s left leg.



He was forced to return for treatment in the US, leaving behind a large collection of belongings where his son claims to have found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child abuse images.

Meghan’s father lived in the city of Rosarito at the time the hard drives were allegedly loaded with content.

Yesterday we reported that cops in the Philippines have been granted a warrant to search Thomas Snr’s computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes.

Cops in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.

Thomas Snr’s belongings — itemised in 80 categories on a police inventory list — are being combed through by Cebu’s Regional Anti Cybercrime Unit 7.



Data checks appeared to show all of the illegal material was downloaded in 2014 and 2020 — long before he moved to the Philippines with his son Thomas Jnr, 60, in January last year.

IT experts have already established hard drives among the haul contain “hundreds, if not thousands” of abuse pics and videos, including the worst illegal content.

Sources in Cebu City, the Philippines, where he lived until recently said the dark discoveries made so far may represent only “the tip of a huge iceberg”.



Thomas Jnr told The Sun previously: “It’s been a long process but I’m determined to cooperate fully in the hope that justice will be done.

“It took nine hours to sign all the documentation as I handed over all that stuff but I was relieved to get it off my hands.

“I think it will take months to check all these items and confirm my father is the disgusting monster I’ve now disowned.

“But if it transfers to the US, I’d be prepared to fly to Florida, or wherever he is, to see him in court.”

A police forensic trawl began after Philippines interior minister Jonvic Remulla said all signs point to Markle Snr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.



FBI investigators have confirmed their interest amid concerns about potential offences while Markle Snr was living in Chicago, Hollywood and Pennsylvania.

Meghan, 45, told 82-year-old Markle Snr it would be the last time he ever heard from her — and that she would never allow him to meet his grandchildren – in a letter last year.

He received the letter while in hospital in the Philippines after his leg was amputated in December 2025.



The bombshell revelations came as the Met Police was under scrutiny for failing to investigate child-sex claims made in a 2019 letter.

Meghan said she was “concerned” no action had been taken by Scotland Yard to alert other authorities.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

An Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) spokesperson said: “Following a voluntary conduct referral from the Met Police, we have decided an independent investigation is required into its failure to pass on allegations of serious offending, contained in a letter it received in 2019, to relevant overseas authorities at the time.

“We have decided that a further conduct matter – relating to an alleged data breach where information was passed on to a third party – should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with including via its data breach policies if required.”

News.title: Sick paedo who placed hidden cameras in bathroom to secretly film young girls showering & using the toilet is jailed
News.content:
VILE STASH Sick paedo who placed hidden cameras in bathroom to secretly film young girls showering & using the toilet is jailed







Next

A SICK paedo who planted hidden cameras to secretly film young girls has been jailed.

Gaven Clarke, 41, of Norfolk, recorded children over a five-year period, capturing videos and photos of girls as they showered or used the toilet.



His offending – between 2020 to 2025 – came to light when one of the girls discovered a phone camera hidden behind toiletries on a bathroom shelf, Norfolk Police said.

When she checked what was on the phone she found footage of herself that she did not know had been filmed.



She told her parents and it was reported to police.

Clarke was arrested in May 2025 and his phone and digital devices were seized, the force said.



When officers examined the devices, they found images of other victims, none of whom knew they had been filmed, and hundreds more indecent images of children that had been downloaded.

The 41-year-old, of Drayton, near Norwich, previously admitted two counts of voyeurism, four counts of making indecent images of children and three counts of taking indecent images of children, police said.

At Norwich Crown Court on Thursday, Clarke was sentenced to three years and eight months in prison.

In a statement read in court, one of his victims said: “I felt disgusted by his behaviour. I was extremely shocked by what I had found. I was physically shaking.



“In the weeks after discovering the videos, I kept asking myself, why me?

“I couldn’t get my head around what had happened. Now when I walk into a public toilet I am constantly looking around to check if there are any devices.”

The mother of another victim said she felt “sick to my stomach” when she was told what had happened.

In a statement on Friday, Norfolk Police urged other victims of voyeurism to come forward.

Detective Sergeant Ash Parker added: “I’d like to thank the victims for their bravery and resilience throughout this investigation.



“Clarke’s offending was a deeply disturbing violation of the victims’ privacy and dignity.

“He deliberately invaded spaces where young girls had every right to feel safe, subjecting them to an experience that has had a lasting and significant impact on them.”

Clarke was also put on the sex offenders’ register for life and made the subject of an indefinite restraining order and a 10-year sexual harm prevention order.

News.title: Dolphins around Britain could have regional accents just like humans, study shows
News.content:
Next

DOLPHINS around Britain may have regional accents just like humans.

Bottlenose specimens in Cardigan Bay make faster, higher-pitched calls than those elsewhere, giving them a distinctive “Welsh accent”.



The BBC’s Countryfile is revisiting 2021 show Wonders of the Celtic Deep, in which scientists filmed 240 dolphins.

They found some whistles were too high-pitched for human ears — but Laura Palmer, who studied dolphin sounds at Bristol University, said the squeaky chat could help them pull.



She said: “It could be that the higher frequency whistle makes them stand out more. Perhaps that’s more attractive to potential mates, for example.”

Another theory is that the dolphins, which develop their own call to use like a name, stick close together so have less need to be heard over long distances.

Ms Palmer explained to BBC Radio Wales: “Higher-frequency whistles don’t travel so far underwater.”

Channel Islands dolphins have a local twang, too.

Expert Paul Chambers previously said: “Just as regional isolation in humans produces different speech accents, the same is true for dolphins and porpoises.”

A 2007 study also found dolphins in the Channel whistled at higher frequencies than those in the Celtic Sea, possibly to be heard above shipping noise.



Regional differences have also been found among dolphins in the Med, Japan and New Zealand.

News.title: Miliband blasts Putin to face of Russian foreign minister during G20 meeting as he slams butcher Vlad killing civilians
News.content:
Next

ED Miliband has blasted Vladimir Putin to the face of his crony at a heated G20 summit – telling him “we all know you are the aggressor”.

Confronting Russia‘s foreign minister he slammed the Kremlin’s relentless bloodshed in Ukraine and warned “you are not winning this war”.



The fiery comments come just one day after Putin’s forces brutally bombed a railway station in Dnipro, Ukraine – killing 15.

Horrifying photos show multiple double decker buses and trucks engulfed in flames and shooting hellish black-orange plumes into the skies.





Speaking at the summit in Atlanta, Miliband said: “Only yesterday your drones attacked and killed 15 people.

“And there are countless examples like this of you killing innocent civilians throughout this war.”

In a fiery face-to-face with Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov he continued: “We all know you are the aggressor. We all know you started this war four and a half years ago with the full scale invasion of Ukraine.”

Russia has lost over half a million people to its senseless war with more than a million more injured.



Putin has even been forced to import thousands of prosthetic arms and legs for his maimed troops from Nato – despite being at war with Europe.

Miliband told his Russian counterpart to pass on a message to Putin: “You are not winning this war.”

In a veiled swipe at Donald Trump – who recently struck a huge diesel deal with Putin – the Brit politician urged all countries to choke off the funds that “perpetuate this barbaric war”.



Miliband made the comments at a meeting of foreign ministers from the world’s leading economies.

Controversy over whether Russia should have been invited to the G20 summit culminated in a scrapped group photo after Miliband and others refused to be pictured alongside Russia’s Lavrov.

In December, Trump is hosting a G20 summit of world leaders at his golf club in Miami.

It is unclear whether Putin will accept the US president’s invitation.

It comes as the world leader halted fresh sanctions against the Kremlin just three days before the limits were due to be imposed.



The measures would have imposed tariffs of up to 100 per cent on five Russian oil companies.

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky blasted the decision, warning it “only encourages Putin to keep attacking”.

Relations between the world leaders have sunk to an all time low after Elon Musk‘s Starlink programme mysteriously blacked out – leaving Ukraine more vulnerable to deadly drone strikes.

Vladimir Putin was delighted by the shock move and hailed the tech tycoon as “a real genius”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Kyiv’s military uses the satellite system for battlefield comms and to guide drone interceptors which down deadly Russian attacks.



Elon Musk and the US government have each blamed one another for the devastating slowdown in Starlink services.

News.title: Trump’s rare win in Memphis is huge lesson for all major cities – so why are the Republicans facing a Midterms pasting?
News.content:
Next

“IT was tense. Everybody was on their guard, head on a swivel. There were car thefts, carjackings, shoplifting raids.

“Ladies especially were afraid — to just go pump gas, afraid to go shopping, afraid to go out to dinner because, when you’d come out to the parking lot, your window was going to be broken into.”



Josh Hammond was talking as he showed me a damaged pillar inside his high-end off-licence in downtown Memphis, where a truck was driven through the front windows by a gang of raiders.

Josh added: “You’d walk around the city and, in any parking lot there was broken glass from these ram raids.



“In 2023, there were 200 liquor store burglaries — we were number 45.”

Describing the hit on his shop, he said: “There were maybe five or six [raiders] — they rammed a truck through these beautiful windows we have. It caused about $30,000 of damage, and they took off with about $20,000 of stock.”



His popular store, Busters, has been family-run for three generations — and is famed in Memphis for selling pretty much every tipple imaginable.

But the shop has now been the target of several raids — reflecting a violent crime epidemic in the city that has turned this birthplace of rock ’n’ roll into the gang capital of the American South.

The home of Elvis’s mansion Graceland has become a byword for gun violence. An underfunded and overwhelmed law-and-order machine often detains criminals only to release them on to the street within hours, to re-offend.

Leslie Taylor, a fed-up mum who founded the Memphis Crime Beat volunteer group, paints a dark picture.



She said of the troubles that inspired her community work: “In my neighbourhood, hearing gunshots was a regular occurrence. Hearing people drag-racing was a regular occurrence. It was not uncommon for people to be pulled over on our highways because they were hanging out car windows, shooting automatic weapons.”

Meanwhile Josh Hammond — faced with both insurance companies and customers abandoning his business out of fear — resorted to paying out for full-time security and installing bollards around his shop — but just two years later he has let the heavies go.

In September 2025, the US Government flooded ­Memphis with more than 1,200 National Guard troops, US Marshals and FBI agents as part of the new Memphis Safe Task Force.



“Memphis is deeply troubled,” said Donald Trump, announcing the task force.

“For years, our ­leaders allowed entire cities in America to be destroyed by crime, drugs and gang ­violence.

“Tolerating this violence was always a choice.”

Although political opponents howled, the statistics speak for themselves.

Both the White House and the independent Memphis Crime Commission have separate data showing overall crime has fallen by more than a third — back to levels last seen in 2011.



Murder is down more than 36 per cent, and burglaries are down by a quarter. Two of the thugs who smashed up Busters are now serving double-digit jail terms.

“There’s no question things are so much safer,” Hammond tells me.

“I can’t speak for everybody, but for the things that I see in my business, my family, the neighbourhoods we’re in, things have definitely changed, and I hope that’s the case throughout the city.”

So, while Trump faces a pasting in Tuesday’s Midterm elections, what are the potential political gains for him of his policy win in Memphis?



“Without question, the ­numbers work, and the task force has been a godsend,” says John Covington, vice president of the Memphis Police Association which represents the city’s 1,900 boys and girls in blue.

While local Democrat politicians and party activists branded sending in the troops “fascism”, the officer welcomed the National Guard’s arrival.

He said: “They’re out there on the streets — it’s visibility, reporting, deterring, support for us. But when you arrest people, you’ve got to ­follow through with the cases and put people in jail — the FBI has been huge with that.”

“Bringing in some federal prosecutions, too, we’re seeing people being put away for a long time. The really, really dangerous, violent people — we were able to put them away for years, so it’s been huge.”



Covington adds that his force is 600 short of its 2,500-officer recruitment target, so it has hugely benefitted from the back-up. He said: “It’s just all this extra manpower, it basically has made us fully staffed.

“We thought we would never see low crime again, and here we are. It’s amazing.”

Despite the results, the task force remains highly controversial — mostly because it has the name Donald J Trump attached to it.

Yet Covington is scathing about the criticism it has faced.

He said: “If you ask the progressive radicals, the liberal politicians, it’s been terrible. It’s been ‘fascist’. They find a way to ignore the numbers.



“But if you talk to the ­people, to law enforcement, they will tell you the real story — that it has had a huge impact. People are able to take their kids out to parks, and not hear gunfire at night and not fear bullets coming through their windows.”

Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District covers Memphis and is the Democrats’ only House of Representatives seat in the whole state.

Yet, thanks to the task force, and some boundary changes, it is one of a tiny handful of seats the Republicans could gain on Tuesday — which is expected to be a very tough night for Trump.

While he was re-elected in 2024 on a hardline platform of fighting immigration and crime, the cost of living and war in Iran have overshadowed clear successes on those fronts.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But regardless of the politics, there are huge lessons for all major cities from the Memphis story: officer numbers, and proper deterrents, work.



As happy copper Covington says: “It’s not rocket science.”

News.title: Burnham promised radical change but has instead proved he’s a PM without a plan – and Britain is paying the price
News.content:
Burnham: The PM in a pickle







Next

THIS was the week when Andy Burnham was exposed as a man without any plan.

The self-proclaimed “King of the North” had been exalted as a saviour by Labour MPs who toppled Sir Keir Starmer for being a dreary plodder.



His “radical” vision might, at face value, have seemed attractive to some. Promising to end the stasis stifling the economy, ease the suffocating cost of living crisis, and get Britons into jobs.

Then reality bit. His Chancellor’s blink-and-you’d-miss-it Budget was spectacular only in its lack of boldness and ambition.



Far from setting the nation on course for calmer waters, he is steering us towards still more treacherous economic rocks — with seemingly no idea of how to avoid them.

The PM has managed to exasperate absolutely everybody. Well, everybody except for benefits claimants, his Left-wing backbenchers and gherkin connoisseurs.

In an ITV interview yesterday, Burnham tried to mop up the mess, only to make himself look even more detached from reality.

How could he seriously grumble that his Budget wasn’t sufficiently radical when he’s ultimately in charge of it?

Hard-toiling taxpayers are raging at being treated like a never-ending cash machine to fund Labour’s unfair policies.

Look at who is picking up the tab. Workers have been betrayed over tax thresholds. Businesses are hit by hidden levies. Savers have been fleeced.



Anybody who enjoys a bet is going to find it harder to locate a high street bookie.

Growth is being strangled.

Yet, held hostage by his own bleeding-heart backbenchers, Burnham refuses to reduce the sky-rocketing welfare bill that is bankrupting the country.



He has no clear and coherent plan for anything. Look at the EU. In the past week, the PM has argued that the only way for the UK to flourish is to get closer to the collapsing bloc.

However, his own Budget policy of cutting import tariffs, to reduce the cost of living, would be IMPOSSIBLE without Brexit.

And what about our Armed Forces? While the Defence Secretary solemnly warns us to stockpile essentials to prepare for war by 2030, Burnham is dragging his feet on properly funding our hollowed-out military.

Burnham is also floundering on migration. He is set to water down the Home Secretary’s flagship crackdown, which would make some migrants wait longer for permanent residency here and reduce their right to benefits. Why?

Because he is scared of upsetting 100 left-wing MPs opposed to the change. Yet this sticks two fingers up at a public which has repeatedly demanded tougher immigration rules.



TikTok-loving Burnham has lofty rhetoric, vibes and musings galore.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But when it comes to dealing with the colossal issues he is an empty vessel.

In the 100 days or so he has been PM, he has shown his government has no serious answers.

News.title: How Kim Jong-un is making North Korea the ‘world’s first hacktocracy’ after stealing $6.3bn in biggest bank heist ever
News.content:
Next

KIM Jong-un’s gang of cyber pirates are feared to be turning the Hermit Kingdom into the “world’s first hacktocracy” after plundering up to £6billion, experts warn.

The tubby tyrant’s shady Lazarus Group are the prime suspects in today’s £4.7billion Binance crypto heist dubbed “the largest bank heist in history.”



Speaking to Sam Homewood on From The Newsroom, The Sun’s new YouTube channel, Investigative Cyber Journalist Geoff White said the hacker squad are estimated to have stolen up to £6billion in total.

He added: “If you could fast forward a few years, you could get to the point where North Korea is the world’s first hacktocracy.”



Targeting Binance overnight, Lazarus’ affiliate TraderTraitor are believed to have stolen nearly £5billion in assets in just 20 minutes.

The heist had all the hallmarks of a North Korean job, White said.



North Korea has spent years fine tuning its cyber warfare and hacking capabilities to turn digital theft into a sophisticated state industry.

Kim is even said to be conscripting primary school prodigies as young as five and grooming them to become the world’s next superstar hackers.

White said: “Some people claim North Korea makes some five percent of its GDP out of hacking.

“We could get to the point where 100 percent of North Korea’s GDP comes from hacks. I think North Korea was going in that direction.”



Paralysed by international sanctions, the regime has to connive a way to fund Kim’s ambitious nuclear programme.

“Hackers go out and steal the money to keep North Korea afloat,” White explained.

“Billions of dollars go into the treasury, they will be spending it missiles, weapons, but also nuclear material.”



Despite a large percentage of the country’s population being shut off from the outside world entirely, the select few are handpicked to become global hackers excel.

White said: “North Koreans are extremely resourceful people. They’re very good at bootstrapping their way up.

“Fundamentally, to carry out a hack, what do you need? A laptop and Internet connection and some brains.

“The first two aren’t particularly expensive. And the third one, North Korea’s got that. They’re innovative, smart thinking people.”

Kim Jong Un’s crypto crooks plundered billions from trading platform Binance in just 20 minutes.



The company admitted that the total estimated impact is around $6.3billion (£4.7bn).

It is not the first time North Korean cyber pirates have raided billions in crypto currency.

The shady Lazarus group nicked a staggering $1.5billion – of which 300million was cashed in – to fund the tubby tyrant’s war chest.



White explained it was “the previous biggest theft of all time” until it was trumped by today’s brazen crypto grab.

“Fast forward a year. This is four times bigger than that. Absolutely astonishing” said White.

He added: “If you fast forward within a few years, maybe five, maybe 10 years, you could get to the point where North Korea is the world’s first hackocracy.

“A government entirely supported by the proceeds of hacking.”

Kim Jong Un is also selling North Koreans to Russian businesses to fund his ballistic missile programme, a new report has found.



The tyrant has hatched a sick plot with Vladimir Putin to bypass international sanctions and bolster each other’s war chests.

The twisted scheme gives Putin a brutally controlled workforce while Kim Jong-Un steals their wages to fuel his own military agression.

The shocking plot was uncovered by the Global Rights Compliance (GRC).

RECOMMENDED STORIES

GRC Legal Advisor Elise Lauriot Prevost, who worked on the investigation, told The Sun: “Cooperation between the DPRK and Russia is only getting stronger.

“The DPRK is getting hard cash and fuel while Russia is getting workers to supplement its manpower shortages.”

News.title: Shabana Mahmood’s tough immigration crackdown faces major climbdown amid fears of huge Labour rebellion
News.content:
Next

SHABANA Mahmood’s immigration crackdown is set to be watered down amid fears of a huge Labour rebellion.

The Home Secretary wants to double the wait for permanent residency from five to ten years.



Some lower-paid migrants would have to wait 15 years for indefinite leave to remain (ILR).

But proposals to apply the changes retrospectively face being softened with Housing Secretary Angela Rayner already calling the plan “un-British”.



The Sun understands that Government whips have been scrambling to head-off a revolt by sounding out Labour MPs.

Opposition is thought to stretch well beyond the 100 who signed a protest letter, with others unwilling or unable to put their names to it.

A Government source said: “The PM is tougher on migration than many people think but on ILR there’s a clear direction of travel. It will now be more surprising if we stick with the proposals.”

About 1.6million migrants from the “Boriswave” are forecast to qualify between now and 2030, including hundreds of thousands of lower-paid workers and their dependants.

Permanent residency opens the door to claiming benefits.

Ms Mahmood herself has admitted this will cost taxpayers £10billion for low-wage care workers alone.



Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp accused her of preparing to “surrender to the open- borders Left, led by Angela Rayner”.

Talks are going down to the wire.

A Government source said: “It’s a stand-off between the Treasury and the Home Office.”

News.title: Telephone kiosk 'at centre of Britain' protected for future generations
News.content:
Telephone kiosk 'at centre of Britain' protected for future generations

The KX100 kiosk at Dunsop Bridge in Lancashire, was the 100,000th telephone kiosk installed in the country. It was officially opened in 1992 by explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, who was the first to use it to make a call

Sir Ranulph Fiennes Interview

A telephone box at the geographic centre of Great Britain has been given Grade II-listed status.

‌



‌



The KX100 kiosk at Dunsop Bridge, in Ribble Valley in Lancashire, was the 100,000th telephone kiosk installed in the country.

‌



It was officially opened in June 1992 by explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, who made the first call from the kiosk.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

He was joined by children from nearby Thornleyholme RC Primary School.

Jayne Rimmer, Historic England's north region listing team leader, said: "As part of the last generation of the public telephone box, it is a nationally significant kiosk."

‌



The Twentieth Century Society (TCS), which champions outstanding examples of modern design, had applied for it to be listed.

Campaigns director Oli Marshall said he was "absolutely delighted" by their success.

‌



View 3 Images The KX100 kiosk at Dunsop Bridge, in Ribble Valley in Lancashire, was the 100,000th telephone kiosk installed in the country. (Image: James Maloney/Lancs Live)

Avoiding awkward conversations about money costs Brits nearly £1,600 a year READ MORE :

He said: "There's no small irony that it was the arrival of the KX100 that first spurred the Society into action back in 1985.

‌



"Once the slayer of traditional red telephone boxes, that we fought vigorously to repel, now itself being given heritage protection.

"While widely unloved and underappreciated in comparison to the classic red telephone boxes, the ugly duckling KX100 model has developed a cult following."

‌



The Tour de France is "passing through Dunsop Bridge next July," he added.

"We hope the kiosk will form the centrepiece of the village's celebrations, as well as being the centre of Great Britain".

‌



Ribble Valley Borough Council leader Simon Hore said the phone box had "a special place in local people's hearts".

View 3 Images Dunsop Bridge is at the geographical centre of Great Britain (Image: James Maloney/Lancs Live)

‌



A plaque states the payphone "marks the centre of Great Britain" First introduced in 1985, the KX100 design has large glass panels and was designed to be easier to clean and more accessible than the previous red model.

The kiosk is of particular importance as it featured "a bespoke, site-specific design" featuring "key places in Britain radiating from the BT 'Piper' marque and Dunsop Bridge".

‌



The phone box was officially opened in June 1992 by explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes.

View 3 Images Sir Ranulph Fiennes with King, then Prince Charles back in 2012. (Image: Getty Images)

‌



The Lancashire village was named as the nearest settlement to the geographical centre of Great Britain following work by national mapping agency Ordnance Survey (OS).

Its calculations put the centre at Whitendale Hanging Stones, about 4.3 miles (7km) north-west of Dunsop Bridge.

‌



The title has been disputed, with other places also making a claim, including Haltwhistle in Northumberland.

OS later stated there could be "no absolute centre for a three-dimensional land mass sitting on the surface of a sphere and surrounded by the ebb and flow of sea water" and "different projections, scales and methods of calculation will all produce different results".

Article continues below

Dunsop Bridge was the result of defining Britain as "the mainland and the 401 associated islands", a spokesperson said in 2014.

They added that "looking only at the mainland of Great Britain", the location was a little further south, lying about 2.5 miles (4km) north-west of Whalley.

News.title: Inseparable couple die within 33 hours of each other - 'couldn't bear to be apart'
News.content:
Inseparable couple die within 33 hours of each other - 'couldn't bear to be apart'

The devastated family of beloved Staffordshire couple Doug and Jean Seabridge said the pair died within two days of one another, after Mrs Seabridge announced her husband's death

View 2 Images Doug and Jean Seabridge died within an hour of one another (Image: GoFundMe)

A married couple who "couldn't bear to be apart" died within 33 hours of one another, their family has said, shortly after marking their 53rd wedding anniversary.

‌



‌



Doug and Jean Seabridge, from Burton upon Trent, Staffordshire, married on September 22, 1973, and were inseparable "best friends" up until Doug died earlier this month. Jean announced his death on Facebook on October 10, saying he passed "peacefully after a short illness", adding the post was "one of the hardest things I have had to write".

‌



The beloved couple's grieving family sadly announced less that two days later that the two would be "together in eternity" after Jean also died.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images The couple had been married for more than 50 years (Image: GoFundMe)

Posting on a GoFundMe campaign set up on October 16, the couple's family said their hearts were broken to announce both Jean and Doug had died. They said in a statement: “Together in life, together in eternity – taken within 33 hours of each other.

‌



"Our hearts are broken, and we reach out to you today with immense sadness to share the devastating news that we have lost both our beloved Mum and Dad, Grandad and Grandma, Auntie and Uncle, brother and sister and dear friend to many.

"Our wonderful Doug and Jean Seabridge.” The couple’s family said losing them during the same weekend had left relatives overwhelmed emotionally and practically.

‌



They have launched a fundraiser to help cover the costs of giving the late couple a joint send-off, and have so far raised nearly £1,800 of a £3,000 target. They said: "If you are able to help, no donation is too small — every single penny will go toward giving them the beautiful, dignified send-off they so deserve.

"And if you cannot donate, please keep us in your thoughts, share this with others, and know that your kindness means more than words can say."

Article continues below

Remembering the couple, the family added: "They were inseparable. They built a life full of love, kindness and laughter. They were each other’s best friend, and it showed in everything they did. When one left this world, it felt as though the other simply couldn’t bear to be apart.

"They have gone home together, hand in hand, just as they lived.” Anyone who would like to donate to the couple's GoFundMe campaign can do so via the link here.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors final LIVE: Two missing from reunion as winners revealed after shocking twist
News.content:
The Celebrity Traitors have crowned their winners - as Sebastian Croft and Romesh Ranganathan took home the prize money for charity after last minute drama from James Blunt

Celebrity Traitors final LIVE: Two missing from reunion as winners and their chosen charities revealed

Celebrity Traitors 2026 has been won by the Faithfuls - as Sebastian Croft and Romesh Ranganathan take home the prize money for charity.

News.title: Bomb squad called to 'neighbour dispute' as 999 crews swarm and street evacuated
News.content:
Bomb squad called to 'neighbour dispute' as 999 crews swarm and street evacuated

Around 40 properties were evacuated in the area of Sawyers Hall Lane in Brentwood, Essex, following an alleged neighbour dispute, as a man and a woman were arrested

View 3 Images A police cordon on Sawyers Hall Lane in Brentwood (Image: Essex Live / BPM Media)

A bomb squad has been called to reports of an alleged neighbour dispute with a massive cordon put in place and dozens of homes evacuated.

The dramatic incident unfolded in Sawyers Hall Lane, Brentwood, as police cars and a bomb disposal van were spotted on the road from 7.30am.

Essex Police said officers forced entry to an address. A man and woman were arrested.

A search of the address revealed a small number of suspicious items which required specialist assessment, police said.

View 3 Images Around 40 properties were evacuated (Image: Essex Live/BPM MEDIA)

Around 40 homes were evacuated as a precaution during the operation. An Essex Police spokesperson said this afternoon: "We’re continuing to work alongside partners to ensure the safety of residents following the discovery of several suspicious items at an address in Brentwood.

"A 100-metre cordon remains in place across much of Sawyers Grove and small parts of Sawyers Hall Lane and Highland Avenue. Around 40 properties are affected, with occupants evacuated as a precaution while Explosive Ordnance Disposal experts safely assess a number of small items.

"A man and a woman remain in custody after officers forced entry to an address this morning, Friday 30 October. Residents whose properties are within the exclusion zone can go to a rendezvous point at King George’s Playing Fields Pavilion while the cordon remains in place.

"We appreciate the disruption this is causing and thank residents for their patience. We’ll continue to provide updates and hope to have the cordon lifted as soon as possible."

Article continues below

View 3 Images A number of small items were being investigated by Explosive Ordnance Disposal teams (Image: Essex Live/BPM MEDIA)

The street is located close to Merrymeade Country Park, and there is a pathway leading to the park that has also been cordoned off by officers, Essex Live reports. Some parts of surrounding roads have also been closed.

News.title: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself during major race makes grim eight-word admission
News.content:
Hyrox athlete who soiled herself during major race makes grim eight-word admission

Joanna Wietrzyk said she had been left traumatised by the backlash and has said she put others at risk while competing in the Hyrox Beijing event

View 4 Images Joanna Wietrzyk won a Hyrox race in September after soiling herself (Image: VCG via Getty Images)

An athlete who controversially soiled herself during a public long-distance race has admitted that she put others at risk during the event.

‌



‌



Joanna Wietrzyk, a 24-year-old elite athlete from Melbourne, Australia, surged to infamy in September when, while competing in the Hyrox Beijing event in China, she soiled herself during a bout of food poisoning. Ms Wietrzyk would go on to win the race covered in her own faeces, triggering outrage when, after fellow runners reportedly slipped in the liquid excrement, she declared: "Go hard or go home...a win is a win."

‌



But despite her confident exclamation, she was left "traumatised" by the ensuing backlash, and on reflection has concluded she made "the wrong decision".

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race reacts to fierce backlash and makes announcement READ MORE :

View 4 Images Ms Wietrzyk sparked massive controversy with her decision to finish the race (Image: BBC)

Speaking to the BBC ahead of her Hyrox return, Ms Wietrzyk said her determination had clouded her judgement on race day. She told the broadcaster she was "truly sorry" after she prompted a firestorm over her move, saying: "I didn't really think about those around me…

‌



"The decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect." Ms Wietrzyk is returning to Hyrox after massive public backlash to the incident.

Onlookers were left shocked by what happened and racers were outraged that they were exposed to it after paying to enter the race. Among them was competitor Joe Ho, who said athletes had been failed.

‌



View 4 Images The athlete said she regrets continuing the race after her bout of diarrhoea (Image: VCG via Getty Images)

He said in an Instagram post following the event that athletes could suffer "physical and psychological consequences".

‌



It ultimately forced Hyrox organisers to issue a public apology, saying in a statement that they "made a mistake" by not intervening, and vowing that rules would be changed. Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste said in a statement: "Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race.

"In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not." He added: "As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again."

‌



View 4 Images Ms Wietrzyk said she is excited to return to Hyrox (Image: Getty Images)

While she was sorry for what happened, Ms Wietrzyk added that she had received a lot of support going back into the sport.

‌



She told the New York Times : "I've had some time to reflect over the past six to eight weeks on everything that happened in Beijing, and firstly I just want to say that I’m truly truly so sorry to everyone that I affected whether they were spectators or participants out on that race floor for my decision to choose to continue to race.

"Having that time to reflect I've really learned a lot from the situation and I am very very sorry for it all. But I also want to say thank you to every person who has reached out to support and given me this overwhelming amount of support over the past couple of weeks.

Article continues below

"It's been a very hard situation to navigate for me and very confronting as well so all the support, whether it was personally or through my team has been honestly so incredible and it goes a lot longer than I can truly express right now.

News.title: Charles could be ditched as King by Bahamas as country's PM breaks silence
News.content:
Charles could be ditched as King by Bahamas as country's PM breaks silence

King Charles visited The Bahamas over two days earlier this week, with the country's Prime Minister Philip Davis saying the future of the monarchy there was "a question for my people"

The Prime Minister of The Bahamas has said he is open to losing the King as head of state and becoming a republic.

‌



Charles was welcomed to the island nation over two days earlier this week, where he frequently spoke of the shared history and deep bond between our two nations.

Yet, despite the warm welcome, Philip Davis has said the future of the monarchy in The Bahamas was "a question for my people" and that he would be "guided by the will" of Bahamians on whether to force a new future. The Prime Minister also addressed growing calls across the Caribbean for the King to apologise for slavery and for reparations to be paid.

Sarah Ferguson seen in public for first time with Beatrice and Eugenie after fleeing UK over Epstein scandal READ MORE :

View 4 Images King Charles in The Bahamas earlier this week (Image: Ben Stansall/Press Association)

He said the King "acts on the advice of his government" and was awaiting that advice until what he called "respectful dialogue" on reparations was complete.

Mr Davis said repair "is not absolutely money, simply, money" and could mean "acknowledgement, education, training, things of that nature."

He pointed to research tracing the largest export of cotton to Liverpool back to a plantation on Long Cay, near Crooked Island, and said the family "might want to consider" repair. But he admitted financial reparations could be "challenging for government", adding: "As a citizen, I would question why my tax payment ought to go to satisfy the debt of my ancestors 200 years ago."

Asked whether the slave trade was lawful at the time, he said: "I don't think so." He cited the King's Trust providing scholarships for Commonwealth citizens to study at Commonwealth universities, saying: "That could be a form of repair."

View 4 Images The King with Prime Minister Philip Davis in Nassau earlier this week (Image: Chris Jackson/Press Association)

On his visit earlier this week, the King made clear that leaders at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) will discuss matters around the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua and Barbuda.

His comments, made in an interview with Sky News, come days after the King began a nine-day Caribbean tour in Nassau, his first official visit to The Bahamas as monarch.

Asked whether The Bahamas still wanted the King as head of state, Mr Davis said: "I think we have some very passionate Bahamians who say we should be a republic. Equally, we have many passionate Bahamians saying that we ought not to rid ourselves of part of our history."

He said any move to a republic would require a referendum, adding: "Referendum in this country is not fared well, but that question would be a question for our people."

View 4 Images The King gives a speech in Cllifford Park (Image: Getty Images)

Within hours of touching down in Nassau on Tuesday, Charles made a speech at a youth rally where he said “It is only right that we acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond”.

However, before the King left Britain, talk of his visits to The Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda was dominated by calls for the monarch to deliver an apology for Britain and the monarchy's historic role in the slave trade as well as calls on the government to pay reparations. Activists in The Bahamas said the King had not gone far enough with his speech and said the issues were far from being resolved.

Mr Davis, who was re-elected in May, said a vote on the monarchy was not currently on the table because "my mandate did not include a referendum on whether we should keep the King or not." But he added: "If it comes up, certainly, but again, I'll be guided by the will of my people."

View 4 Images Charles spent two days in The Bahamas earlier this week (Image: AP Photo/Tim Aylen)

Pressed on his own view, he said he was "quite agnostic" about the issue. When asked whether he would be open to losing the King as head of state, he replied: "I'm open to it, yes."

And to those in Britain who believe there is no need for an apology, he said: "I think they have to appreciate the weight of that history and that ancestors like ourselves continue to bear."

The Bahamas gained independence in July 1973. On his visit this week the King returned to Clifford Park, where he last officially appeared as Prince of Wales in 1973 when the country gained independence after 300 years of British rule. On that occasion he delivered a formal message from Queen Elizabeth II to Bahamians.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Mr Davis said the country had "thrived" since then. "We have a tremendous advancement, development, and you can see how we have developed," he said.

But his remarks suggest the nation's relationship with the Crown could yet take a different course, following Barbados, which became a republic in 2021.

After The Bahamas, the King's tour moves on to Guyana and then Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, where Queen Camilla will join him.

News.title: Farmer's 'blazing row' with dad before strangling him and leaving body in shallow grave
News.content:
Farmer's 'blazing row' with dad before strangling him and leaving body in shallow grave

Charles Wright, 52, strangled Brian Wright, 82, and left his body in a shallow grave at Hall Farm near Newark in Nottinghamshire

View 3 Images Brian Wright was 82 when he was killed by his son (Image: Nottinghamshire Police / SWNS)

A man killed his father and buried him on the family farm before taking his own life following a "blazing row" over money, an inquest heard.

‌



‌



Charles Wight, 52, saw a "flash of red" when he felt his father, Brian, 82, was "cutting him out" of the family's business. He choked him to death to death placed his body in a shallow grave at Hall Farm near Newark in Nottinghamshire.

‌



Two days later, Charles took his own life. Nottingham Coroner's Court heard today that, in a voice message left by Charles for police, he said his father was "thinking of replacing him" and "giving the lion's share of the farm to another family member".

‌



In the note, which was sent on November 22, Charles said: "I just had a flash of red and after 25 years and everything I have given him, he was just cutting me out like that. I just saw red, dragged him out of the car and throttled him."

View 3 Images Police near the scene where Brian Wright was buried in Nottinghamshire (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

The inquest was told Brian had called Charles "useless" and "not capable of farming" and said it was a "mistake to let him farm that land" during the heated argument. Detective Chief Inspector Ruby Burrow, of Nottinghamshire Police, told the court of the voice message: "Charles stated that he had killed his father and intended to kill himself.

‌



"He described that his father Brian had criticised him and there had been a disagreement about finances. He stated he had buried his father Brian on the family farm."

Brian was reported missing to police shortly before midnight on November 20 as he had failed to take his wife to a hospital appointment. The next day, Charles, his brother James Wright and a colleague who worked on the family farm as a mechanic spoke to police officers.

‌



DCI Burrow told the inquest that Charles, who was interviewed the day before he took his own life, "was able to assist by describing difficult family dynamics and difficulties in relationships over the years, including issues around finances and also working arrangements on the farm". She continued: "We had a number of interactions with Charles.

"Charles provided similar contextual information about relationships within the family. He described an argument he had had with his father. He described his father had been critical towards him and he, himself, had taken some time to calm down."

‌



View 3 Images Police near the farm following the two deaths (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

Charles Wright told police his father had "left in the opposite direction after the small argument", the court heard. Later on November 21, Brian's vehicle was reported as appearing "out of place" where it had been left overnight, and his body was discovered buried on the farm four days later.

‌



His cause of death was found to be pressure applied to the neck, the inquest heard. Ms Burrow said there had been a report on November 22 of "a collision between a vehicle and two gentlemen", where the vehicle was driven at them "apparently deliberately".

She stated that Charles had driven his vehicle at his brother James, who was running alongside a friend, "causing injury". Charles Wright took his own life later that same day, with his body discovered in an outbuilding area on Hall Farm.

Article continues below

Senior coroner for Nottinghamshire Mairin Casey ruled that Brian Wright had been unlawfully killed, while his son's death was concluded to be suicide. Addressing the family members present in person and those joining via video-link, she said: "The horror of this, I'm clear in my mind, will have affected all of those who have survived in a very deep and painful way."

Samaritans can be contacted for free, day or night, 365 days a year, on 116 123, or visit samaritans.org to find your nearest branch.

News.title: Russell Myers: King Charles in danger of being remembered as monarch who didn't apologise
News.content:
As the King stood in reflection in Georgetown, on the very ground where enslaved Africans were executed after the Demerara uprising of 1823, it was impossible not to be encapsulated by the moment.

Even before Charles' arrival in The Bahamas earlier this week and Guyana today, this tour has been dominated by the issue of slavery and reparations.

I have no doubt that Charles' personal feeling over slavery is deeply felt and perhaps, given the freedom to do so rather than being restricted by the government, he would feel moved to issue an apology for Britain and the monarchy's historic role in slavery.

King Charles reflects at spot where slaves were publicly executed after uprising READ MORE :

King Charles' popularity sinks to lowest level of reign amid Harry and Meghan return READ MORE :

View 3 Images King Charles in Guyana today (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Indeed, within hours of landing in Nassau on Tuesday, he told a youth rally: "It is only right that we acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond". Yet, however heartfelt his words, they have not quietened the clamour that has followed him across the Caribbean.

At a Junkanoo parade in Nassau, one sign in the crowd read simply: "Pay us what you owe us." In Guyana, President Irfaan Ali has welcomed the King's past expressions of regret but made clear an apology must be the next step. And today came perhaps the most striking intervention of the tour so far.

Speaking to Sky News, Bahamian Prime Minister Philip Davis said he was open to losing the King as head of state, just days after giving him the warmest of welcomes.

View 3 Images Protestors hold up posters during the King's visit to Guyana (Image: Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

‌



The future of the monarchy, he said, was "a question for my people" and he would be "guided by the will" of Bahamians. Asked directly whether he was open to it, he replied: "I'm open to it, yes."

Mr Davis was careful. He described himself as "quite agnostic", noted that a referendum was not part of his mandate and acknowledged that many Bahamians did not want to "rid ourselves of part of our history".

But his message to Britain was unmistakable. To those who see no need for an apology, he said: "I think they have to appreciate the weight of that history and that ancestors like ourselves continue to bear."

Here lies the King's dilemma. He acts on the advice of his ministers, and the Government has ruled out both an apology and reparations, fearing a legal precedent that could open the floodgates for former colonies around the world.

‌



View 3 Images Charles during a visit to Umana Yana in Guyana (Image: Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

Mr Davis himself recognises that. He said the King "acts on the advice of his government", and conceded that financial reparations could be "challenging". Repair, he suggested, might instead mean acknowledgement, education and training, even pointing to the King's Trust scholarships as "a form of repair".

That is perhaps the most hopeful note for Charles. There is a path between apology and silence, and it is one he has walked for years.

He has also confirmed that Commonwealth leaders will discuss the legacy of slavery in Antigua next week, at a summit he will preside over.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Yet the ground is shifting beneath him. Barbados left in 2021. Jamaica is pushing towards becoming a republic and now the leader of a nation that welcomed him so warmly this week admits he is open to the King's departure.

None of this is of Charles's making. He has gone further than any monarch before him in confronting the past.

But history rarely judges kings on intentions alone. If Chogm ends with warm words and little else, the danger is that his reign in the Caribbean will be remembered not for the moments of reflection, but for the apology that never came.

‌

News.title: Driver guilty of hitting cyclist and dragging him to death under car
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A man has been found guilty of murdering a head teacher who was dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car.

Simon Richardson crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins, who was cycling home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on the evening of 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.

Prosecutors claimed Richardson, 35, fled the scene of the crash before stopping to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist and then driving on with Mr Mullins still lodged underneath the vehicle.

Richardson was also convicted of dangerous driving and will return to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to be sentenced on Monday.

There were shouts of "Yes!" from the court's public gallery as the guilty murder verdict was announced.

Others could also be heard crying.

The judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, told Richardson that there was only one sentence for murder, namely life imprisonment.

News.title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
News.content:
Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.

One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".

Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".

"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.

The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.

Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

News.title: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
News.content:
The King has made a poignant visit to the site where a Guyanese slave rebellion was violently resisted by British authorities, making the stop during his tour of the Caribbean.

He visited Independence Park in Georgetown to remember the Demerera Slave Rebellion of 1823, which saw an uprising by thousands of enslaved people.

Accompanied by Guyana's Culture Minister, Steven Jacobs, he was told how hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders during the rebellion and many of those who survived were executed close to where the King stood.

Above the King was a sign that he took time to read.

"This ground was used as a public execution site," it said, "where enslaved persons...were condemned to death and hung."

The moment of reflection was what Buckingham Palace had described as the King "not shying away from the UK's colonial legacy" and described today as a chance for the King to reflect on Guyana's history of slavery and resistance.

In 2022, Charles described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to "deepen my own understanding of slavery's enduring impact", in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.

Independence Park, which is now a sports ground, drew a crowd of dozens of schoolchildren. The King stopped to talk to many of them asking them about their homework, their holidays and if they'd had a day off school.

News.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
News.content:
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).

Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.

Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.

While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.

Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.

Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (Â£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.

At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.

The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

News.title: Democrats in the US have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix
News.content:
James Stevens calls himself a democratic socialist. The 24-year-old film student is the type of Democrat who recalls watching the provocative left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker six years ago, "before he became relevant in politics". Last year, James flew up from his home in Georgia to New York City to canvass for Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign.

His mother, Tamara, 56, is a loyal Democrat too. But of a different ilk. She grew up Republican then switched to the Democratic Party after seeing Barack Obama on Oprah. These days, she's a loyal party woman, championing reproductive rights, attending campaign rallies and donating to local candidates.

Both mother and son want Democrats to win control of Congress at Tuesday's midterm elections, but they don't entirely agree on what they want their Democratic Party to be.

"I'm very sick of how compromising Democrats are to Republican policies that don't benefit a large group of people," James told me, as his mother looked on. "There needs to be a bold vision for the Democrats," he says, arguing that the party should adopt policies affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a left-wing splinter group. In his view, that means anti-Zionism, getting corporate money out of politics, and government-run free healthcare.

The conventional wisdom in Washington is that Democrats are well-positioned to take control of the House, and possibly even the Senate, after the vote next week.

Underlying conditions are in Democrats' favour â Republican US President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low for a president heading into a midterm, comparable to George W Bush in his final term in 2006; the Iran war still isn't over and it's proving unpopular with American voters; and this has led to higher gas prices, which are frustrating an electorate that is already worried about the cost of living. Traditionally, the midterms are a referendum on a sitting president. In 18 of the last 20 US midterm elections, the party in power has lost seats in the House.

News.title: Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86
News.content:
Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".

Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."

Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".

"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.

Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.

The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."

The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.

Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".

Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".

"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.

News.title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
News.content:
Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.

In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".

Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings".

Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.

Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.

She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".

None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."

Referring to Brand's accusers' evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality changeâ¦

"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.

She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushingâ¦ thrusting".

"In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."

The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened.

"There is no magic force in this documentary", she added.

"What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."

She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."

She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit.

"The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."

News.title: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
News.content:
The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".

The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.

He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".

On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.

The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.

The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".

Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.

Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".

The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.

The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.

The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".

The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.

The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.

Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".

"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."

Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.

Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.

Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.

However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".

News.title: Stabbed boy felt Huntingdon train attacker 'was not sane', court hears
News.content:
A 14-year-old boy stabbed by a man who went on to attack people on a train said he did not feel the knifeman was "mentally sane", a court heard.

The teenager was attacked in Peterborough the day before Anthony Williams is accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon in November 2025.

In a video recorded interview played to jurors at Cambridge Crown Court, the boy said: "This random guyâ¦ he just pulled out a knife and stabbed me."

Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder - four of which concern attacks prior to the mass train stabbing.

At the time of the attack, the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was waiting with a friend on a footbridge over the River Nene, before going trick or treating.

Williams drew a knife from his waistband, he said, and "because I was closest to him, he's just stabbed me".

"I didn't feel like he was mentally sane. His eyes were wide open, like he was on something," he said.

"My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'."

"When he stabbed me, it's like he was there for a knife fight. Like he was waiting for me to pull out something."

The teenager said he had "so much adrenaline" that it felt "like a poke in the chest".

The jury heard the pair ran away and hid in some bushes, where they called the police.

News.title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
News.content:
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.

"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.

He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".

In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.

Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.

The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".

Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.

He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.

The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.

News.title: Wettest week for two years but still not enough rain to get out of drought
News.content:
The recent stormy weather brought England's wettest week in two years, according to the Environment Agency.

However, despite the rain, Wales and most of England are still in drought with parts of southern England in severe drought.

Met Office provisional statistics for October show that the UK received above average rainfall.

However, the National Drought Group have said it will take sustained and above average rainfall over a seven month period for conditions to improve to normal.

Over the last week we had the first two named storms of the season - Austen and Boelo - which gave much of the UK significant and much needed rain.

Rainfall totals ranged from 38mm in central England to 87mm in the south-west and according to Enviroment Agency (EA) monitoring, it was the wettest week across England since October 2024.

In some parts of southern England there was nearly 50% more rainfall than normal throughout the month.

As a whole, England has had 111% of its long-term monthly rainfall, according to the EA.

News.title: Ministers vow online safety action after teen sextortion victim took own life
News.content:
The UK government has said it remains committed to making the online world as safe as possible for young people following the death of a teenager who took his own life after he fell victim to an online sextortion scam.

Cai Davies, 18, died in June 2025 after he had sent messages to a woman he believed had a romantic interest in him.

South Wales Central Coroner's Court heard he had been targeted by scammers operating from Africa, who demanded money from him and said intimate photos would be sent to his friends and posted on YouTube.

The coroner addressed a Regulation 28 preventing future deaths report, external to the UK and Welsh government with her concerns about how Cai had fallen victim to the scam.

Assistant coroner Rachel Knight recorded a conclusion of suicide after Davies, from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, died.

Knight said it was "more likely than not" that personal stresses in his life together with falling victim to the sextortion scam "more than minimally contributed" to his death.

She wrote of the scammers: "Conversation quickly turned sexual and she asked him for intimate images, which were then used to blackmail him for money by threatening to send the images to his family and friends, and to upload them to a YouTube channel.

"The images were indeed sent to at least one of Cai's Facebook friends by the scammer.

"Cai was bombarded with video calls and messages via Facebook Messenger and WhatsApp over a very short period of time making demands for money."

News.title: County Down man among three jailed for planning mosque attack
News.content:
A County Down man is among three men who have been jailed for attempting to engage in a terrorist activity, specifically damaging a mosque in Galway.

Garrett Pollock (36) of Kilhorne Greene in Annalong was sentenced to 10 and a half years with the last year suspended.

Darren Gorman (34) of O'Moore Place in Portlaoise was sentenced to eight years with the last year suspended and Karolis Peckauskas (39) of Newfoundwell Road in Drogheda was sentenced to eight years in prison with the last year suspended.

They had made advanced plans to blow up the Maryam Mosque on the Monivea Road between 4 and 5 November 2025 when they were arrested, the Special Criminal Court in Dublin heard.

Pollock also pleaded guilty to possessing an explosive substance which was found in four glass jars hidden in a drawer in his van on 4 November.

On Friday, Ms Justice Caroline Biggs said that modern Ireland is a multicultural and diverse country and that the actions of this group bring shame on the country.

It was, Biggs said, attempted arson with a terrorising message to be spread worldwide.

She added that it was clear that this was intended to be the first of many attacks.

News.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Trump approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Kyiv days after calling for Zelensky to go
