In 2021, Switzerland’s Federal Criminal Court found Kosiah, now 51, guilty of multiple atrocities committed during the first of Liberia’s back-to-back civil wars, in which about 250,000 people died between 1989 and 2003.

In 2023, the court’s appeals chamber upheld his 20-year sentence for war crimes and, for the first time in Swiss history, also made a new ruling that Kosiah was guilty of crimes against humanity.

The Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland was asked to review the case, and its verdict, dated September 28, was published on Friday.

The court “rejected the appeal filed by a high-ranking Liberian military official challenging his conviction for violations of the laws of war committed between 1993 and 1995 during the first Liberian civil war”, it said in a statement.

“However, the court has acquitted the individual of the charge of crimes against humanity, based on a strict application of the principle of non-retroactivity.”

Switzerland recognises the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows it to prosecute individuals suspected of international crimes, regardless of where those crimes were committed.

The court said the offence of crimes against humanity – introduced into Swiss law in 2011 – could not be applied to acts committed before then.

Kosiah’s conviction for violating the law of war was upheld, as was the maximum 20-year custodial sentence imposed.



“The decision makes final the first war crimes conviction ever handed down by a Swiss civilian court, and the first conviction anywhere of a Liberian for war crimes committed during the country’s civil wars,” said the Swiss organisation Civitas Maxima, which works to bring perpetrators of international crimes to justice.

Kosiah settled in Switzerland in the late 1990s and was arrested in 2014.

“Today the survivors of Alieu Kosiah’s crimes have final justice,” said Civitas Maxima director Alain Werner, who represents victims in the case.

“We are, however, deeply disappointed by the acquittal on crimes against humanity. What happened in Lofa between 1993 and 1995 is the very definition of a crime against humanity.”

Like war crimes, crimes against humanity refer to atrocities, including murder, torture and rape. However, instead of isolated or sporadic events, the charge is used for incidents carried out in a widespread or systematic way.

In the 2021 verdict, Kosiah was found guilty of a slew of war crimes committed as commander of the United Liberation Movement of Liberia for Democracy rebel group.

He ordered or participated in the killing of 17 civilians and two unarmed soldiers, as well as rape and the deployment of a child soldier, the court ruled.

He had also ordered looting and repeatedly ordered, or had himself inflicted, cruel and humiliating treatment of civilians and mishandled corpses, according to the verdict.

World.title: US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots
World.content:
The 9th Circuit Court calls the petition to remove 20,000 ballots from California’s vote count unconstitutional.

Share US appeals court again rejects Trump bid to set aside California ballots on social media

For the second time in less than a week, a United States appeals court has rejected a petition from the administration of President Donald Trump to set aside 20,000 ballots in California over concerns about non-citizen voting.

The decision came down on Friday, with less than four days until the November 3 midterm elections.

The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Trump’s request would violate the US Constitution and risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

“The consequence of the United States’s request is not merely ballot segregation, but ultimately both the cancellation of the ballot and the removal of voters from the voting rolls,” the majority wrote in its ruling.

Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez – appointed by Trump and his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden, respectively – formed the majority.

A third judge, Trump appointee Patrick Bumatay, issued a dissent, saying the administration’s petition was a “reasonable request”.

The Trump administration has claimed that nearly 20,000 “likely non-citizens” received mail-in ballots to vote in California’s midterm elections on November 3. It sued the state on October 15 to prevent those ballots from being counted.

But the accuracy of the Trump administration’s list has been called into doubt, as have its claims of widespread non-citizen voting.

Election fraud in the US is extremely rare. So is non-citizen voting, despite Trump’s assertion earlier this year that as many as 278,000 foreign nationals across the country were registered to vote.



Like California, states such as Nevada and Washington have also received lists of alleged non-citizen voters, but officials there have found the documents largely inaccurate.

In Nevada, for instance, state authorities issued a statement in September saying the Trump administration had erroneously identified citizens as non-citizens on its list. Not a single name was correct, according to the statement.

California, a Democratic stronghold, will elect 52 members of the House of Representatives, one of Congress’s two chambers, on November 3.

The state has long been Trump’s target for criticism, with the president accusing its Democratic leadership of “cheating” in elections.

But California officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, have countered that the Trump administration is seeking to meddle in the state’s elections to sow voter distrust and undermine the results.

“This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters,” Newsom said in a news release after the October 15 lawsuit.

Non-citizen voting in federal elections is against the law in all 50 US states, including California.

The Constitution’s Elections Clause also grants states exclusive authority to administer elections, though it does allow for Congress to pass regulations concerning voting procedures.

The Trump administration initially sent California its list of 20,000 “likely non-citizens” on October 12, barely three weeks before the midterm election.

California officials refused the administration’s demand to set aside the 20,000 ballots, requesting proof that the names on the list were indeed foreign nationals. According to the California government, no such evidence has been provided.

The Trump administration last week charged 28 foreign nationals in California with election-related infractions, but some of the accused told the Los Angeles Times they had never registered to vote.

The newspaper’s reporting suggested some of the non-citizen defendants shared the same name as eligible voters.

As the October 15 lawsuit navigated the court system earlier this month, the Trump administration sought an emergency ruling from the 9th Circuit Court to suspend the 20,000 ballots.

But the appeals court rejected the petition on Monday, saying the Trump administration had not given lower courts adequate time to weigh the matter.

A lower court ultimately ruled against the Trump administration on Wednesday, and the administration again appealed to the 9th Circuit Court.



In its majority decision, the appeals court framed the Trump administration’s lawsuit as an attempt to violate the Constitution’s Elections Clause.

“We decline the United States’s invitation to contravene the Elections Clause by undermining the Constitution’s plain text,” the majority wrote.

The majority also wrote that it had “major concerns” that granting the Trump administration’s request would “harm the public interest by risking the disenfranchisement of eligible voters and putting the entire tabulation process in jeopardy”.

World.title: G20 drops group photo as Europeans refuse to stand with Lavrov
World.content:
Share G20 drops group photo as Europeans refuse to stand with Lavrov on social media

The United States has scrapped a traditional group photo of foreign ministers after European officials refused to be pictured alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

The move exposes deep rifts at the heart of the Group of 20 (G20), whose foreign ministers are meeting in the southern city of Atlanta in the United States for talks overshadowed by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“There will be no family photo featuring our European partners together with Mr Lavrov,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, according to the dpa news agency.

Lavrov, who remains under Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arrived in Atlanta ahead of the talks, Russian state media reported. Moscow said on Thursday that he would use his speech to argue against international sanctions. Ukraine was not invited, the Abu Dhabi-based newspaper The National reported.

A diplomatic source told the AFP news agency that Russia’s presence at the G20 “in no way legitimises its actions”.

The European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas pledged on Thursday to urge G20 partners to strengthen support for Ukraine and pursue accountability through a special tribunal and claims commission, after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian railway station killed at least 14 people earlier that day.

The meeting also comes weeks after US President Donald Trump issued sanctions waivers allowing Russia to export diesel to ease fuel prices before the November 3 midterm elections.

Opening the talks, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged members to cooperate on economic and geopolitical crises threatening global trade, energy and food supplies, and freedom of navigation, dpa reported. Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz after US-Israeli strikes began in late February, and global energy prices have risen sharply since.

“Both maritime and food security drive economic security,” Rubio wrote on X.



No joint statement is expected. A diplomatic source told the AFP news agency that Washington will instead publish a chair’s summary it has drafted. The source added: “The G20 is no longer really a forum where foreign ministers can reach agreement on a statement.”

No government has said whether Rubio and Lavrov will hold a formal bilateral meeting.

China sent Executive Vice Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu in place of Foreign Minister Wang Yi, according to a delegation list released by the Department of State. South Africa, a founding G20 member, has been excluded by Washington, and the African Union is represented by Burundi’s Edouard Bizimana.

The Atlanta talks are the last ministerial meeting of the US G20 presidency before leaders meet in Miami on December 14 and 15.

World.title: Rubio hosts G20 talks as Russia’s Lavrov presence sparks tensions
World.content:
NewsFeed Rubio hosts G20 talks as Russia’s Lavrov presence sparks tensions

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged G20 officials meeting in Atlanta to work together to confront threats to the economic order. The US scrapped the traditional group photo after several European officials objected to being pictured with Russia’s Sergei Lavrov.

World.title: Port Sudan families can barely afford water as shortages persist
World.content:
Port Sudan, Sudan – Every day, Amina Khalafallah spends 10,000 Sudanese pounds ($1 at the parallel market rate) on water for herself and her four children. Over a 30-day month, that amounts to 300,000 pounds ($30) – the equivalent of her entire monthly salary.

Khalafallah lives in the Deim Mayo neighbourhood of Port Sudan, in eastern Sudan, where her home is not connected to a piped water network. Instead, she depends on street vendors, who charge 1,000 pounds ($0.10) for 18 litres.

Khalafallah works in a cafeteria at a private institution, while her husband works in another state and sends money to help her out when he can.

Between them, the family barely scrambles enough money to get by, but Khalafallah says she often has to borrow money. It’s a typical story in Sudan, where, according to the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the country’s more than three-year-long war has pushed average incomes back to levels last seen in the early 1990s.

The hotter months bring additional challenges, as water prices rise and vendors become harder to find.

“We make sure to set aside money for water in the summer before covering our other household needs, even if that means going without some essentials,” Khalafallah told Al Jazeera.

According to the African Development Bank (AfDB), access to safe water is one of Sudan’s most urgent needs, with millions of children at risk of waterborne diseases.

In Port Sudan, relatively safe from the fighting that has plagued other areas of the country, the arrival of people displaced by the war has put additional pressure on already fragile infrastructure. The AfDB has reported that the city’s water supply was meeting less than 40 percent of demand.



One of the major issues Port Sudan has faced is the collapse of the Arbaat Dam. Located in the Red Sea Hills northwest of Port Sudan, it once supplied half of the coastal city’s daily water needs.

But in August 2024, heavy rainfall and flooding caused the dam to collapse, destroying villages downstream and damaging pipelines and wells.

As a result of the collapse, entire neighbourhoods are dependent on expensive water deliveries by truck.

Rising costs for water vendors

Ahmed Osman, 30, has spent the past three years working at a water distribution station that supplies street vendors who deliver water to households.

When Sudan’s war began in April 2023, Osman said he charged vendors 4,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.40) to fill a donkey-drawn cart carrying at least 250 litres of water.

Those prices have since risen sharply, he said, because of increasing operating costs, particularly the fuel needed to transport water to his distribution station.

“A water tanker carrying 50,000 litres of water now costs 1.5 million Sudanese pounds [$150], compared with about 450,000 pounds before the war,” Osman told Al Jazeera.

Osman keeps the water in storage tanks before pumping it into the vendors’ carts. He charges 16,000 pounds ($1.60) to fill a cart carrying 250 litres.

After his expenses, Osman typically makes a profit of about 70,000 pounds ($7) per day, split between him and his partner.

Repairs yet to end water shortages

Rehabilitation work has restored parts of the damaged water network.

According to the UNDP, the restoration work has included drilling or rehabilitating 15 boreholes, laying 17 kilometres (10.5 miles) of new pipelines, as well as installing solar-powered pumps.

The UNDP said the restored system could supply water to nearly 230,000 people.

However, that would still not be enough to supply water to all of Port Sudan, which the UNDP estimates to now have a population of one million people.

Other projects are therefore necessary to meet the water needs of residents – including one launched in June by the AfDB and UNICEF, which intends to expand access to safe water for up to 750,000 people in the city.

Water shortages threaten public health

Emad Hafez, medical director of the emergency department at Port Sudan Teaching Hospital, told Al Jazeera the water crisis poses serious risks to public health, increasing the risk of waterborne diseases and making it harder for families to maintain basic hygiene.



He warned that disruptions to water supplies can force families to rely on untreated water, increasing the risk of cholera and other diarrhoeal diseases, particularly during the rainy season and in overcrowded displacement camps.

“Water shortages can also make it harder for families to maintain adequate hygiene, increasing the risk of skin infections and other hygiene-related illnesses,” Hafez said. “Meanwhile, storing water in uncovered containers can create breeding sites for mosquitoes, raising the risk of vector-borne diseases such as malaria and dengue fever.”

Water shortages also threaten healthcare services, Hafez said, explaining that hospitals require reliable supplies for infection prevention, cleaning and patient care.

“Beyond its immediate health consequences, water insecurity can worsen food shortages and malnutrition by disrupting agricultural activities and placing additional financial pressure on already vulnerable households,” he said. “Children under five and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the effects of inadequate nutrition.”

World.title: EU and Canada seek deeper ties amid worsening global uncertainty
World.content:
The European Union and Canada have launched what they described as an Alliance for the Future, as Ottawa prepares to become the bloc’s first so-called “associate member”.

Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted the Canada-EU summit in Montreal and signed a digital trade deal, alongside other agreements. Also at the Friday summit were European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

The term “associate member” has no legal basis and is contested by some EU states. However, its use underscores the desire of Canada and the EU to forge closer relations, as United States President Donald Trump continues to threaten Washington’s traditional allies with trade tariffs if they do not play by his rules.

“Canada and the EU are working to establish the closest possible partnership, which will be far from full membership, but which will make Canada the first associate member of the European Union,” Carney posted on X.

“Today in Montreal, we have taken a major step forward by establishing more than twenty measures that will increase affordability, create opportunities and ensure our sovereignty on both sides of the Atlantic.”

In a joint statement following the summit, the two sides announced an agreement under which the European Investment Bank will invest in critical Canadian resources, particularly raw minerals. They also said they would advance cooperation on artificial intelligence security and safety.

“A more dangerous and divided world has fundamentally changed the requirements of sovereignty. It is no longer enough for nations to feed, fuel and defend ourselves,” the statement said.



It added that “true sovereignty” requires secure access to critical minerals, semiconductors, payment systems, energy, vaccines, space-based communications and AI.

Ukraine was also on the meeting agenda, with Carney announcing Canada’s participation in the EU’s 90 billion euro ($103bn) support loan for Kyiv. Carney said Canada would make an initial contribution of 500 million euros ($558m).

Opportunities for students in Canada and the EU were also discussed. Both sides said they would launch negotiations aimed at deepening Ottawa’s participation in Erasmus+, the EU’s flagship student exchange programme.

Carney and Trump are currently engaged in a trade dispute, with talks under way to reach a deal between the two countries.

World.title: How 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli is making F1 history
World.content:
NewsFeed How 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli is making F1 history

Kimi Antonelli had an F1 licence before he could legally drive on the road. Now 20, the Mercedes driver is on the brink of becoming Formula One’s youngest-ever world champion. Al Jazeera’s Basel Ghazoghli traces his rise.

World.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
World.content:
The US has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks, after Kyiv said deliveries had been delayed in recent months.

The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (Â£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly urged the US to speed up deliveries of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.

The latest move comes just days after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump, with the US president saying it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to try to end the war with Russia.

In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".

It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".

The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".

Zelensky said earlier this week that his country had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies.

And in a Telegram post late on Friday, the Ukrainian president reported that earlier in the day Russian ballistic missiles had struck two of the country's regions.

"They continue to carry out terrorist strikes against our cities," he said.

Zelensky has recently admitted that Ukraine was running critically low on Patriots, as Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.

It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.

Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.

In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.

World.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
World.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.

The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.

Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (Â£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.

The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.

While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.

The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle â cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.

Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".

It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".

World.title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
World.content:
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".

Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he responded.

Speaking about the state's response to what happened to Pike, Mann said: "I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out."

She added: "What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her."

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.

It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.

Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess".

She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology.

"All I wanted was justice," Martinez said.

Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.

Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.

The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.

In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.

World.title: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
World.content:
Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".

A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Friday morning.

"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."

Ukrainian military positions lie 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.

They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.

Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.

World.title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
World.content:
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.

In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.

"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.

In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."

President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, ordered his plane be turned back to Warsaw on his way to Senegal to attend the Summer Youth Olympic Games.

The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.

Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.

The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.

Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.

Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.

One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.

World.title: They strangled us, says founder of Russian newspaper shut under pressure from authorities
World.content:
At the editorial offices of Novaya Gazeta, they are packing up and shutting down.

Everywhere I look there are cardboard boxes and plastic bags. Everything must go.

For thirty years this has been Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, featuring investigative journalism fiercely critical of those in power.

Now Novaya Gazeta is being evicted from its home of three decades. The paper also says it's been blocked from receiving donations.

It's accusing the Russian authorities of killing it off.

"There are different ways to commit murder," journalist and co-founder of the paper Dmitry Muratov tells me. "They chose to strangle us."

"First, they blocked our websites and banned the paper edition. Then they revoked our media licence. One by one we were declared 'foreign agents', and our journalists were attacked.

"Now we can't earn any more money. The banks are refusing to accept donations from our readers. In our country there are political repressions going on. Those have reached us."

In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".

The award didn't stop the Russian authorities from designating him a 'foreign agent' in 2023. The label is often used to punish critics of the government.

Over the years Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.

The paper says that six colleagues were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty". Those journalists include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block twenty years ago this month. She had written extensively on the wars in Chechnya.

As I walk down a corridor, I spot the office Anna had used. Following her killing, the room and all the items in it were preserved and became a museum in her memory. Since the eviction order, most of the objects have already been removed. All that's left is the desk and, lying on top, a portrait of Anna.

World.title: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
World.content:
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.

Ãscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.

"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.

The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.

Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.

A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV becomes first pontiff to vote in a US election
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has submitted his mail-in ballot in Illinois, for the midterm elections, becoming the first-ever pope to vote in a US election.

"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement.

The Chicago-born pontiff is the first US citizen to hold the Vatican's highest seat, after his selection in May 2025.

Since then, he has clashed with the Trump administration over various issues, including immigration enforcement and the US-Israel war with Iran.

"Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the press office said, including during his years in Peru.

The US midterm elections will determine which political party controls Congress and have a significant impact on the final years of Donald Trump's presidency.

Elections will be held nationwide on 3 November, but early voting has begun in most states.

According to NBC News, the Pope requested his mail-in ballot from the Will County Clerk's Office on 3 October.

Less than two weeks later, the Vatican announced he had surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung after he was diagnosed with lung cancer.

The Vatican confirmed last week that the Pope, aged 71, will travel as planned to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru in early November.

Tensions escalated between the Pope and the US president in April, after the Pope called for peace in the wake of US-Israeli strikes on Iran.

"I don't think he's doing a very good job," Trump said about the Pope afterwards.

"We don't like a Pope that's going to say that it's OK to have a nuclear weapon," he continued. "I'm not a big fan of Pope Leo."

Pope Leo followed with his own remarks later, saying: "The mission of the Church is to preach the Gospel, to preach peace," according to Reuters.

"If someone wants to criticise me for preaching the Gospel... I hope simply to be listened to because of the value of God's words."

World.title: Abiodun’s Road Revolution: From forgotten communities to connected economic corridors, By Kayode Akinmade
World.content:
Infrastructure development is one of the most visible measures of governance because its impact is felt in the everyday lives of citizens. A good road connects communities, shortens travel time, facilitates commerce, improves access to healthcare and education, enhances security and creates opportunities for economic growth. Beyond the convenience of transportation, roads are critical instruments of social integration and economic transformation.

For Ogun State, whose strategic location places it at the intersection of major commercial and industrial activities in Nigeria, road infrastructure is particularly important. Sharing boundaries with Lagos, the country’s commercial nerve centre, and serving as a major gateway to the Southwest and other parts of the country, Ogun requires an extensive and efficient road network to sustain its expanding population, growing industrial base and increasing commercial activities.

It was against this background that Governor Dapo Abiodun placed infrastructure development at the centre of his administration’s development agenda upon assuming office in May 2019.

The task before the administration was enormous. Years of inadequate maintenance, increasing population pressure, rapid urbanisation and the expansion of commercial activities had left several roads across the state in deplorable conditions. Many communities, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, had endured prolonged difficulties accessing neighbouring towns, markets, schools, healthcare facilities and other essential services.

For some communities, travelling a few kilometres could become an exhausting experience, especially during the rainy season. Farmers struggled to move their produce to markets, traders incurred additional transportation costs, while residents of emerging urban settlements faced the daily frustration of deteriorating roads.

The Abiodun administration therefore adopted a statewide approach to road development, recognising that infrastructure should not be concentrated in a few urban centres but distributed across the state’s 20 local government areas.

More than seven years into the administration, the scale of the intervention is reflected in the approximately 1,700 kilometres of roads constructed or rehabilitated across the state since 2019. The government has set a target of delivering 2,000 kilometres before the end of its tenure.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The figures represent an extensive infrastructure programme involving the construction of new roads, reconstruction of failed roads, rehabilitation of existing routes and the provision of supporting infrastructure.

But beyond the kilometres, the more important story is what these interventions mean for communities and the state’s economy.

CONNECTING COMMUNITIES, OPENING UP OPPORTUNITIES

One of the defining features of the administration’s road programme is its attention to communities that have historically struggled with poor road access.

In Ogun West, the reconstruction of the Ilaro–Owode Road has strengthened connectivity across the Yewa axis, while the completion of the Odo-Afa and Afon bridges along the Imeko-Afon corridor has addressed critical transportation challenges in rural communities.

Other interventions, including the General Hospital–Aferiku Road and Oke Erinja–Erinja Road Phase 2, have improved access to communities in Yewa South.

These projects demonstrate the importance of infrastructure beyond major urban centres. For farming communities, an accessible road can determine how quickly agricultural produce reaches markets, how much farmers spend on transportation and how much value they ultimately derive from their investments.

In a state with considerable agricultural potential, connecting farming communities to markets is central to food security, rural development and poverty reduction.

The same development philosophy is evident in other parts of the state.

In Obafemi-Owode Local Government, the Mowe–Ofada and Siun–Owode roads have improved access within rapidly developing communities. The Siun–Owode–Ofada corridor is particularly significant because of its connection to economic activities and settlements along the Lagos–Ibadan Expressway.

In Ifo Local Government, the rehabilitation of roads such as Akute–Gbero–Isase, Alhaji Kosoko, Ajuwon–Akute and other adjoining routes has addressed long-standing transportation difficulties in communities experiencing increasing population growth and urban expansion.

For residents of these communities, road infrastructure is not an abstract government achievement. It is about spending less time in traffic, reducing vehicle maintenance costs, improving access to workplaces and making daily commercial activities less stressful.

REBUILDING THE INDUSTRIAL CORRIDORS

Perhaps nowhere is the economic significance of road infrastructure more evident than in Ogun’s industrial belt.

Ogun is home to several manufacturing clusters, industrial estates and commercial centres, many of which depend on efficient road networks for the movement of raw materials, finished products, workers and other logistics.

The reconstruction of the Ota–Abeokuta Road, a major 70-kilometre corridor, is one of the significant interventions in this regard. The road serves communities and commercial establishments across the Ado-Odo/Ota and Abeokuta axes.

Similarly, road projects around Lusada, Alapoti, Igbesa and other industrial communities are important to the continued expansion of manufacturing activities in Ogun West.

The Lusada–Alapoti Road and other adjoining routes are particularly relevant to industrial development in the Agbara–Ota axis, where manufacturing companies depend on reliable transportation infrastructure.

The administration’s road programme also complements its broader efforts to attract investments and position Ogun as a preferred destination for industrial and commercial enterprises.

The relationship between roads and investment is straightforward. Investors require access to industrial locations, efficient movement of goods, dependable logistics and connectivity to major markets. Without these, the cost of doing business increases and the attractiveness of an investment destination diminishes.

This explains why road infrastructure remains an essential component of the administration’s economic development strategy.

The emerging industrial developments around the Gateway International Airport, the proposed Gateway Deep Sea Port and the Blue Marine Economic Zone further underscore the importance of expanding and improving road connectivity across the state.

These projects require an integrated transportation network capable of supporting industrial production, maritime activities, warehousing, distribution and international trade.

URBAN RENEWAL AND THE GROWING POPULATION

Ogun’s proximity to Lagos has created enormous demographic and economic opportunities, but it has also placed considerable pressure on existing infrastructure.

Communities such as Mowe, Ibafo, Magboro, Arepo, Akute, Ajuwon, Alagbole, Ijoko and Ota have experienced rapid population growth as more people seek residential accommodation outside Lagos.

This expansion has increased demand for roads, drainage, public transportation and other essential infrastructure.

The administration’s interventions in these areas are therefore significant to the management of urban growth.

The reconstruction of Magboro Road, Alagbole–Ajuwon Road, Akute–Ajuwon Road and other connecting routes reflects the government’s response to the transportation challenges associated with expanding settlements.

These projects are expected to improve connectivity within the communities and strengthen their links with Lagos and other parts of Ogun State.

In Abeokuta, the state capital, several road projects have also been undertaken to improve mobility and enhance the urban environment.

Similar interventions across Sagamu, Ijebu-Ode, Ikenne and other major towns form part of the wider effort to improve road infrastructure throughout the state.

FROM ROAD CONSTRUCTION TO ECONOMIC TRANSFORMATION

The significance of the road revolution should ultimately be measured by its contribution to economic and social development.

A road connecting a rural community to a major market is an economic asset. A road providing access to a hospital can make a difference in emergency situations. A road linking an industrial estate to a major highway can improve productivity and reduce logistics costs.

These are the practical outcomes that give meaning to infrastructure investment.

The Abiodun administration has consistently argued that its infrastructure policy is designed to democratise development by ensuring that communities across the three senatorial districts benefit from government interventions.

With approximately 1,700 kilometres of roads constructed or rehabilitated since 2019, the administration continues to pursue its 2,000-kilometre target.

The government has also incorporated inherited road projects into its programme, demonstrating that infrastructure development requires continuity and sustained investment beyond political and administrative transitions.

Nevertheless, the scale of the remaining infrastructure needs must not be overlooked. Several communities continue to demand improved roads, while increasing traffic, population growth and heavy-duty industrial vehicles place additional pressure on existing infrastructure.

The challenge, therefore, is to sustain the pace of construction, ensure quality delivery, maintain completed roads and prioritise projects according to their economic and social importance.

Road construction must also be accompanied by adequate drainage systems, proper engineering standards and effective maintenance arrangements to ensure that public investments deliver lasting value.

THE ROAD AHEAD

As Ogun State moves towards the final phase of the Abiodun administration, the ambition of delivering at least 2,000 kilometres of roads provides a measurable benchmark for assessing the government’s infrastructure programme.

But the broader significance of the initiative extends beyond the numbers.

From the rural communities of Yewa to the industrial clusters of Agbara and Ota, from the expanding settlements along the Lagos–Ibadan Expressway to the commercial centres of Ijebu-Ode and Sagamu, road infrastructure is an important part of the state’s evolving development story.

The objective is to create a connected Ogun where communities are not isolated by poor roads, farmers can move their produce more efficiently, businesses can operate with reduced logistical constraints and residents can enjoy improved access to opportunities.

The journey is far from complete. The demands of a rapidly expanding state will continue to require investment, planning and sustained attention to infrastructure.

Yet the approximately 1,700 kilometres of roads already constructed or rehabilitated provide a substantial basis for examining the administration’s road development record.

Ultimately, the true measure of a road revolution is not simply the number of kilometres delivered. It is the number of communities connected, the economic activities stimulated, the transportation difficulties reduced and the opportunities created for the people.

That is the larger development story behind Abiodun’s road infrastructure programme: moving Ogun from isolated communities towards an increasingly connected network of economic corridors.

World.title: Zamfara is evidence of transformational leadership under Gov Lawal, says EFCC Chairman
World.content:
The Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Mr Olanipekun Olukoyede, affirmed the presence of transformational leadership in Zamfara State under Governor Dauda Lawal.

The EFCC Chairman delivered the keynote address at the 30th anniversary of Zamfara State, held at the Grand Chamber of the Government House in Gusau.

Other notable speakers at the anniversary lecture are Professor Tijjani Muhammad Bande, Professor Sulaiman Kura, Professor Murtala Rufai, Professor Taofik Aminu, among others.

Mr Olukoyede stated that he conducted due diligence on Zamfara State and its governor before accepting the invitation to serve as a keynote speaker.

He said, “By virtue of the ethical demands of my office, I don’t attend political events; I don’t go to the government house as a matter of principle. But when I received this invitation, something told me to accept and see what was going on there.

“I did a little due diligence on His Excellency and the state. I saw when the state was created and noticed the drastic change over the past 3 years. And I made up my mind. I went to meet my boss, Mr President, and he said, go. I told him what I have seen about Zamfara and the need to support the work His Excellency, Dauda Lawal, is doing in this state.

“I am deeply honoured to be with you this morning. My acceptance to be with you today stems from two distinct realities: first, my professional engagements rarely bring me to this vibrant part of the nation because my office is based in Abuja. This is my first time in Zamfara State.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“As I arrived in Gusau, the first thing I noticed was the new airport. It is noticeable even to first-time visitors. The capital city speaks of visible transformation, as we have seen. Newly paved roads align with street solar lights.

“Zamfara unfortunately ranked near the bottom, not for lack of natural allure, but because the perception of rigid social tendencies overshadowed its immense natural potential.

“Even after becoming a state capital in 1996, transformation was gradual. For years, despite the efforts of previous governors, Zamfara remained among the country’s less-developed states.

“However, today, the contemporary outlook is shifting; indeed, the physical evolution of Gusau serves as a powerful metaphor for the broader Zamfara State.

“I am incredibly encouraged to learn that Zamfara has steadily improved its performance in critical national examinations like NECO and WAEC. Public infrastructure is expanding, positively impacting people’s daily lives. These strides are rightfully attributed to the consolidation of the deliberate reform initiatives and align perfectly with the theme of today’s celebration titled ‘accountability and responsibility in transformational government’.

“Despite the ethical standards of the office I occupied, it will take a serious-minded, committed democrat, a transparent governor, to have the temerity and audacity to bring the Chairman of the EFCC to address the people of the state.”

In his remarks, Governor Lawal emphasised that the anniversary theme, “Reflections, Achievements, and the Future,” is meant to examine the challenges that have shaped the state’s experience and to consider what leaders must do to secure a better future.

He said, “I’m pleased this commemoration has fostered serious intellectual engagement beyond ceremony. Today’s papers address key government responsibilities: public accountability, community involvement in tackling insecurity, preserving our history and culture, and linking security with socio-economic development.

“These discussions guide this administration. Our Six-Point Rescue Agenda addresses the State’s challenges. At the same time, the Zamfara State Development Plan 2025–2034 provides a long-term roadmap for the economy, infrastructure, social welfare, human capital, governance and environmental sustainability. We must turn these commitments into measurable improvements in people’s lives.

“I sincerely appreciate all the presenters for the knowledge and experience they have brought to this occasion. I also thank the Chairman of the Occasion, the discussants, the organising committee and the Sub-Committee on Lecture and Publications for their contributions to this event. To all our guests and participants, I am grateful for your presence and participation.”

World.title: Super Eagles defender Ogbu highlights importance of financial planning for footballers
World.content:
Super Eagles defender Igoh Ogbu has reiterated the need for Nigerian footballers to develop the habit of saving and investing early in their careers, warning that high earnings can leave players financially vulnerable if they fail to prepare for life after football.

The Slavia Prague centre-back said young players should not wait until they secure lucrative contracts or join big European clubs before learning how to manage their money.

In an interview with the American sports website RG.org, where he discussed various issues, Ogbu said he was concerned that some footballers get carried away by their earnings and neglect to prepare for retirement.

“A lot of footballers earn a lot of money and that makes them forget that they have to prepare for the rainy days,” he said.

The 26-year-old advised players to make saving and investing a priority from the beginning of their professional careers, regardless of how much they earn.

“You need to understand that the moment you come to Europe, the first thing you need to learn is to start saving and learn about investing. You have to invest,” he said.

Ogbu also challenged the mindset among young players that financial planning should begin only when they start earning substantial salaries.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“When I talk about investment, people say, ‘Oh, I haven’t been in a big club,’ but I want you to learn something when you have little, not when you have much. Because when you have much without having learned when you had little, you won’t be able to do much when you have much.”

He warned that expecting regular paydays could encourage players to spend without considering the uncertainty of their careers.

“Nowadays, young players always think the next payday is too close — after a few trainings, I’m going to get another one,” he said.

“This mentality is somehow bad. So when we get older, when we are playing, and it is time for us to leave the stage, we force our bodies to keep going because we are not ready to accept reality and tell ourselves, ‘Now it is time to let go.’ But a good farmer always saves seeds for the next season.”

Financial security after football

Ogbu’s warning reflects wider concerns about professional footballers’ preparedness for life after retirement.

A 2021 survey published by the global players’ union, FIFPRO, found that 67 per cent of 282 active and retired footballers surveyed across 33 countries were unsure about their career paths after football. The survey also found that 54 per cent had received no assistance with planning for a second career.

Research has also highlighted concerns about financial literacy among professional footballers in Africa.

A 2023 study involving 300 professional footballers in Ghana’s Premier League found low levels of financial literacy and poor financial behaviour among respondents. The researchers identified savings and investment habits as important factors in achieving financial well-being.

Case study

Former Super Eagles defender Ben Iroha offers a practical example of how such preparation can shape life after football. In an interview with PREMIUM TIMES, Iroha said he began planning for retirement while he was still an active player.

After Nigeria made its World Cup debut in the United States in 1994, Iroha identified Dallas, Texas, as the city where he wanted to settle. He was impressed by the Nigerian community there and the support the Super Eagles received during their opening match against Bulgaria.

He bought a house before retiring and eventually moved to Dallas with his family, where he established a spare parts and car business. According to Iroha, the move and the business were part of a plan he had discussed with his wife long before he left professional football.

His experience has informed his advice to current players. While acknowledging that modern footballers have better access to managers and financial advisers, Iroha warned that their income and lifestyle could change significantly after retirement.

“The money’s gonna go,” he said, urging players to control their spending and invest in property and other businesses.

He also warned that letting spending rise alongside earnings could leave even top-level players bankrupt.

Ogbu, who joined Slavia Prague in January 2023 after spells with Norwegian clubs Levanger, Rosenborg, Sogndal and Lillestrøm, has made 87 appearances for the Czech club across all competitions.

World.title: NIPRD records gains in research, staff welfare, public health
World.content:
The National Institute for Pharmaceutical Research and Development (NIPRD) says it has recorded progress in research, staff welfare, infrastructure and public health interventions under the leadership of its Acting Director-General, Philip Builders.

The institute highlighted the reforms in a statement issued on Friday, citing improvements in staff welfare, restoration of basic infrastructure, efforts to strengthen research funding and intellectual property management, and its recent response to the Ebola outbreak.

“His administration is committed to strengthening the Institute’s capacity to fulfil its mandate and contribute to Nigeria’s pharmaceutical development, scientific innovation, and improved healthcare outcomes,” it noted.

One of the administration’s interventions has been the constitution of an Ebola Response Team, headed by Peters Oladisu, Director of the Department of Microbiology and Biotechnology.

NIPRD said it also supplied 17 cartons of hand sanitiser gel and 2,000 educational posters on Ebola symptoms and preventive measures to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare.

The institute said the intervention is part of its contribution to public awareness and prevention of emerging health threats.

Staff welfare

NIPRD also cited improvements in staff welfare as part of the changes under Mr Builders.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The institute said it conducted its 2025 staff promotion exercise and addressed outstanding staff claims.

It also said salary arrears owed to security personnel, cleaners and gardeners had been settled.

Beyond staff-related measures, the institute said it restored electricity and water supply, which it described as critical to creating a more conducive environment for research and other activities.

Research and innovation

NIPRD said it was also strengthening its research and innovation ecosystem by restructuring its Intellectual Property and Technology Transfer Office and Grant Office.

It has established an Office for Strategic Partnerships and Commercialisation, headed by Adeola Jegede, a scientist with experience in policy, monitoring and evaluation.

The office is expected to facilitate partnerships, attract research opportunities and support the commercialisation of products developed from research carried out by the institute.

An example of the institute’s research efforts is the success of its scientist, Isaac Ajeh, who won a NASENI Innovation Grant for research into converting plantain peels into pharmaceutical products.

The project seeks to explore how agricultural waste can be transformed into useful pharmaceutical products, highlighting the potential intersection between local research, healthcare and sustainable innovation.

NIPRD said it was also expanding its digital capacity through upgrades to its NCC Centre, computer-based testing facilities and other information and communication technology infrastructure.

According to the institute, the facilities will support computer-based examinations, digital research and technology-driven learning, while providing access to ICT facilities for schools in surrounding communities.

The administration has also supported researchers to participate in national and international training programmes, which the institute said would expose them to global best practices and strengthen scientific collaboration.

“Under Professor Builders’ leadership, NIPRD continues to pursue initiatives aimed at strengthening local pharmaceutical production, translating research into practical solutions, and improving Nigeria’s healthcare capacity,” it noted.

World.title: FG begins N50,000 monthly cash payment to vulnerable Nigerians – Official
World.content:
The federal government has commenced a monthly cash relief programme, offering N50,000 to vulnerable households to cushion the effects of rising living costs.

The Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Bernard Doro, announced this in a statement issued on Friday in Abuja.

Mr Doro said the National Emergency Relief and Stabilisation Intervention (NERSI) is a presidential initiative aimed at providing immediate financial support to millions of vulnerable Nigerians.

He explained that the intervention was introduced in response to global food inflation and the rising cost of essential goods, which had continued to put pressure on household incomes.

“Under this intervention, eligible beneficiaries will receive N50,000 monthly, providing direct assistance to help meet essential needs and ease the burden of living costs,” he said.

The minister said the programme would be reviewed periodically to reflect changes in the cost of living, adding that beneficiaries would be notified directly before any adjustments were made.

According to him, the ministry is collaborating with licensed digital financial service providers to ensure secure, timely and transparent disbursement of the funds.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He explained that beneficiaries would receive text messages from the service providers seeking their consent before payments were made directly into their bank accounts or mobile wallets.

Mr Doro emphasised that beneficiaries were not required to submit applications, pay fees or register through agents to access the intervention.

He also warned Nigerians against fraudsters, urging them not to disclose their Personal Identification Numbers (PINs) or Bank Verification Numbers (BVNs) to anyone.

“If you are unsure about any message, or anyone asks you for money, call the official NERSI helpline on 0700-022-2222,” he said.

The minister described NERSI as complementary to existing federal government social protection and economic support programmes, noting that it was designed to strengthen household resilience and promote economic stability.

He added that the intervention aligned with President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda and reaffirmed the ministry’s commitment to implementing the programme with dignity, transparency and accountability.

(NAN)

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: Inside NSCDC’s Niger cell where 14 children, 19 other detainees died
World.content:
About 50 men and boys were confined in a cell measuring roughly 12 square metres at the Niger State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Minna, Niger State. Thirty-three of the detainees died in custody between 16 and 17 September 2026, a federal investigation has found.

PREMIUM TIMES reported earlier on Friday that the committee found that 14 of the 33 deceased persons were minors. They also included persons displaced from their communities by bandits.

The cell had a solid metal door, poor ventilation, no running water and no functioning toilet. Food and drinking water were either unavailable or grossly inadequate, according to the investigation committee.

The Jonathan Kure-led 10-member committee’s final report, obtained by PREMIUM TIMES, described the detention conditions as cruel, inhuman and degrading, and concluded that the deaths were foreseeable and preventable.

The report was submitted to the Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, on 27 October.

Inside the cell

Investigators inspected the detention facility in Chanchaga, Minna, on 25 September, taking measurements, photographs and video recordings and preparing a floor plan.

The committee estimated that about 50 detainees occupied the male cell, roughly five times the maximum occupancy of 10 it considered appropriate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Survivors described extreme heat and dehydration. They could barely move in the crowded cell, and some collapsed as conditions worsened, according to the report.

The cell also had poor lighting. Children were held alongside adults, which the committee found breached child-protection requirements.

Female detainees were temporarily moved elsewhere because of overcrowding but were subsequently returned.

The committee also found that detainees in the male cell drank their own urine or sweat because they had no access to drinking water.

The probe panel also said it found that officers responsible for the cells failed to reduce the overcrowding, “ignored prolonged cries and banging of the cell door and wall and did not provide emergency help.”

Mining raids and unlawful detention

The detentions followed NSCDC raids on suspected illegal mining sites in and around Minna on 15 and 16 September, after complaints from residents around the M.I. Wushishi area.

The panel confirmed that the mining sites were licensed to Ozams Consult and Services Ltd and Prixair Resources Ltd.

However, the operations proceeded without an approved operational order, adequate planning or consultation with the relevant mining authorities. The specialised Mining Marshals Unit was not involved, and NSCDC National Headquarters had not been informed beforehand.

Men, women and children were arrested. By the evening of 16 September, 75 people had been detained. One was released, leaving 74 in custody overnight, about 50 of them in the male cell.

The committee confirmed 33 deaths and identified 41 survivors. Fourteen of those who died were children.

Some detainees were internally displaced persons who had turned to artisanal mining to survive, the report found.

One victim, Emmanuel Emeka, 25, had been held since 12 September over a private debt complaint unrelated to mining. The panel found his detention unlawful.

Other detainees had been held beyond the permitted period without a court order or remand warrant.

The command’s legal officer had raised concerns about the detention of children and advised that the suspected mining offence was bailable. His advice was ignored, according to the report.

The committee found that the duration and conditions of detention breached constitutional safeguards, the Administration of Criminal Justice Act and child-protection requirements.

Warnings of suffocation

On the evening of 16 September, Mariam Etang Nelson, a nurse attached to the command, warned cell guards that overcrowding could cause suffocation. She advised leaving the metal door unlocked to improve ventilation.

The warning was ignored, the committee found.

Evidence from survivors and officers indicated that signs of distress began shortly after 7 p.m. Detainees shouted for help, banged on the door and walls, and pleaded for water.

A female detainee, Alheri Dauda, recalled hearing cries and banging from the men’s cell from about 8 p.m.

Two armoury guards told investigators that between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m. they urged the officer on duty to open the cell after hearing screaming and banging. He refused, citing instructions not to open it without armed backup. A telephone call to his superior went unanswered.

The guards said the screaming stopped at about 2.30 a.m. Ms Dauda placed the end of the disturbance at approximately 2 a.m.

Neither account established the precise time of death.

The cell was opened the following morning. The committee found that officers had failed to reduce overcrowding or arrange an adequate emergency response.

Medical findings and their limits

Investigators interviewed 29 survivors, including nine children. Six survivors received treatment at General Hospital Minna and were subsequently discharged. Hospital records confirmed that 33 bodies were brought in dead.

Post-mortem examinations were conducted on only three bodies. The remaining 30 had been buried before the medical team arrived.

The medical findings were most consistent with respiratory failure caused by a lack of oxygen in the overcrowded cell, described in the report as environmental asphyxia. Heat stress and dehydration were identified as probable contributing factors.

The report states that the individual causes of death of the 30 unexamined victims could not be determined medically. Their shared detention conditions and the timing of the deaths suggested the same mechanism as in the three examined cases.

The medical conclusions remained provisional pending toxicology results.

The panel found no evidence supporting a disease outbreak as the cause of the deaths.

Some survivors alleged that an aerosol substance had been sprayed into the cell, but the committee considered the allegation unproven and improbable on the available evidence.

The medical section separately recorded eye and throat irritation. Toxicology results were outstanding when the report was submitted.

Eight survivors reported being beaten during arrest. The committee distinguished those allegations from its medical assessment, which did not identify physical assault as the immediate cause of death.

Alterations before inspection

Before independent forensic inspection, the detention cells had been scrubbed, washed and disinfected.

Additional ventilation openings had been introduced, other alterations made and numbers painted above the cell doors.

Investigators documented the changes by comparing the facility with earlier images taken by first responders. The panel found that the cleaning and alterations interfered with physical evidence and limited aspects of the forensic assessment.

The detention register for 16 September, when most of the suspects were taken into custody, was also unavailable to investigators.

The missing register and changes to the cells meant investigators could neither examine the detention area in its original condition nor consult a complete detention record for the day preceding the discovery of the deaths.

Nevertheless, the committee concluded that the overcrowding, inadequate ventilation and failure to respond to repeated warnings had made the deaths preventable.

World.title: Hamzat unveils 100-point manifesto, pledges child protection agency, state wealth fund
World.content:
The Lagos State All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate, Obafemi Hamzat, has unveiled a 100-point manifesto, promising to establish a child protection and nutrition agency, create a state wealth fund and introduce a public service delivery office within his first 100 days in office if elected governor.

Mr Hamzat announced the proposals on Friday at the launch of his manifesto and campaign theme, Lagos, Forward Together, organised by the Lagos State APC PBAT-KOH Campaign Council 2027 at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, Iganmu, Lagos.

The manifesto, which he described as ‘The Lagos Promise’ and called the Hamzat Compact, contains seven pillars covering people, infrastructure, economic opportunities, government operations, inclusion, security and citizenship.

Mr Hamzat said 87 of the 100 pledges were firm commitments within the powers of the state government, while the remaining 13 were aspirations dependent on consultations with the federal government and other institutions, including the courts.

He promised to publish a scorecard against which residents could assess his administration’s performance.

“If one of them is not delivered, it will be noted, and I must own it,” he said.

For his first 100 days in office, Mr Hamzat said he would send a bill to the Lagos State House of Assembly to establish a Child Protection and Nutrition Agency. The proposed agency, he said, would ensure that every child below 18 was either in school or learning a trade and had adequate food.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He also promised to establish a Lagos State Service Delivery Office through an executive order. The office, to be chaired by the governor, would publish baseline figures for assessing the administration’s commitments.

The third proposal is a state wealth fund, which, he said, would have an independent board and publish its accounts to preserve resources for future generations.

Mr Hamzat said his administration would introduce service charters in government offices, setting out the services residents should expect and the standards to be met. He promised that complaints would be acknowledged within 48 hours, answered within seven days and resolved within 30 days.

“Accountability will not wait for the end of my term. It begins in my first 100 days. My manifesto is a promise to Lagosians. The promise, as we all know, has seven letters, seven pillars, and 100 pledges. Inside there are 100 pledges. So as we know, P stands for People First. R stands for Renewal. O stands for Opportunity. M stands for Machinery of Government. I for inclusion. S for security and resilience. And E for every citizen. So seven letters, seven pillars, one word,” he said.

Healthcare, education and jobs

On healthcare, Mr Hamzat promised to increase the number of maternal and child centres from six to 15, complete ongoing hospital projects and build two new general hospitals in Ogombo and Ibeju-Lekki.

He also pledged to upgrade 100 primary healthcare centres to flagship status and recruit more doctors, nurses and midwives.

Among the projects he cited were the new Massey Children’s Hospital, which he said would have 150 beds, and another general hospital project with 280 beds. He also mentioned the Shomolu General Hospital project, expected to provide 150 beds.

“Our promise is that we will deliver two new general hospitals at Ogombo and Ibeju Lekki, expand the capacity of existing general hospitals, and upgrade 100 primary healthcare centres to flagship status. We will strengthen the health workforce. We will hire more doctors, more nurses and more midwives,” he said.

In education, the candidate promised to strengthen the EkoEXCEL programme in public primary schools, improve teaching and learning outcomes and expand opportunities for technical and vocational training.

He said his administration would pursue plans for a University of Medicine and Health Sciences in Lagos and ensure that children remained in school. Mr Hamzat also promised to review teachers’ compensation packages.

“We will review your compensation package, so that your pay matches the work we demand from you,” he said.

On employment, he argued that businesses would create most of the jobs needed in Lagos and that government should focus on removing obstacles to their growth.

He proposed a single schedule of local government charges, easier business permits, improved access to credit and a defined share of state procurement for qualifying small businesses.

He also promised to introduce a vocational placement scheme under which students in technical schools would spend between six and 12 months with employers, with the state paying 40 per cent of their stipends.

For artisans, he proposed free skills certification at their workplaces and in languages they understand.

Mr Hamzat said the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund had provided more than N15 billion to over 21,000 businesses, while businesses supported through the scheme had created more than 300,000 jobs. These figures were presented as part of his account of the administration’s achievements.

Transport, housing and environment

On transportation, Mr Hamzat said his proposed administration would extend the Blue Line rail service to Okokomaiko and work with the federal government to advance the Green Line from Marina to the Lekki Free Trade Zone.

He also promised to connect the Blue and Red rail lines at the National Theatre station, expand ferry services and introduce integrated ticketing across road, rail and water transport.

“Lagos, we must know, is a water state. The lagoon must therefore be our third highway,” he said.

He pledged to dredge an additional 140-kilometre water corridor, optimise ferry routes and procure 75 riverine vessels.

On roads, he promised to prioritise inner roads in collaboration with local governments and local council development areas, while accelerating work on major road projects, including the coastal road along the Lekki-Epe axis.

The candidate also promised to complete ongoing housing projects and develop additional homes through partnerships with the private sector. He proposed mortgages requiring a 10 per cent deposit, single-digit interest rates and longer repayment periods.

On security, he said he would strengthen the Lagos State Neighbourhood Safety Agency and extend its presence to wards across the state’s 20 local government areas and 37 local council development areas. He also promised to expand street lighting and CCTV coverage.

For the environment, Mr Hamzat set a target of 95 per cent waste collection coverage through improved operations by private sector participants. He promised to complete waste transfer facilities, develop a waste recovery facility and complete a waste-to-energy project at Agbowa.

“On waste, we will strengthen community collections, reach 95% coverage by optimizing the PSP, that is the private sector participant deliveries, and make Lagos cleaner. We will complete the transfer loading stations at Olusosun and Solous III in Alimosho.

“We will deliver a recovery facility and complete the waste-to-energy facility at Agbowa. 30,000 Lagosians already collect and sort this state’s waste, and we will bring them into the system, and we train them, equip them, and pay them properly. Essential work deserves recognition,” he said.

The pledge comes amid persistent challenges with waste collection and disposal in Lagos, where gaps in the state’s waste management system have left some communities struggling with irregular collection and inadequate disposal services.

A Premium Times investigation found that waste collection services remain uneven across the state, with some households receiving regular services while others have limited or no access to formal collection. The investigation also highlighted the pressure on existing disposal infrastructure and the difficulties residents face in managing refuse.

Sanwo-Olu backs Hamzat, cites years of working relationship

Earlier, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu urged Lagos residents to support Mr Hamzat, describing him as an experienced public servant who had been involved in major decisions and projects during their seven years working together.

The governor recalled that Mr Hamzat had sought the governorship in 2018 but stepped aside after party leaders asked him to allow Governor Sanwo-Olu to emerge as the candidate.

He said Mr Hamzat accepted to serve as his running mate and had remained loyal throughout their time in office.

“In seven years, there has not been one day, not one, when I had to wonder whose side my deputy was on,” Governor Sanwo-Olu said.

He cited the COVID-19 response, the development of the Blue and Red rail lines and the arrival of the first ship at the Lekki Deep Sea Port among the major events in which Mr Hamzat had been involved.

The governor described the candidate as a key participant in the administration’s planning and project implementation, particularly in technical matters.

He framed Mr Hamzat’s candidacy as a continuation of the APC’s successive administrations in Lagos, from Bola Tinubu to Babatunde Fashola, Akinwunmi Ambode and himself.

“There has been one government. There has been one direction. There has been one voice. This is not the time to experiment with Lagos. This is the time to consolidate,” he said.

APC chairman, former deputy governor endorse candidate

The Lagos APC chairman, Cornelius Ojelabi, described the manifesto as a covenant between the party, its candidate and the electorate.

Mr Ojelabi said the APC administrations in Lagos had recorded achievements in infrastructure, transportation, education, healthcare, housing and economic development.

ALSO READ: Otedola recalls sharing bunk bed with Hamzat 49 years ago

He called for continuity but said it should not prevent the government from addressing shortcomings.

“Continuity must not mean complacency. It must mean building on proven achievements, correcting identified shortcomings, and pursuing greater progress with renewed determination,” he said.
