World.title: 'You can't just get out': How 2 boys were recruited into the drug trade at the age of 12
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kai was 12 years old when he began to warn his mother he might not make it home.

"[If] I don't make it home by four o'clock, just know that I got snatched and somebody put me in their car and kidnapped me," he would tell her.

His mother, whom CBC's the fifth estate is calling Aria for her protection, moved her family to another city when Kai was a boy to disconnect from his father, who had a criminal past and street associations.

She enrolled Kai, whose name has also been changed for his protection, in community centres and drop-in spaces in Winnipeg to keep him busy and away from trouble

But Aria believes those spaces exposed her son to people who would exploit him.�

Watch the full documentary, "Missing Boys: Lured into Danger," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

She believes some staff abused their positions, allowing gang members to manipulate her son and coerce him into the drug trade — sending him thousands of kilometres away from home.

Fifth estate host Mark Kelley, left, sits down with a boy who was recruited by a gang when he was 12. He says he has been sent out of town to sell drugs more times than he can count. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Kai said men in their 20s and 30s presented themselves as people he could trust.

"People call it grooming, people call it using. There's many words for it, but it's just being taken advantage of because you're innocent," Kai said.

For the last two years, the fifth estate has investigated the disappearances of young Black boys from the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) who are groomed and lured into drug trafficking networks in Ontario cities as far away as Sarnia and Thunder Bay, and sent further north into Indigenous communities like Ginoogaming, a First Nation.

Now, the fifth estate has heard directly from boys who live this dangerous life and say they were sent across the country to sell drugs, revealing a network that reaches even farther.

We now know of this activity taking boys as young as 12 as far west as British Columbia, as far north as Yellowknife and as far east as Halifax — places where drugs are sold at exponentially higher prices — up to 10 times the price in some cases.

The business of going OT

In an interview with CBC's the fifth estate, Kai recounts his first trip out of town, also known as “going OT,” when he was 12.

"You don't know what's in those bags. You don't know what you're delivering for people … you just think, 'I'm helping the older guy, because I want to be cool like him,'" he said.

Kai said the older men picked him up, told him where he would stay and expected him to sell drugs. He was left in a remote community eight hours north of his home in Winnipeg.

LISTEN: The Missing Boys: When It All Went Wrong

Kai said he did not fully understand what he was getting into. He had to figure it out in a place where he did not know anyone and his family was out of reach.

"You're not telling family members," he said. "Because not only do they not know where you are, you don't know where you are."

The first trip taught him more about what he calls the rules of "the game," where the three outcomes are freedom, jail or death.

And he says he was forced to gamble for the gangs.

"You can't just get out ... whoever sent you there is expecting you to come back with a prize," Kai said. "And if you don't come back with anything … God forbid something happens to you."

Now 14, Kai has made more trips out of town than he can count.

WATCH | Sent north by gangs: On the front line of the drug trade | Duration closed caption 0:49 Kai, not his real name, 14, says he has been sent by gangs to remote northern communities where drugs can sell for 10 times the price.

Jamal, another teenager whose name has been changed for his safety, started going OT at 12. He had been away from home for more than a week and his mom reported him missing.

The now-18-year-old who lives in the Toronto area said he has been sent to communities in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.

Jamal's farthest trip took him to Yellowknife. He was even convinced to pay his own way.

Like Kai, Jamal said it was in Grade 7 when he was first approached to work for a gang. His family had spent a year bouncing between houses and he grew close to older people in his neighbourhood who were often around his cousins.

"I always just had the respect and looked at them like an older role model," he said.

Jamal said those role models could offer him an escape from the instability at home.

"If things were stable at home, I wouldn't really have a reason to go outside," he said.

Jamal said the adults he worked for were selling drugs bought internationally — and worked with cartels.

Then Jamal tells the fifth estate how the boys cross the country — a key piece of information — as many families are baffled as to how their boys are boarding planes and driving to remote locations when they are too young to have a driver's licence and don't have identification.

Jamal said fake names and identification are provided for them.

"It doesn't even matter who you are, how young you are. You can go anywhere in Canada," he said. "It's actually quite easy."

The adults behind the operation

The fifth estate previously found adult traffickers use the boys as disposable mules and legal shields that often take the fall when police make drug busts.

A 2026 federal Justice Department report found that the proportion of Black youth in correctional supervision in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia remained at around 12 to 13 per cent from 2019 to 2024. That's almost two times more than their combined share of the population for that age group, across all four provinces.

Black boys often face well-known socio-economic challenges including high unemployment , and bias within justice and educational systems that can make them more vulnerable to the pull of organized crime.

"Many of these [youths] are exploited … they're seen as disposable to the people who are running these networks," said Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski.

Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski tells the fifth estate the drugs supplied by gangs have been linked to international cartels. Young boys are often used for street-level dealing so gang members don't have to expose themselves to violence or being arrested. (Oliver Walters/CBC)

In May, Ewatski led a team involved in what police called Manitoba's largest drug bust. Investigators seized 525 kilograms of cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl in Winnipeg.

Those arrested included people associated with Canada's highest ranks of organized crime including the Hells Angels, Wolfpack Alliance and a Mexican cartel.

"Most of the drugs of cocaine and methamphetamine will come from Mexico up to the U.S. and into Canada," Ewatski said.

He described a sophisticated network where multiple drug trafficking organizations are working together to move drugs into remote communities.

He says it's associates of these international criminal networks who are recruiting and using boys.

For more on the story, listen to "The Missing Boys," a four-episode series on the new CBC podcast When it All Went Wrong.

Ewatski said boys are used for street-level dealing and to work in stash houses. He said they often don't know who they are working for.

"These kids are used so [those running the networks] don't have to expose themselves to being arrested or being shot."

Leaving a gang can be just as dangerous. Ewatski said some boys become trapped by debts they are told they owe their recruiters.

“If they're out, they're going to be out in a violent way," he said. "Possibly even dead."

Denny Heathen, a reformed gang member, now counsels youth and leads prayer circles in his community of Prince Albert, Sask. (Shelley Ayres/CBC)

Denny Heathen spent much of his 20s working for a gang in Prince Albert, Sask. He said some recruiters targeted boys between 15 to 18 and told us that the boys who were targeted had a look of desperation.

"They wanted purpose," Heathen said.

Recruiters offered attention, money and the promise of protection, presenting themselves as brothers or older mentors.

"These are puppets," he said. "You just got to make them feel like they're appreciated, like they are going to be taken care of."

WATCH | A price for getting out: What it takes to get out of a gang | Duration closed caption 0:24 A former gang member tells boys in the drug trade that getting out will come with a price.

Kai remembers the grooming process well.

“You're a little kid in a community centre trying to play basketball and then you see these guys … walking around with the large prize in their hand."

The prize was money — an amount that felt impossible to a boy too young to get his first job.

During his interview with the fifth estate, Kai pulled out a thick stack of $100 bills to demonstrate how quickly money could influence a boy to sell drugs.

"All it takes is this and you're influenced."

He said the amounts involved can be enormous in First Nations communities where an oxycodone pill can sell for $200.

"That substance that is being put in these boys' pockets and these boys' hands to go deal over the province … people will do anything for."

The boy who never came home

On March 27, 2025, Jay'siiah Webb-Long walked out of his family's home in Brampton, Ont., carrying a single duffel bag that appeared nearly empty.

Doorbell camera footage provided by the family to the fifth estate shows the 15-year-old placing a single box in the recycling bin on his front porch, scanning the street before disappearing out of frame.

His story made national headlines.

Jay'siiah Webb-Long, 15, was last seen outside his home in Brampton, Ont. on March 27, 2025. (Saskatchewan RCMP)

"Somebody had sent me photos after his disappearance," said Shenice Long, his mother.

"She had sent photos of him holding stacks of money. So, at that point, I said, 'OK, somebody has sent him far out … to make money.'"

Long said she remained in contact with her son for weeks after he left home. But he would not tell her where he was.

Jay'siiah's family told the fifth estate they are frustrated with action from Peel Regional Police and the RCMP in Saskatchewan, citing for example that it took Peel police eight weeks to alert the public that Jay'siiah was missing.

Long said police used a phone number she never had for her son to trace his location to Pelican Narrows, Sask., a northern community about 3,000 kilometres from his home in Brampton. This number only surfaced when the public alert came out and a young woman came forward.

"I heard of Saskatchewan, but … I don't have family there. I don't know anyone there," Long said.

In July 2025, Saskatchewan RCMP took over the file as a homicide investigation. They didn't alert the public of this shift until September 2025.

Police told the family a search was delayed by winter weather. In the spring, investigators told the family they planned to search near Pelican Narrows — led with cadaver dogs.

Pelican Narrows, Sask., a community of about 4,000 and located about 500 kilometres north of Saskatoon, is part of the Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

On May 13, human remains were found near a sewage lagoon just outside the community. An autopsy confirmed two days later that the remains belonged to Webb-Long.

RCMP believe his death was a homicide. The investigation is ongoing and no charges have been laid in connection with his death.

Missing — and not always reported

In 2024, 322 male youth were reported missing to Toronto police. Statistics Canada data shows Black boys account for almost half of those missing, despite representing less than 10 per cent of the city's population of that age group.

The fifth estate has found not every family reports their youth missing. In the case of Jay'siiah Webb-Long, his mother didn't file a formal report until three weeks after he had left home. She told the fifth estate she had called Peel Regional Police after 48 hours but they dissuaded her because she was still in contact with him.

"One youth missing is too [many]," said Christene Lewis, who is a violence intervention specialist and works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas. She supports many families who have youth that go missing and go "OT." It's a life she knows because she lived it.

"I come from the gang culture," Lewis said. "I come from feeling isolated, I've come from feeling like the streets were more loyal to me than my own family was."

Christene Lewis, a violence intervention specialist, works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas who have youth who go missing. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Lewis said some parents hesitate reporting their child missing because they fear their kids will be treated as runaways rather than young people at risk. Others feel shame and embarrassment.

Lewis said there is also a breakdown of trust between marginalized communities and police.

"They don't feel like the police even care."

Lewis's advice to parents: Always report a missing kid and keep following up.

"If they didn't hear you the first day, call the next day," she said. "Don't give up."

WATCH | Parents urged to be vigilant: A message for parents of missing kids | Duration closed caption 0:30 A woman who works with the families of missing kids says they should stay vigilant and always report to police.

Aria remembers when it first became clear her son had gone to a First Nations community to sell drugs.

"He was telling stories like he came back from camp," she said.

He would leave home sporadically, returning home with designer clothing and money.

Aria said she has also had the windows of her home shot at three times.

Now, when Kai goes missing, she reports him and collects evidence that might help police locate him.

"This is not something you make peace with," she said. "This is something that's wrong."

'Nobody's just going to let you go'

Jamal said the people who recruited him continue to contact him and tell him he owes them money.

''They're going to keep texting you, telling you that they got this opportunity … nobody's just going to let you just go."

Kai has also tried to leave. He spent the summer away at camp and returned determined to get out of gang life.

"Now that I realize what kind of hell on earth is like … I never want to go back there," he told the fifth estate in August.

But Aria said the messages continued.

She found text messages about Kai from a sibling that read: "I will not be returning your little bro" and "he's my slave.”

She believes the messages are proof her son is being trafficked.

Aria, a Winnipeg mother whose name has been changed for protection, worries gangs will never loosen their grip on her son. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Kai left home again the night before he was set to start Grade 10. He returned home and left again several times.

Aria fears that even if Kai manages to break free from the gangs, they will continue to chase and manipulate him, tempting him with money and a sense of belonging.

Kai is facing drug trafficking charges.

"This monster exists and it's going to exist on his path as a young man, as an adult," Aria said. "I don't think that this monster ever goes away."

World.title: Alberta separatist Jeff Rath kicked out of governing United Conservative Party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Separatist leader Jeff Rath, who rose to prominence in the lead-up to the Alberta referendum in his white cowboy hat, has had his membership revoked by the governing United Conservative Party.

In an email sent to Rath on Thursday and viewed by CBC News, Dustin Van Vugt, the party's executive director, said that Rath's "words and actions have made clear" that he does not support the party or its objectives.

"Your public conduct in relation to our party and leader has not met the basic standard of decency we expect of our members when they disagree or otherwise."

His membership was revoked immediately, Van Vugt wrote.

After Albertans voted decisively to remain within Canada on Oct. 19, Premier Danielle Smith made it clear the UCP would be a federalist party going forward. But with pre-referendum polling suggesting that independence was popular among UCP members, there's been much speculation about how she would address the separatist faction within her base.

Ahead of next month's party AGM, any aspiring board members are now required to sign a declaration that they'll abide by the results of the referendum.

Rath is the first separatist leader to be asked to leave.

In a phone call, Rath said his ouster had less to do with his separatist beliefs than with how he's expressed his criticisms more broadly.

"I'm a very loud and effective critic of Danielle Smith," he said.

"She obviously does not want free speech in the party."

In an email, a party spokesperson said the decision was made because of Rath's "public conduct toward the party and its leader."

Rath said he also received an email from the UCP notifying him the party had refunded the $239 he paid in order to attend next month's AGM.

Rath and Smith have publicly sparred over their differing views on Alberta’s place in Confederation. Rath has dismissed the premier as an "avowed federalist" and mused about trying to push her out of the party leadership.

Smith, meanwhile, has maintained that she was always on team Canada and, after the referendum, warned anyone not on board that they would need to join a different party.

But their debates have occasionally veered into more personal territory.

Earlier this week, Rath accused Smith of colluding with federalist leader Thomas Lukaszuk in a personal text exchange he posted online. When pressed by NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi during question period Thursday, Smith appeared to try to distance herself from Rath by noting his past financial contributions to the Opposition party.

"He's actually an NDP supporter," she said.

Rath told CBC News he once attended a leadership event for then-NDP leader Rachel Notley, largely because, he said, she was once his classmate in an honours political science class.

Speaking to reporters Friday, Smith confirmed the party's executive director had pulled Rath's membership.

"He’s never supported me ... He never supported me during the leadership, he never supported me in my time in office, and he certainly doesn’t support me now," she said.

"That’s irrelevant," she added. "What is relevant is that he has said publicly things like he wants to come to the AGM to turn the UCP into an independence party. And we are not an independence party."

Rath says he will be consulting with legal counsel and will "likely" file an appeal of the decision.

Either way, he says his work trying to speak to members and have Smith replaced as party leader isn't over.

World.title: Carney says, unequivocally, Canada seeking to become the EU's 1st associate member
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is working to become the European Union's first associate member, his most definitive statement on the issue to date after hosting the bloc's leaders in Montreal this week.

It still remains unclear what that would look like and cost.

This year's Canada-EU summit saw Canada and European officials finalize a number of negotiations and launch a long list of new commitments as part of a deeper alliance, but the issue of what to call the allies' deeper partnership has somewhat overshadowed the work between Ottawa and the 27-member bloc given some members are against the proposal.

"We are working toward the deepest possible partnership, short of accession because of our geography, with Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member," said Carney in his closing remarks.

"Over the coming months, we will determine the substance, scale and scope of this form of membership."

WATCH | Canada and EU launching 'alliance for the future,' Carney says: Canada and EU launching 'alliance for the future,' Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:22 Standing with the presidents of the European Commission and European Council in Montreal, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the EU are 'working towards the deepest possible partnership, short of accession… with Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member.'

Carney previously stayed away from using the "associate member" title, instead arguing the nomenclature doesn't matter.

By Friday, though, he he added a timeline to the debate, saying the plan is to conclude negotiations in June, when he'll join European Council meetings.

He also said he, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will convene the College of the European Commissioners and Canada's federal cabinet in March.

Von der Leyen first raised the prospect of making Canada an associate member — a status that doesn't currently exist in the bloc — in a speech last month and has continued to spearhead the initiative despite objections from some members, notably Germany.

No talk of cost

Speaking on background after the news conference, a Canadian official couldn't answer what what legislation would be needed in Canada and across the EU member states.

"It's a concept," the official said, noting there's no existing formal process to becoming an associate member.

Asked what the cost of joining as an associate member could be, Carney said "we don't view this as paying for something, we view this as coming together."

While von der Leyen, Costa and Carney are all now championing the title, it's far from a done deal. EU members would have to vote, and Carney has said a new partnership with the European Union will be put up for debate and a vote in Canada's Parliament.

"Canada is by far the most European of the non-European countries," Costa said on Friday morning.

Canada-EU sign agreements

Division over what to call the partnership was apparent in the crafting of the joint statement released at the end of the summit.

Sources with knowledge of what happened said the "associate member" term was removed from the draft version, given some members' disapproval. One source said Germany called it a red line. Instead, the final document calls for "an ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself."

Outside of the title, the document makes clear Ottawa and Brussels have lots to agree on as they move ahead on what's being dubbed the "alliance for the future"

On Friday the two sides announced they finished negotiations between Canada and the European Investment Bank to support investment in critical Canadian resources, notably critical raw materials and another on countermeasures to fight anti-competitive activity.

They also wrapped negotiations on a digital trade agreement between the EU and Canada meant to improve legal certainty and facilitate cross-border data flows, as well as finalized an agreement giving Canadian researchers and businesses access to European supercomputers.

Canada will also join a EU program for aid to Ukraine, called Ukraine Support Loan.

When it comes to next steps, the two sides have agreed to expand opportunities for Canadians and Europeans to study, work and conduct research. There's also a promise to launch talks to secure international connectivity between Canada, Europe and Asia through new subsea cable infrastructure.

The document includes commitment on a long list of other areas, including the Arctic, foreign information manipulation and interference and advancing co-operation on artificial intelligence (AI) security and safety.

It also calls for reforming the World Trade Organization instead of replacing it, and doing more on border security and fighting climate change.

"It means, at its base, sovereignty," said Carney. "Greater resilience [and the] ability to withstand shocks together."

But it is unclear how much all the new programs will cost either.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne dodged questions on Thursday, saying Canadians should see only "opportunities."

WATCH | EU chief revisits 'associate membership' for Canada: EU chief floats 'association without accession' for Canada | Duration closed caption 0:58 After Canada's 'associate membership' of the EU was reportedly removed from a proposed joint statement on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen mentioned the idea again on Thursday, suggesting a partnership 'that comes closer to membership than anything we've done before.'

Canada's Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre said the summit featured "big talk" but a lack of concrete results.

"There was a lot of talk at the summit about aligning Canada with the insane European taxes, debt, immigration and anti-oil and gas policies that have left parts of Europe bankrupt and burning," he posted on social media Friday.

"Does any of this lower your mortgage payments, rent, grocery bills or gas prices, back here in the real world? Of course not."

Carney points to EU's strong belief in democracy

The summit was billed as a way to deepen ties with like-minded leaders in the wake of an unpredictable and volatile White House under U.S. President Donald Trump.

While the three leaders in Montreal were in step around their common goals, shifting political winds on the continent could test that alliance, notably in France and Germany — both heavyweights within the bloc.

In France, presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally is leading in polls ahead of the spring 2027 election. Le Pen, an advocate for strict immigration limits, has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact.

In Germany, the far-right and isolationist Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues to gain ground in regional parliaments and national polls.

Asked Thursday if he has concerns about dealing with a potentially different political makeup, Carney praised the EU's adherence to democratic values.

"One of Europe's strengths is democracy, freedom and a core belief in the rule of law. There will always be different governments, governments of different stripes in Europe," he told reporters.

"Over the course of decades, the European Union has continued to develop, and strengthen, throughout, and be enriched by the national democratic processes of those countries."

Carney also downplayed the notion he was looking to secure commitments with the EU before the French election. "We're not tying it to any political cycle, but to the fundamentals of what they deliver … for Canadians," he said.

Asked earlier this week about the summit potentially attracting retaliation from Trump or right-wing leaders in Europe, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the gathering isn't directed against anyone, but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.

World.title: Some Backstreet Boys fans consider refund after Live Nation relocates them to cheaper, still-obstructed seats
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some Backstreet Boys fans aren't happy with their new seats for the group's Toronto residency. They say presale tickets they bought were later reclassified as partially obstructed. Live Nation promised to relocate them to better seats, but some say their new seats are actually worse. CBC's Tyler Cheese reports.

These Backstreet Boys fans say their 'obstructed view' seats were relocated to worse spots

Some Backstreet Boys fans attending one of the group’s Toronto shows aren’t happy with their seat change after Live Nation relocated fans who unknowingly bought tickets that had an obstructed view.

Betsabe Bustillos from Welland, Ont., said she originally bought four seats in the second row of section 130 at Toronto's Rogers Centre during the presale period for around $1,300.

Days after the presale ended, dozens of fans flooded social media with complaints that Ticketmaster failed to indicate their seats had an obstructed view and that after the presale, similar seats were selling for a discounted price. That prompted calls for the vendor to issue an apology and rectify the problem, either through refunds or exchanges for different seats.

After seeing the reports on social media, Bustillos said she checked her own tickets, which, much to her surprise, had also been marked as partially obstructed. She says she then reached out to Ticketmaster, where she was told she would be relocated to an unobstructed seat.

Instead, Bustillos says she was moved to a row much farther back and the view from her new seats is also obstructed.

"This is insane," she said. "It's destroying the entire experience."

In a statement to CBC Toronto Thursday, Live Nation spokesperson Shabnum Durrani apologized for the situation. (Paul Sakuma/The Associated Press)

Rogers announced earlier this month that it was the organizer bringing the Backstreet Boys to Toronto in 2027. Its announcement offered Rogers customers "exclusive" access to the Oct. 5 presale.

Live Nation oversees the concerts, and its subsidiary, Ticketmaster, operates the ticketing platform.

'There is no option at all': ticket holder

The Backstreet Boys are expected to play 12 shows across four consecutive weekends in Toronto, from February to March 2027.

In a statement to CBC Toronto Thursday, Live Nation spokesperson Shabnum Durrani apologized for the situation.

"We are always happy to work directly with fans to review individual concerns and explore available options," Durrani said. "We understand this has been frustrating and appreciate the patience of fans as we work to resolve these issues."

Bustillos says a couple of friends backed out after they found out about the issues, meaning she was forced to sell two of the tickets. But she said she was really excited, which is why she’s not keen on a refund.

"That's not my goal. I want to go and I want to enjoy the concert," she said. "It's not great that we have to do all this work for something that we already paid for."

Bustillos says she will need to give Ticketmaster a response on whether she wants a refund or a relocation by Nov. 22.

"There is no option at all," she said. "You go with this bad view or you don't and you stay home."

The Backstreet Boys are expected to play 12 shows across four consecutive weekends in Toronto, from February to March 2027. (backstreetboys.com)

"If I don't get the solution that is fair for me as a purchaser, as a buyer, for this ticket, I will definitely get a refund and not go and miss it, unfortunately," Bustillos added.

Customer hoped for more solutions

Backstreet Boys fan Giulianna Heto said she was also blindsided by the partially obstructed seating. She told CBC Toronto Friday she had to talk to three different people before she finally spoke with someone at Ticketmaster willing to help her with her two tickets. But the suggestion was far from ideal, Heto says.

"It came to, 'Oh, you should list it, sell it to get your money back,'" she said. "I was told several times in that call to lie and to not mention that it was obstructed."

"That's pretty crazy," she added. "It's not fair."

Heto says some of the solutions she would have appreciated include an ability to pick her new seating, a chance to change the date she’d be attending or a difference in the price between her old and new tickets.

"It should have been announced [as] obstructed. There's other concerts that were," she said. "I just want Ticketmaster [to] take ownership for it."

In a statement Friday, Durrani said the Ticketmaster team connected with Heto Thursday night and are "working with her to explore available options."

World.title: Canadian Crime Stoppers Association advises chapters to accept tips by phone only
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) is advising its local chapters to solely accept tips by telephone instead of online, it said in a statement to CBC News on Friday.

The "interim telephone-only approach … will allow participating local programs to receive tips without using Navigate360’s P3 platform," reads the statement, referring to the third-party U.S. company's tip management platform that suffered a massive data breach in March.

It appears to be a shift for the not-for-profit organization, which had previously issued guidance to local programs that if members of the public asked about the breach, they should express their confidence in Navigate360's security improvements and say the platform "remains secure and appropriate for continued use."

In the Friday statement, the CCSA asked that the public now call 222-TIPS to submit tips anonymously. For programs that have been paused, there will be local announcements about when telephone reporting will resume, it said.

"Local programs will keep new information under their control and share it securely with law enforcement," reads the statement from CCSA president David J. Forster.

"This change cannot undo the exposure of information already taken. We will continue pressing Navigate360 for answers while working to rebuild trust in a program that has long helped communities prevent and solve crime."

The extent of the breach was revealed in a CBC investigation published last week, which found that over 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years had been hacked.

To date, more than 40 local Crime Stoppers chapters and police agencies in five provinces have temporarily paused their intake of anonymous tips or their partnerships with the organization. Meanwhile, the privacy commissioner is investigating the breach , focusing on Navigate360 and its security safeguards at the time of the hack in March.

"It's hard to imagine [Crime Stoppers] ever getting back to where they were in terms of trust," said Randy Lippert, a criminology professor at the University of Windsor in Ontario, in an interview with CBC News before the Friday statement was released.

At least 13 programs not accepting tips in any form

Before receiving the CCSA statement, CBC had attempted to contact all 64 Crime Stoppers chapters we identified as having compromised tips. (Six do not have publicly listed contact information.)

To date, 13 Crime Stoppers programs in Ontario and Saskatchewan said they would no longer accept anonymous tips.

The latest addition to the list was Ontario's Brant-Brantford Crime Stoppers chapter, which made the announcement on its Facebook page .

Three Crime Stoppers chapters explicitly confirmed they were still accepting anonymous tips: New Brunswick and the districts of Thunder Bay and Sault Ste. Marie and Algoma.

The latter two programs both have statements on their websites — published before the Friday statement — stating that they were unable to accept tips intended for their local police services, which had paused their participation in Crime Stoppers. But they said they would still accept tips for "other participating police services in our region."

CBC News has reached out to the three chapters about whether they will reconsider the decision, in light of their national organization's new guidance.

OPP 'pausing the promotion' of program

CBC also contacted the biggest municipal police departments in the country that hadn't yet commented on the breach to ask them if they intended to suspend their use of anonymous tips as a policing tool. Crime Stoppers sends tips to law enforcement when deemed necessary, but it works independently of the police.

At least 29 police units across Ontario, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and British Columbia said they had suspended their partnership with the Crime Stoppers program.

However, some, such as Calgary and Charlottetown, said they would continue accepting Crime Stoppers tips and that their use of the program "has not been paused."

WATCH | Privacy commissioner investigating Navigate360: Federal privacy commissioner investigating Crime Stoppers data breach | Duration closed caption 1:11 The office of Philippe Dufresne, Canada's privacy commissioner, said Tuesday it is opening an investigation into a massive data breach. The probe will focus on Navigate360, an American company hired to manage Crime Stoppers tips.

Meanwhile, the Ontario Provincial Police confirmed that it was pausing the promotion of the Crime Stoppers program. However, people can still use it if they prefer to, a spokesperson said in a statement, and the agency will assess the information "as appropriate."

The RCMP did not explicitly confirm whether it was still using anonymous Crime Stoppers tips for active investigations. Instead, it said it was aware that several chapters had paused their tip intake, and advised any potential tipsters to avoid sharing any identifiable information in their reports.

Lippert said that there could be long-term implications from police agencies' distancing from Crime Stoppers, going beyond the use of anonymous tips in policing, due to the program's "strong overlap" with law enforcement.

"It's just hard to imagine Crime Stoppers being able to survive without a lot of the support," he said.

For example, while Crime Stoppers' reward money does not come from the police, many agencies do give their local chapters funding for other matters, such as special events or marketing campaigns, he said. Some have provided their chapters with physical offices, or have even assigned officers to serve as program co-ordinators and help investigate tips.

CCSA previously insisted on 'continued operations'

The CCSA previously appeared take a different approach to how it addressed the breach and its relationship with Navigate360, even with the fallout after CBC's initial investigation.

In an internal memo to local programs dated Oct. 22 and obtained by CBC News, president David J. Forster had advised them to direct all media inquiries to the national association, saying one of its key messaging points would be that Navigate360's "security improvements support continued operations."

The memo, which was sent the day after Toronto Crime Stoppers paused accepting tips, included a suggested response to potential questions from the public about why other local chapters continued to accept tips: "We continue to receive tips because of our confidence in the technical work completed by our third-party software provider, together with stronger procedures for handling information within Crime Stoppers."

CBC News has reached out to Navigate360 for comment on the Friday statement.

World.title: Montreal police chief defends push to change force's culture, weed out bad apples
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As accusations of misconduct against Montreal’s police service mount, Chief Fady Dagher says he is taking concrete steps to bring change from the ground up while investigating and potentially prosecuting those "one per cent" of officers who "tarnish the uniform."

This comes after new allegations arose at Station 39 in Montréal-Nord, which has been at the centre of a major racism scandal since June.

Now, the Quebec Crown prosecution's office is investigating an officer who, according to Radio-Canada sources , allegedly deleted evidence from a victim's phone in a case of domestic violence in 2025.

Also in recent news, Quebec's domestic security minister has ordered two separate investigations into a Montreal police officer who allegedly urinated on homeless people while in uniform.

But the latest claims are not the first time the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) has faced accusations of misconduct, having been the subject of serious allegations of police brutality and discrimination in the past.

In a news conference Friday, Dagher insisted he has been working tirelessly to not only weed out those on the force who are breaking laws and policies, but also prevent more such officers from being hired.

"We have reviewed everything," Dagher said, citing recruitment, training and promotion processes. "It didn’t happen in a day. It took several years, and believe me, it’s not over."

The SPVM, he said, has overhauled the internal investigative norms and standards. Dagher said the police service also put tools in place so officers can flag their colleagues for misconduct, and "the 99 per cent responded" by reporting those who break protocol or the law.

The majority of officers, he explained, do admirable work, day after day, risking their lives to protect others.

"I have always told my police officers since I was hired that I would always defend them in the context of their work during emergency responses," he said, noting mistakes are inevitable.

"But I say again today, that I will be merciless to those who intentionally and deliberately conduct themselves in a way that tarnishes the uniform."

He defended his actions back in June when a 16-member patrol unit from Station 39 was suspended following allegations of discrimination and misconduct. More suspensions followed as the investigation continued in the weeks and months since.

Some question why he didn’t fire these officers immediately, he said, but "I wanted to do more." That includes a thorough investigation into not just the individuals, but any potential accomplices.

"And an investigation of this kind takes time," he said. He acknowledged that many people are impatient, especially the victims, who have been "waiting too long."

He said more information will be released in November.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada has come out in support of Dagher, saying she is confident in his effort to bring cultural change to the SPVM and rid the service of "bad apples."

"I think we have someone who wants to tackle this culture. So, let's give him the chance to do that," she said.

"Let's give him the chance to speak to the citizens and strengthen their sense of security towards their police service."

Dagher was promoted to the role of police chief in November 2022.

Opposition Leader Ericka Alneus said the most recent allegations "shatter the confidence of people in vulnerable situations who need to feel that society is behind them."

She said the mayor "must take responsibility, show leadership and summon the police chief to an extraordinary city council meeting to answer public questions."

World.title: North American stocks sink, Wall Street suffers worst day since June amid tech sell-off
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A sell-off for tech stocks got even worse Friday on worries that Wall Street's frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high.

The S&P 500 tumbled about 1.8 per cent Friday for its worst day since June. The weakness of technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 2.9 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.1 per cent.

Canada's main index, the S&P/TSX composite, bounced back from its afternoon drop of 2.3 per cent to close down 1.7 per cent.

Intel's stock led the way lower and plunged 28.6 per cent for its worst drop since 1974. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts' expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Amazon sank 1.4 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon's reporting that it burned through $42.4 billion US of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion US on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.

WATCH | A breakdown of Anthropic's IPO and its single 'God share': How Anthropic's IPO creates a single 'God share' | About That | Duration 2:49 Andrew Chang breaks down how Anthropic's unique ownership structure works as the AI giant prepares to go public — and why it's nearly impossible to overrule its founders. Images provided by The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images

A day earlier, Alphabet's stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and almost single-handedly dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI.

Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centres have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centres.

"We're moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the 'show me' phase," said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors.

A drop of 4.2 per cent for Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, outweighing even Intel.

In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 US from more than $86,000 US earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that affected more than $6 billion US worth of crypto at Binance.

Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell.

WATCH | What happens to the U.S. economy if the AI bubble pops?: If the AI bubble pops, will the whole U.S. economy go with it? | About That | Duration closed caption 25:53 As investors pour billions into artificial intelligence, warnings of a looming AI bubble are intensifying. Andrew Chang breaks down what's fuelling those fears. Plus, how one reporter’s question struck at the core of U.S.-Saudi relations.

ExxonMobil climbed 2.2 per cent, and Chevron added 1.8 per cent after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.

Mondelez International rose 3.9 per cent due to better than expected growth and Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.3 per cent after higher prices for its products helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected.

Expectations are high for U.S. companies' ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of a safer option. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month.

In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Europe following sharper swings in Asia. South Korea's Kospi dropped due to AI worries, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng climbed slightly.

World.title: Dune 3 popcorn buckets are even more unhinged than the original
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Remember when Dune: Part Two gave the world that suggestive popcorn bucket that stopped you in your tracks and made you wonder: is this even allowed? Well, it's back. And this time it brought a friend.

Yes, you read that right. The movie merchandise widely deemed to be NSFW is making a comeback ahead of Dune: Part Three. And movie theatre chains didn't dial it back. They've doubled down.

Clearly, simply putting popcorn in a bag just doesn't cut it anymore.

Riding the viral success of the last movie's merchandise, two new suggestive designs are being sold — and they've already got people talking.

First up is a "shareable" popcorn tub featuring not one, but two sandworms. According to American theatre chain AMC, the design makes it "easier to share."

Cineplex is also rolling out an updated version of the original single-worm bucket, complete with a functional vibrating 'sandworm thumper'. (Cineplex)

And if two sandworms weren't enough to get the internet talking, Cineplex is also rolling out an updated version of the original single-worm bucket, complete with a functional "sandworm thumper."

For anyone who hasn't seen the film, a thumper is the device used to pound the desert and attract giant sandworms. The best (or worst) part of the sandworm thumper bucket? It has a working design: this one vibrates. Yes, you read that correctly.

The memes are so back

The original popcorn bucket kicked off countless memes when it dropped in 2024. Director Denis Villeneuve, in an interview with the New York Times, said his reaction to the bucket was: "Hoooooly smokes. What the [expletive]!?"

It even inspired a sketch on Saturday Night Live, which featured a teenager with a rather unconventional use for the popcorn bucket — proving everyone on the internet was thinking the exact same thing.

Naturally, fans took zero time reacting to the latest designs, flooding social feeds with unhinged memes and 18+ reactions.

For this story's purposes, we're keeping it PG. You can dive into that wormhole at your own risk.

"What if we both reached for more popcorn and accidentally touched hands inside the DUNE: PART 3 popcorn bucket 👉🏻👈🏻 >.<🩵✨" one user wrote on X . "Holding my wife's hand in the Dune 3 popcorn bucket, you sick freaks should take notes," another joked.

Over on Instagram, the comment sections were just as suggestive as you might've guessed.

"Double the worms double the fun," one user commented on Cineplex's post.

"Ya'll play too much 😂." said another. "Me ordering 12 of them 🧐🧐🧐," a third added.

Movie theatres have been selling novelty popcorn tins and containers for years. But the success of the previous Dune bucket seemingly inspired theatre chains to get more creative — and increasingly outrageous — with the designs.

Other notable mentions include: an entirely transparent bucket for You Can See Everything; a giant dinosaur footprint bucket for Jurassic Park Rebirth; a Trojan horse bucket for The Odyssey; and a red purse for The Devil Wears Prada 2.

Hitting theatres December 18, Dune: Part Three continues the sci-fi saga based on Frank Herbert's novels.

WATCH | Trailer for Dune: Part Three:

Directed by Villeneuve, the film has a star-studded cast featuring Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson, Florence Pugh, Anya Taylor-Joy, Jason Momoa, Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin and Rebecca Ferguson.

"We love that merchandise has become part of the moviegoing experience, giving fans an interactive way to enjoy concessions", Michelle Saba, vice-president of communications for Cineplex, wrote in a statement to CBC News.

The new merch will be up for grabs at most Cineplex locations across Canada starting Dec. 17, while supplies last.
