SOUTH AFRICA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country South Africa, Africa’s most industrialised economy, is led by President Cyril Ramaphosa.

Producer prices Factory-gate inflation jumped to 6.2% in September from 5.0% in August.

The driver Fuel, chemicals, rubber and plastics rose 19.1% in a year and lifted the index 1.0% in September.

Lending Bank credit to businesses and households grew 6.23% in September, down from 7.47%.

Money supply The broad money measure M3 grew 7.93% in September, down from 8.89%.

South Africa’s producer prices rose 6.2% in September 2026 from a year earlier, while lending and the money supply both slowed. Stats SA, the national statistics office, published the producer price figures on Thursday 29 October 2026 at 11:30 local time.

For US readers, the three releases set the scene for the next interest-rate decision of the South African Reserve Bank, the central bank, in November and for the rand, which Americans trade through exchange-traded funds and ADRs (US-listed shares of foreign companies). They also arrive days before Washington decides on Monday 2 November whether South Africa keeps duty-free access under AGOA, the African Growth and Opportunity Act, as we explain in South Africa Awaits US Trade Ruling Monday.

What Happened

The Producer Price Index, which tracks the prices factories, mines and farms receive before goods reach shops, showed annual inflation of 6.2% for final manufactured goods in September, against 5.0% in August. Prices rose 1.0% in one month, according to Stats SA.

The Reserve Bank, South Africa’s central bank, published its money and credit data for September on the same Thursday. Private Sector Credit, the stock of loans and other claims banks hold on companies and households, grew 6.23% from a year earlier, compared with 7.47% in August.

The M3 Money Supply, the broadest count of cash and bank deposits in the economy, grew 7.93% in the year to September, compared with 8.89% a month earlier. Both measures lost speed in September, which points to weaker demand for money and loans.

In plain English Producer Price Index: A measure of what producers charge, often an early warning for shop prices.

A measure of what producers charge, often an early warning for shop prices. Private Sector Credit: How fast loans to firms and households are growing compared with a year ago.

How fast loans to firms and households are growing compared with a year ago. M3 Money Supply: The total of cash, bank accounts and other deposits in the economy.

The total of cash, bank accounts and other deposits in the economy. Policy rate: The Reserve Bank’s main interest rate, formerly the repo rate, which sets the cost of loans across the country.

Fuel and Chemicals Drive Producer Prices

Stats SA says coke, petroleum, chemical, rubber and plastic products were the main force behind the September jump. Their prices were 19.1% higher than a year earlier and added 4.1 percentage points to the 6.2% headline rate.

The same group rose 4.2% in September alone and supplied the whole of the 1.0% monthly gain. Metals, machinery and computing equipment, up 3.4% in a year, added a further 0.5 of a percentage point.

Prices of intermediate goods, the materials that factories buy to make other products, grew 7.8% in a year, slower than 8.8% in August, and edged up 0.1% in the month. Mining prices grew 7.3%, unchanged from August, with non-ferrous metal ores up 15.0% and coal and gas up 11.1%.

Farm-gate prices swung from a 1.8% annual fall in August to a 2.5% rise in September. Electricity and water prices were 8.4% higher in a year, although the index fell 17.7% in the month because of a 20.5% monthly drop in electricity prices.

Lending and Money Supply Cool

A fall in credit growth from 7.47% to 6.23% is a sharp one-month slowdown. A slower pace usually means households and companies are borrowing less, because loans cost more or because they are less confident about the economy.

South Africa’s consumer price inflation was 4.5% in September, up from 4.4% in August, Stats SA reported on Wednesday 21 October. Our report on that release has the detail.

What It Means for You

If you hold South African stocks or bonds through US funds, the producer price jump is a warning that consumer inflation could rise in the coming months. The Reserve Bank raised its policy rate, formerly called the repo rate, by 0.25 percentage points to 7.25% on Wednesday 23 September, and its final policy meeting of 2026 takes place in November.

Higher factory costs and slower lending pull in opposite directions for the central bank, because one argues for higher rates and the other for patience. The rand, South Africa’s currency, usually firms when interest rates rise and weakens when they fall.

US companies that buy South African chemicals, plastics and metals may see higher quotes. Travelers will not notice the data directly, although a weaker rand would make safaris and wine tours cheaper in dollar terms.

The US trade angle matters as well. AGOA, the African Growth and Opportunity Act, lets eligible African countries sell many goods in the United States without import duty, and the annual decision on South Africa is due on Monday 2 November.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the Reserve Bank will raise, hold or cut its policy rate in November, because the central bank has not signalled a decision. It is also unclear how much of the September fuel and chemical price rise will reach shop shelves.

The split of September credit growth between households and companies was not available to us at publication. The US decision on AGOA for 2027 is also unknown.

More: South Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Was South Africa’s Producer Price Inflation in September 2026?

Producer price inflation for final manufactured goods was 6.2% in September 2026, up from 5.0% in August. Stats SA published the figure on Thursday 29 October 2026.

How Fast Did Private Sector Credit Grow in September?

Private sector credit grew 6.23% from a year earlier, down from 7.47% in August. M3 money supply grew 7.93%, down from 8.89%.

Why Does This Matter for the Rand?

Rising producer prices can push the Reserve Bank toward higher interest rates, which usually supports the rand. Slower lending points the other way, so the November meeting is the next test.

World.title: Uruguay Trade Gap Narrows to US$35 Million
World.content:
Aerial file photo of the La Teja oil refinery on Montevideo Bay, with the city of Montevideo in the background. (Photo: Marcelo Campi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

URUGUAY · TRADE

Key Facts The country Uruguay, a country of about 3.5 million people between Brazil and Argentina, lives largely from farm and forestry exports.

What happened Uruguay’s goods trade deficit narrowed to US$35.3 million in September 2026; market calendars had forecast US$181 million.

Exports Goods exports rose 7.8% to US$1.14 billion, led by meat and manufactured goods.

Imports Imports edged down 0.6% to US$1.18 billion, as oil purchases fell 53%.

The bigger picture The deficit for January to September is US$1.26 billion, more than three times last year’s.

Power Index Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 45.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Uruguay’s goods trade deficit narrowed to US$35.3 million in September 2026, far smaller than the US$181 million that market calendars forecast, the Banco Central del Uruguay (BCU), the country’s central bank, reported on Friday 30 October. Exports rose 7.8% to US$1.14 billion, while imports edged down 0.6% to US$1.18 billion.

For US readers, the report shows a small, farm-driven economy between Brazil and Argentina that sells beef, soybeans and wood to the world and still buys more than it sells. It matters to US buyers, because Uruguayan shipments to the United States jumped 33.7% in the month to US$123.2 million.

What Happened in September

Customs data compiled by the BCU show goods exports of US$1,140.2 million in September, up from US$1,057.6 million a year earlier. Imports valued free on board, meaning without freight and insurance, were US$1,175.4 million, down 0.6%, and with freight and insurance they were US$1.27 billion, up 0.1%.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Uruguay ranks 7th of 14 with 45.9 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (88); weakest: future resources (23). Alignment group: Hedging. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The deficit was US$35.3 million, compared with US$124.5 million in September 2025 and the US$42.8 million deficit we reported for August. The result beat the forecast by about US$146 million.

From January to September the goods deficit is US$1.26 billion, against US$369 million a year earlier. Over the 12 months to September it is US$1.80 billion, with exports up 1.9% and imports up 9.0%.

Why the Gap Narrowed

Two things closed the gap: stronger exports and a sharp drop in oil purchases. Imports of oil and fuels fell 53.3% to about US$74 million after the surge of crude shipments that widened the August deficit.

Without oil, fuels and electricity, imports actually rose 7.7% to US$1.20 billion measured with freight. Consumer goods rose 9.9%, led by cars and other transport vehicles, which jumped 28.1%, while machinery and equipment fell 8.4%.

China supplied US$363.5 million of imports, up 17.1%, and Brazil US$252.3 million, up 2.1%. Argentina sold Uruguay US$212.6 million, down 5.7%.

The company operates twelve international airports in the Pacific and Central region of Mexico; and two international airports in Jamaica. It also offers aeronautical services, such as passenger, aircraft landing, parking charges,…

Beef, Wood and Farm Exports

Manufactured goods, a group that includes meatpacking, rose 11.5% to US$700.7 million, about three-fifths of all exports. Meat products rose 11.4% to US$284.9 million, the largest single line in the BCU table.

Primary products from farms and forests rose 2.0% to US$425.6 million. Forestry and wood grew 16.5%, while crops fell 2.8% to US$243.9 million and dairy exports dropped 22.1% to US$65.3 million.

Brazil, Argentina and China

Brazil was the biggest buyer in the customs data, taking US$217.1 million, up 47.0%. China took US$176.9 million, down 16.8%, and Argentina took US$47.6 million, down 17.8%.

The United States bought US$123.2 million, up 33.7%, and the European Union US$83.9 million, up 14.9%. Exports of transport equipment jumped about 264% to US$67.6 million, a sharp swing for a small line.

Why Another Measure Looks Different

The US$35.3 million is the BCU’s own measure, exports minus imports valued free on board, under a United Nations trade system that leaves out goods made in the production free zones, such as the big pulp mills. Even with freight and insurance added to imports, the BCU deficit would be US$129.4 million, still well below the US$181 million forecast.

We could not establish how the US$181 million forecast was built, so the gap may reflect a different definition, such as one that counts free zones, or simply a forecast miss. Uruguay XXI, the government export-promotion agency, does count free zones, and its goods-export total for September was US$1,398 million, up 10%.

Uruguay XXI names soybeans, beef, pulp, dairy products and drink concentrates as the main sales of the month, and puts January to September exports at US$10.37 billion, up 1%. The two agencies count different things, so their September export totals differ by about US$258 million.

What It Means for You

For US importers, Uruguay is a steady meat supplier, and the BCU data show US purchases of Uruguayan goods up 33.7% to US$123.2 million in September. Buyers of wood pulp and soybeans watch the same figures, because Uruguay’s shipments to China and Europe set the supply on those markets.

For investors, a smaller deficit should ease pressure on the Uruguayan peso, but a 12-month goods gap of US$1.8 billion is still large for a country of 3.5 million people. The strong sales to Brazil show that Uruguay still depends on its two big neighbors, while the 17.8% drop in sales to Argentina shows how weak demand there remains.

Travelers and expats need not change plans, because the report does not affect prices for visitors or residents. The figures matter most for exporters, shippers and anyone who invests in the region’s currencies.

What Would Change the Picture

A new crude oil cargo could widen the gap again in a single month, as it did in August. A larger soybean harvest would lift crop exports in the coming months.

Weaker Chinese demand would hit beef and soy first, and a stronger Brazilian real would help Uruguayan sales next door. Another drop in Argentine purchases would keep the pressure on the border trade.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the fall in oil imports is a lasting change or just timing. The BCU figures are preliminary, and the two agencies’ totals will keep differing because of free-zone trade.

It is also not known how the US$181 million forecast was built, so part of the miss may come from a different definition. The report also does not show services, such as tourism, which are part of the current account.

More: Uruguay news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Uruguay’s Trade Balance?

Uruguay had a goods trade deficit of US$35.3 million in September 2026, according to the central bank. Exports were US$1.14 billion and imports were US$1.18 billion.

What Does Uruguay Export?

Beef, soybeans, wood pulp, wood and dairy products are Uruguay’s main exports. Pulp is shipped from free trade zones, so the central bank’s monthly figures do not include it.

Who Buys Uruguay’s Exports?

In September 2026 the largest buyers in the central bank data were Brazil, China and the United States. Argentina bought less than a year earlier.

Sources: Banco Central del Uruguay, monthly goods trade report, September 2026 (preliminary figures; compiled from National Customs Directorate data), 30 October 2026; Uruguay XXI, monthly foreign trade report, September 2026.

World.title: Colombia Jobless Rate Falls to 8%, Cement Up
World.content:
File photo, 2008. Bogotá seen from the Monserrate hill above the city. (Photo: Jair Hernández Q., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Colombia, a major Andean economy, is led by conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella.

Jobs The unemployment rate fell to 8.0% in September from 9.4% in August; analysts had expected 9.2%.

Cement Gray cement production rose 2.0% from a year earlier in September; the forecast was 1.7%.

The catch Cement shipments to Colombian buyers rose only 1.1%, and unemployment in the 13 biggest cities edged up to 8.3%.

Prediction markets Polymarket gives 55.0% to no change in the central bank’s December rate decision and 31.9% to a quarter-point rise (30 October, 6:12 p.m. ET).

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Colombia’s unemployment rate fell to 8.0% in September 2026 from 9.4% in August, well below the 9.2% that analysts expected, DANE, the national statistics office, said on Friday 30 October. Cement production, a quick gauge of building activity, rose 2.0% from a year earlier and beat the 1.7% forecast.

For US investors in Colombian bonds, stocks and the peso, the two reports show a job market that is firm and a construction sector that is growing slowly. Hours later the central bank held its rate at 12.25% on a split 4-3 vote, as we report in Colombia’s Central Bank Holds Rate at 12.25%.

What Happened With Unemployment

The national unemployment rate was 8.0% in September, down from 8.2% in September 2025 and from 9.4% in August 2026, DANE said. About 24.2 million people had a job, which is 322,000 more than a year earlier.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The participation rate, the share of working-age people who have a job or look for one, was 63.8%, against 63.9% a year earlier. The employment rate stayed at 58.7%, so the yearly drop in unemployment reflects slightly fewer job seekers, not a higher share of people at work.

Women had an unemployment rate of 10.1% in September, against 6.5% for men, a gap of 3.6 percentage points. About 14.1 million men and 10.2 million women had a job.

Why the Rate Fell From August

August was unusually weak, with unemployment at 9.4% against 8.6% a year earlier, and it was also the month of the 10 August 2026 earthquake in western Colombia. DANE data show that factory employment was 240,000 lower in August than a year earlier.

In September factories employed 100,000 more people than a year earlier, and shops and vehicle repair added 162,000 jobs. Transport and storage added 84,000 jobs, which lifted that sector to 1.94 million workers.

Farming went the other way, with 184,000 fewer agricultural jobs than a year earlier. Government employees also fell by 68,000, a loss that the gains elsewhere more than covered.

DANE does not say how much of the rebound is a return to normal after the earthquake month. A swing of 1.4 points in one month is large, so the next report will show whether 8.0% holds.

The Big Cities Tell a Different Story

In the 13 largest cities and their metropolitan areas the rate rose to 8.3% from 8.1% a year earlier. The three-month rate for the whole country to September was 8.5%, the same as a year ago.

Bogotá had the lowest three-month rate at 7.6%, ahead of Villavicencio at 7.7% and Medellín at 7.8%. Quibdó, the capital of the Chocó province on the Pacific coast, had the highest at 23.4%, followed by Cartagena at 13.7% and Tunja at 13.2%.

What Happened With Cement

Colombia produced 1,263.1 thousand tonnes of gray cement in September, 2.0% more than a year earlier, DANE said. Gray cement is the standard cement used in concrete and mortar, so its output is a quick read on building activity.

Shipments to the domestic market, which DANE calls dispatches, rose a smaller 1.1% to 1,194.4 thousand tonnes. The gap of about 69,000 tonnes between production and dispatches is made up of exports and changes in stocks.

Market calendars list this release as cement production, with a 1.7% forecast and a 2.9% prior reading, and we use production (+2.0%) as the headline because it matches DANE’s production figure exactly. The 2.9% prior matches August dispatches as first published, while August production fell 1.9%, and DANE has since revised August with real company data, so the prior may not be a like-for-like comparison.

From January to September production is up 2.1% to 10.59 million tonnes, and dispatches are up 3.6% to 9.87 million tonnes. Over the 12 months to September dispatches rose 4.7%, and all figures are provisional.

Where Cement Demand Is Growing

Ready-mix concrete plants, which turn cement into concrete for large projects, took 7.4% more cement and supplied most of the growth in dispatches. Bagged cement sold to builders and contractors rose 8.2%.

By region, dispatches rose 34.8% in Boyacá, 20.3% in Meta and 18.0% in Atlántico, the department around Barranquilla. They fell 9.3% in the Bogotá area, 4.5% in Valle del Cauca, around Cali, and 4.1% in Antioquia, around Medellín.

Weak orders in the biggest cities fit the small rise in city unemployment, though DANE does not link the two. The data also do not show whether rebuilding after the earthquake has started to lift orders.

What It Means for You

For US investors in Colombian assets, a jobless rate of 8.0% points to steady household income, which supports spending and loan quality at banks such as Bancolombia, the country’s largest bank. It also gives the central bank, which held its rate at 12.25% today while inflation is 6.3%, little reason to rush toward rate cuts.

The peso closed at about 3,167 per US dollar on Thursday 29 October, so 1,000 pesos are worth about US$0.32. Oil prices and the debate in Congress over the Rescue Law explained, a package of spending cuts worth about US$13 billion in 2027, are likely to move the currency more than one month of jobs data.

Cement output of about 1.26 million tonnes a month points to a construction sector that grows slowly, which matters for US suppliers of machinery and building materials. Travelers need not change plans, because nothing in either report affects visas, safety or prices for visitors.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where users bet real money, gave 55.0% to no change at Colombia’s central bank meeting in December and 31.9% to a quarter-point rise as of 6:12 p.m. ET on Friday 30 October. About US$30,000 has been traded on that market.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Would Change the Picture

A rise in unemployment back toward 9% in the next monthly report would suggest that September was the outlier and August the trend. A fall below 8% would point to a labor market tightening further, which would add wage pressure at a time when inflation is more than double the 3% target.

In cement, a lasting rise in dispatches around Bogotá, Cali and Medellín would show that housing and public works are recovering. A US$13 billion spending cut in 2027 under the Rescue Law, if Congress passes it, could slow public works instead.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how much of the fall from 9.4% is a return to normal after the earthquake month. The September jobs figures are survey estimates, and the cement data are provisional and can be revised for up to two years.

It is also unknown whether the weakness in cement orders in the big cities is temporary. The two reports say nothing about wages or informal work, so the quality of the new jobs cannot be judged.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Is Colombia’s Unemployment Rate?

It was 8.0% in September 2026, down from 9.4% in August and 8.2% a year earlier. DANE, the national statistics office, published the figure on Friday 30 October 2026.

How Much Cement Does Colombia Produce?

Colombia produced 1,263.1 thousand tonnes of gray cement in September 2026, up 2.0% from a year earlier. Shipments to the home market rose 1.1%, and all figures are provisional.

Why Does Cement Output Matter?

Cement goes into almost every building, road and bridge, so its output gives an early read on construction. A steady rise suggests housing and public works are growing.

World.title: Chile Industry Falls, Shops Beat Forecasts
World.content:
Railway tracks at the shunting yard of the Chagres smelter in Chile, as described by the photographer. File photo, 1 August 2026; it does not show Centinela. Photo: Santurwar, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

CHILE · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Chile, the world’s largest copper producer, saw its statistics office publish three activity reports on Friday 30 October 2026.

Industrial Production It fell 2.7% in September from a year earlier; forecast was a 1.9% rise, August was -5.7%.

Manufacturing Production It rose 2.0% in September; forecast was 3.0%, August was -2.6%.

Retail Sales Retail activity rose 4.4% from a year earlier (forecast 3.6%, August 3.4%) and 1.0% on the month (forecast -0.3%, August 1.2%).

Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

Chile’s factories grew in September 2026, but its mines dragged the whole industrial sector down, and shoppers spent more than analysts expected. The National Statistics Institute (INE, the government agency that counts the economy) published all three reports on Friday 30 October 2026.

For US investors, the split matters because it shows a Chile that is strong at home and weak where the money is made, in copper. Our report on Chile’s copper output falling 15% in September explains the mining side in detail.

Industrial Production Misses by 4.6 Points

Industrial Production fell 2.7% in September from September 2025, according to INE. Economists had expected a rise of 1.9%, so the result missed by 4.6 percentage points, although it was better than August’s fall of 5.7%.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The index has three parts: mining, manufacturing, and electricity, gas and water. Mining fell 8.7% and took 3.7 percentage points off the total, while manufacturing and utilities both grew.

INE adjusts the data for the calendar as well. September 2026 had one more working day than September 2025, and once that and the usual seasonal swings are removed, output was 3.7% lower than a year earlier but 2.7% higher than in August.

Manufacturing Production Turns Positive

Manufacturing Production rose 2.0% in September, against a forecast of 3.0% and a fall of 2.6% in August. It is a miss on paper, yet it is a clear turn from August, and INE says it was 0.7% higher than in August after seasonal adjustment.

The biggest push came from drinks, up 12.5%, which INE links to more bottled wine sold to foreign buyers. Food products grew 3.2% and paper products 4.7%, while metal products, a group that includes steel parts, fell 7.2% because fewer power-sector projects were being contracted.

Electricity, gas and water together grew 0.8%. INE credits more electricity from hydroelectric plants and more water supplied to homes.

Retail Sales Beat Both Forecasts

Retail Sales were the bright spot, and INE’s retail activity index rose 4.4% from a year earlier. That compares with a forecast of 3.6% and 3.4% in August.

On the month, after seasonal adjustment, retail grew 1.0% when analysts had expected a 0.3% fall. August had risen 1.2%, so retail has now grown on the month two times in a row.

Online and household goods led the gain. Sales by mail and internet were up 20.3%, spare parts and tires for cars rose 15.6%, and electronics and home equipment climbed 8.4%.

Supermarkets were the soft spot, with sales up only 0.4% in the year. INE’s wider commerce index, which also counts wholesale and car dealers, rose 2.7%, with every one of its three branches growing.

Why the Numbers Split

Mining explains almost the whole industrial miss. INE named a temporary stoppage at one large company and lower ore grades at several mines, which means the rock now holds less copper and miners must move more of it for the same metal.

Copper mines made 15.1% less metal in September than a year earlier, the third monthly fall in a row. Shoppers, by contrast, have a central bank that held its key rate at 4.5% on Tuesday 27 October, as our report on the rate decision shows.

Chile’s jobless rate stands at 9.8% for the third quarter, which tempers the picture, as our coverage of the truckers’ strike and unemployment explains. Strong spending next to weak hiring is a gap worth watching, and INE does not explain it.

What It Means for You

If you hold Chile through US funds, the numbers say the economy is not collapsing, but the earnings engine is copper, and copper volumes are shrinking. The iShares MSCI Chile ETF (ECH), a US-listed fund that tracks large Chilean companies, closed at US$35.51 on Thursday 29 October, and the report is unlikely to change that story on its own.

The peso ended Thursday near 988 per US dollar, so 1,000 pesos are worth about US$1.01. Weak mining output means fewer dollars flowing in, which can pressure the peso, while a copper price that stays high, as Chile’s state copper commission now projects, softens the blow to the budget.

US companies that sell consumer goods or online services in Chile get a positive signal, since online sales are growing at about 20% a year. Travelers face no change from these reports.

What Would Change the Picture

A restart at the stopped mine and better ore grades would lift mining quickly, and the industrial index would turn positive again. A further fall in copper output in October, or a drop in copper prices, would deepen the gap with manufacturing and shops.

On the shopping side, a rise in unemployment or in the cost of credit would cool spending. The next big check is the Imacec, the central bank’s monthly estimate of the whole economy, which will show how much of this split reaches national growth.

What Is Not Known

It is not known which company paused mining or for how long, because INE did not name it. The September figures are provisional and INE may revise them when it publishes October data.

It is also unclear whether the jump in retail is a lasting trend. INE gives no reason why supermarkets grew only 0.4% while online sales rose about 20%.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Did Chile’s Industrial Production Do in September?

It fell 2.7% from a year earlier, against a forecast rise of 1.9%. Mining fell 8.7%, while manufacturing and utilities grew.

Did Chile’s Manufacturing Production Grow in September?

Yes, it rose 2.0% from a year earlier, below the 3.0% forecast but a turn from August’s fall of 2.6%. Drinks, led by wine exports, were the main driver.

How Strong Were Chile’s Retail Sales in September?

INE’s retail activity index rose 4.4% from a year earlier and 1.0% on the month, both better than forecast. Online sales grew about 20%, while supermarkets rose only 0.4%.

World.content:
PORT LOUIS · Culture

A public holiday on 2 November, Diwali on 8 November and a month of concerts across Mauritius. The month, day by day.

PORT LOUIS — This monthly guide is for people who live here or are staying for weeks, not for a one-weekend tourist. It gathers the confirmed things to do in Port Louis November 2026 that are worth crossing the city for, with dates, venues, prices and ticket sources from the Otayo ticketing platform.

The month opens with a public holiday, then turns to Diwali and a run of concerts. Many of the biggest concerts this month are outside Port Louis, so the guide names them as island-wide options when they justify the trip.

2 to 8 November: A Holiday, Food and Diwali

Monday 2 November 2026 Arrival of Indentured Labourers Day (public holiday) Mauritius nationwide The day remembers the arrival of indentured labourers from India, which began at Aapravasi Ghat in Port Louis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is a public holiday, so many offices and businesses close.

Saturday 7 November 2026, 11:00 to 23:00 Gourmet Experience 2026 Le Château de Labourdonnais, a historic estate in the north · From MUR 450 (about US$9.50, at about 47.5 rupees per US$, 29 October 2026) · Otayo A full-day food and drink event in the grounds of a historic estate. It is outside Port Louis, so plan transport in advance.

Saturday 7 November 2026, 7:00 p.m. Festival Seggae Zwe Anjalay Coopen Stadium, north Mauritius · From MUR 500 (about US$10.50) · Otayo Seggae blends séga, Mauritius’s traditional music, with reggae. It is outside the capital, so check your return transport before booking.

Sunday 8 November 2026 Diwali Mauritius nationwide Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is a public holiday in Mauritius. Because it falls on a Sunday, check with your employer about any substitute weekday, as we could not confirm one.

14 November: Diwali Night

Saturday 14 November 2026, 6:00 p.m. to 2:00 a.m. The Grand Diwali Night 2026 Valentina Hall, Phoenix · From MUR 1,000 (about US$21) · Otayo An evening-to-2-a.m. celebration at an events hall in Phoenix, a town in central Mauritius.

19 to 22 November: Dance and Spectacle

Saturday 21 November 2026, 2:00 to 11:30 p.m. Takeover: Telfairian × Afro Bros The Residence Hotel, east coast · From MUR 800 (about US$17) · Otayo A day-and-night event at a hotel on the east coast, far from Port Louis. Prices on the ticket page rise above the entry level, so check before you buy.

Saturday 21 November 2026, 6:30 to 10:30 p.m. Le Grand Spectacle J&J Auditorium, Phoenix · From MUR 500 (about US$10.50) · Otayo A stage show at the J&J Auditorium in Phoenix, listed with a four-hour evening slot.

28 and 29 November: Concerts

Saturday 28 November 2026, 7:00 to 9:00 p.m. Rock Meets Classical Serge Constantin Theatre, Vacoas · From MUR 800 (about US$17) · Otayo A rock and classical-music crossover evening in a theatre in Vacoas, a town in central Mauritius. A second show runs on Sunday 29 November from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m., also from MUR 800.

Saturday 28 November 2026, 7:30 p.m. Hariharan Live Trianon Convention Centre, Trianon · From MUR 1,500 (about US$32) · Otayo Hariharan is a well-known Indian playback singer, the voice behind many Bollywood and Tamil film songs.

Sunday 29 November 2026, 3:30 p.m. Anointed Gospel Concert with Gino Belloguet and guests J&J Auditorium, Phoenix · From MUR 500 (about US$10.50) · Otayo A gospel concert in the J&J Auditorium on a Sunday afternoon. Otayo lists Gino Belloguet and special guests.

Planning Your Port Louis in November

Two public holidays fall this month: Monday 2 November for the Arrival of Indentured Labourers and Sunday 8 November for Diwali. Because Diwali falls on a Sunday, check with your employer about any substitute weekday, as we could not confirm one.

Otayo, a Mauritian ticketing platform, lists every event in this guide. Prices are “from” prices in Mauritian rupees (MUR), and higher seat or VIP tiers cost more.

Almost all of the month’s events are outside Port Louis, in the north, in Phoenix, Vacoas and Trianon, or on the east coast. Plan transport before you go and agree a fare or book a driver for the return trip.

We could not confirm any film-festival programme in Port Louis for November 2026, so this guide lists none.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the main things to do around Port Louis in November 2026?

The listed highlights are Gourmet Experience on 7 November, The Grand Diwali Night on 14 November and the Hariharan concert on 28 November. Most are outside the capital.

Is Diwali a public holiday in Mauritius in 2026?

Yes. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November 2026. We could not confirm a substitute weekday, so check with your employer.

Where can I buy tickets for November events in Mauritius?

Otayo, a Mauritian ticketing platform, lists the events in this guide, with prices in Mauritian rupees.

Is Monday 2 November 2026 a public holiday in Mauritius?

Yes. Monday 2 November is the day marking the arrival of indentured labourers.

World.title: Four Detained in Costa Rica Over Sedative-Spiked Rides From Bars
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities detained four men yesterday who are suspected of offering rides to people leaving bars in San José, drugging them with a sedative and then using their phones and bank cards to empty their accounts. Agents from the theft section of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) and prosecutors from the specialized cybercrime unit raided homes in Grecia, in Alajuela province, and in Aserrí, south of the capital.

The suspects are two brothers plus two other men and authorities have identified eight victims so far. Losses are put at about 10 million colones, or roughly $22,000. According to investigators, the suspects approached people who had been drinking outside bars in San Jose during the early morning hours and offered them a private transport service. During the ride, the victims were allegedly given water mixed with drops of clonazepam, a prescription sedative.

Once the drug took effect, the group allegedly took the victims’ cell phones and bank cards. Investigators say the cards were then used for purchases and cash withdrawals, and the victims were left next to the road. The four men are under investigation for alleged computer fraud and aggravated robbery however they have not been charged and the case remains open.

Authorities have not disclosed which bars or neighborhoods were involved, the ages of the suspects, or whether any of the victims were foreign visitors. The case is the latest in a series of thefts in Costa Rica that rely on speed and surprise rather than force, including one this week in which thieves emptied a rental car in eight minutes.

Anyone who believes they were targeted in a similar way can report it to the OIJ through its confidential line at 800-8000-645.

World.title: Costa Rica Celebrates National Masquerade Day With Traditional Parades and Music
World.content:
Costa Rica is celebrating one of its most colorful traditions this weekend as giant masks, lively marching bands and characters from local folklore take over streets and public spaces across Costa Rica. National Traditional Masquerade Day, observed every October 31, brings communities together for a celebration that has been part of Costa Rican culture for generations.

The Ministry of Culture and Youth has organized a series of free activities for today and tomorrow including street parades, musical performances, workshops and cultural exhibitions. The main celebration is scheduled for Friday in downtown San José, where three groups of traditional masked performers and musicians began marching at 11 a.m. from Plaza de la Democracia, Parque Morazán and the Simón Bolívar Urban Nature Park.

The groups then make their way through the capital before gathering around noon at the National Center for Culture (CENAC), across from Parque España. The event is open to the public and will feature the oversized masks and traditional music that have made these celebrations a familiar part of life in Costa Rica.

Unlike Halloween, which shares the same date, Costa Rica’s masquerade tradition has its own history and characters. The masks represent figures from local legends, including La Segua, La Llorona, the Devil, Death and La Giganta, along with a collection of other characters that have entertained and occasionally frightened generations of children.

Some of the figures tower over spectators, with enormous heads and exaggerated facial features made from papier-mâché, fiberglass or other materials. Beneath the masks are performers who dance, chase spectators and interact with the crowds as traditional marching bands, known locally as cimarronas, provide the music.

The bands typically include trumpets, trombones, drums and other instruments, producing the loud, energetic rhythms associated with Costa Rican town festivals. For many Costa Ricans, the sound of a cimarrona approaching is enough to bring back childhood memories of neighborhood celebrations, school festivals and the excitement of watching the masked characters move through the streets.

The tradition has roots in colonial-era celebrations, particularly in Cartago, where Spanish festivities gradually mixed with Indigenous customs and local folklore. Over time, communities such as Barva, Aserrí, Escazú and Cartago became important centers for the creation and performance of traditional masquerades.

The modern national celebration began in Aserrí on October 31, 1996, when local cultural organizers and artisans held a parade to promote Costa Rican traditions at a time when Halloween was becoming increasingly popular. The following year, the government officially declared October 31 National Traditional Masquerade Day through an Executive Decree.

The celebration received further recognition in 2022 when Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly declared traditional masquerades a national symbol under Law 10239, acknowledging their importance to o cultural identity. Today, the tradition remains an important source of work for artisans who design, sculpt and paint the masks, often teaching their techniques to younger generations.

Acting Culture Minister Sally Molina Villalobos has emphasized that the celebrations are not simply about entertainment. They also recognize the craftsmanship and dedication required to keep the tradition alive. This weekend’s activities extend well beyond San José. In Cartago, a free masquerade and cimarrona festival is scheduled for Friday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Plaza Mayor, with traditional performances and workshops.

In Limón, the Civic Center for Peace will offer mask painting, traditional Costa Rican games, storytelling and a parade accompanied by a cimarrona on Friday afternoon, from 4 p.m. to approximately 6:20 p.m. The Public Library in Liberia, Guanacaste, will host a free afternoon of Costa Rican legends on Friday from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m., inviting community members to share traditional stories.

On Saturday, the celebration continues in Escazú, where Escazú Village will host free activities from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. The program includes traditional masked characters, a cimarrona performance, children’s mask-making workshops and costume competitions. Families attending the Escazú event will also find activities designed to introduce younger children to the history and artistic traditions behind the masks.

In the San Carlos area, the community of Marsella will hold traditional games, mask-making activities and a neighborhood parade on Saturday morning. Other cultural institutions are participating with exhibitions and special events, including an artisan mask display at the José Figueres Ferrer Cultural and Historical Center in San Ramón, which continues through November 6.

Not every event is free. The National Band of Guanacaste will perform a special concert at the National Theater in San José on Saturday at 7 p.m., with general admission tickets priced at ₡4,000 and discounted tickets at ₡2,500 for students and older adults. The weekend’s celebrations come at a time when Costa Rica continues working to preserve its traditional arts and customs while welcoming cultural influences from abroad.

For residents and visitors unfamiliar with masquerades, the events offer a chance to experience a side of Costa Rica that goes beyond beaches, rainforests and national parks. The colorful masks, lively music and interaction between performers and spectators are a reminder that our cultural heritage remains an important part of everyday life, particularly in smaller towns where these t

World.title: Lufthansa to Drop Costa Rica Route in 2027 as Sister Airline Adds More Flights
World.content:
German airline Lufthansa will stop operating its flights to Costa Rica in December 2027, but travelers will not lose the connection to Europe. Instead, sister airline Discover Airlines will take over the Frankfurt–San José route and increase service from five to six flights per week. The change, announced on October 29, will take effect on December 14, 2027, with Discover Airlines operating flights to Juan Santamaría International Airport using Airbus A350-900 aircraft.

The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) confirmed that Lufthansa will continue operating the route through December 13, 2027, before handing it over to Discover, which belongs to the same airline group. For anyone flying here, the important point is that the route is not disappearing. Lufthansa Group will continue to fly to Costa Rica from Germany, although the airline operating the flights will change.

However, there is one important difference in the new schedule. Of the six weekly flights, four will operate nonstop between Frankfurt and San José. The other two will follow a route that takes passengers from Frankfurt to San José, continues to Belize City and then returns to Germany. That means passengers leaving Costa Rica for Frankfurt will need to pay attention when booking. Although the total number of weekly flights will increase, two of the return services will include a stop in Belize.

The change follows negotiations between the ICT and Lufthansa Group that began more than a year ago. Tourism officials said the goal was to move the route to an airline more focused on vacation travelers, which better matches Costa Rica’s tourism market. Discover Airlines specializes in leisure travel and operates from Frankfurt and Munich, serving destinations popular with tourists. It is part of Lufthansa Group, allowing passengers to continue using Frankfurt as a connection point for other destinations in Europe and beyond.

Another significant change will be the aircraft itself. Discover plans to introduce the Airbus A350-900 on the Costa Rica route, replacing the aircraft currently used by Lufthansa. The A350 is a modern long-distance aircraft designed to carry passengers across continents with improved fuel efficiency. Discover expects to receive its first A350 in June 2027 and a second aircraft in December, when the Costa Rica service is scheduled to begin.

The airline is gradually expanding its long-distance fleet, with additional A350 aircraft expected in 2028. The announcement comes as Lufthansa is already increasing its presence in Costa Rica. For the current European winter season, which began October 25, the airline expanded its Frankfurt service from three to five weekly flights and introduced Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft with its newer Allegris cabin design.

Germany remains Costa Rica’s largest source of European tourists. According to ICT figures, 54,794 German visitors arrived in Costa Rica between January and September 2026, an increase of 8.1% compared with the same period in 2025. The Frankfurt connection is particularly important because it serves both German vacationers and travelers connecting through one of Europe’s busiest international airports.

For Costa Rica’s tourism industry, the planned increase in weekly service provides another opportunity to attract European visitors, especially during the busy winter travel season. Passengers planning trips for late 2027 should keep an eye on the new schedules as Discover Airlines updates its booking system. The airline has confirmed the planned route changes, but final operating details and aircraft assignments may still be adjusted before the service begins.

World.title: High Tides Flood Homes in Costa Rica’s Puntarenas
World.content:
High tides flooded homes in Puntarenas on Thursday, October 29, with authorities warning that elevated tides could continue along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast through Saturday, October 31. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) reported flooding in Barrio El Carmen and the community of 20 de Noviembre in Chacarita.

Seawater entered homes, and photographs from the affected areas showed flooded patios and corridors, with furniture and household belongings standing in water. Members of the Puntarenas Municipal Emergency Committee visited the communities to assess damage, identify families’ needs and coordinate assistance. Initial reports did not specify the number of homes affected or provide an estimate of financial losses.

Thursday’s flooding followed repeated high tides earlier in the week. Residents of El Carmen described moving appliances and other belongings off the floor and staying awake to monitor water entering their homes. Flooding was also reported earlier in the week at Playa Zancudo in Golfito and Playa Preciosa in Puerto Jiménez, extending the effects beyond the city of Puntarenas.

The University of Costa Rica’s Oceanographic Information Module, known as MIO-Cimar, warned that the period of unusually high tides could last through Saturday. The CNE urged residents of coastal communities with a history of tidal flooding to watch local conditions and take steps to protect their belongings.

The conditions are associated with spring tides, the higher tides that occur around the new and full moon when the gravitational effects of the Sun and Moon reinforce one another. These events occur regularly and are unrelated to the spring season. MIO-Cimar coordinator Rodney Mora said warmer Pacific waters associated with El Niño were also contributing to higher sea levels, worsening the effects in vulnerable coastal communities. Water expands as it warms, allowing high tides to reach farther into low-lying areas.

El Niño does not cause spring tides, but the combination can increase the risk of flooding along the coast. Mora also warned that similar conditions could recur in November and December, urging coastal residents to prepare for further episodes.

World.title: Costa Rica Gas Prices Jump Sharply as Regular Fuel Becomes More Expensive Than Premium
World.content:
Drivers in Costa Rica will soon be paying considerably more at the pump after the public services regulator approved yet another round of fuel price increases, including a 12.38% jump in regular gasoline that will make it more expensive than premium fuel. The Public Services Regulatory Authority (ARESEP) approved the adjustment a couple of days ago, with the new prices announced yesterday. Regular gasoline will increase by ₡89 per liter, climbing from ₡719 to ₡808, while premium gasoline will rise by ₡42, from ₡764 to ₡806.

That creates an unusual situation at Costa Rica’s gas stations. Regular gasoline, traditionally the cheaper option, will cost ₡2 more per liter than premium, while diesel will also reach ₡808 following an increase of ₡23. The higher prices have been approved but will not take effect until the regulatory resolution is published in the official government newspaper, La Gaceta. Under the resolution, the new rates begin the following day. An exact implementation date had not been confirmed as of Friday morning.

At the new price, filling a 40-liter (10.6-gallon) tank with regular gasoline will cost ₡32,320 (about $71), up from ₡28,760 (about $64) today, an increase of ₡3,560 (about $8) per fill-up and with regular. Drivers filling a larger 60-liter (15.9-gallon) tank will pay ₡5,340 more than before.

For those who commute daily, operate delivery vehicles or regularly travel between Costa Rica’s major cities, the additional expense could quickly add up. The increases are not limited to gasoline and diesel. Households that use propane gas for cooking will also face higher costs, with the price of a standard 25-pound cylinder rising by ₡549, from ₡7,172 to ₡7,721.

ARESEP estimates that approximately 53% of Costa Rican households use this type of cooking gas. Restaurants, small food businesses and other commercial establishments that depend on propane will also be affected. The regulator says the adjustments reflect rising international fuel costs, which have been influenced by instability in global energy markets.

Costa Rica imports all of its finished petroleum fuels, making domestic prices especially sensitive to changes in international supply, shipping costs and the exchange rate between the colón and the U.S. dollar. Energy officials pointed to disruptions involving oil shipments from the Middle East, declining global inventories and higher refining and transportation costs. Diesel supplies have faced particular pressure as demand and supply conditions fluctuate internationally.

The latest adjustment was calculated using fuel purchases made by the Costa Rican Petroleum Refinery (RECOPE) between September 11 and October 8. The exchange rate also played a role. ARESEP used an average rate of ₡456.66 per dollar for the new calculation, compared with ₡450.41 in the previous adjustment. Because fuel purchases are made in dollars, that difference increases the amount paid in colones even when the international price of a product remains unchanged.

For Costa Rican businesses, higher fuel prices can create expenses that extend well beyond the cost of filling a vehicle. Transportation companies, agricultural producers, delivery services and businesses that distribute goods throughout Costa Rica depend heavily on diesel and gasoline. When those costs rise, companies may face pressure to adjust their operating budgets or eventually pass some of the increases on to customers.

Tourism operators could also feel the effects. Rental car companies, shuttle services and tour providers frequently travel long distances between Juan Santamaría International Airport, the Central Valley and popular destinations such as La Fortuna, Manuel Antonio, Tamarindo and the southern Pacific coast.

Tourists coming here and are renting cars will find the same regulated fuel prices as Costa Rican motorists. However, any increase in tour prices, transportation fares or rental rates would depend on decisions by individual businesses and where applicable, additional regulatory approvals.

The latest adjustment comes after earlier fuel increases in October, adding to transportation expenses as Costa Rica approaches the busy end-of-year holiday and tourism season. The approved changes also highlight how fuel prices can move differently depending on the type of petroleum product. Although regular gasoline is typically cheaper than premium, international market conditions and the formulas used to calculate domestic prices can occasionally reverse that relationship.

For those who don’t have a diesel car, once the new rates become effective, premium gasoline will actually be slightly cheaper than regular gasoline, but you should still follow the fuel specifications recommended by your vehicle manufacturer. The regulator’s decision covers nearly two million vehicles circulating in Costa Rica, including private cars, motorcycles, buses, trucks and other commercial transportation.

While our government regulates retail fuel prices, those prices are reviewed periodically and can increase or decrease depending on the cost of imported petroleum products and other factors included in the pricing formula. For now, drivers have a short period before the latest adjustment takes effect. Once the new prices are officially published and implemented, a liter of regular gasoline and diesel will both cost ₡808, marking another increase in the cost of getting around Costa Rica.

World.title: Heading Out for Halloween in Costa Rica? Expect More Police on Patrol
World.content:
Heading to a costume party, a beach bash or a masquerade parade this Saturday? Expect to see more police than usual. Costa Rica’s national police are stepping up patrols across our country for Halloween and they will concentrate on the places where crowds gather. The Public Security Ministry said officers will focus on cemeteries, churches, shopping centers and the streets around bars hosting costume parties.

The goal is to prevent vandalism, spot unauthorized parties and head off trouble at large gatherings. When the national police first outlined the plan, it said it would deploy 1,500 officers from today through Sunday. The ministry’s latest statement, issued yesterday, did not give a number of officers.

Because halloween falls on a Saturday, many parties start Friday night, and that three-day window is meant to cover them. Why cemeteries and churches? Police said incidents in past years, including vandalism and rituals at cemeteries, are the reason officers will patrol them through the weekend. César Anchía, deputy director general of the national police, outlined the weekend operations.

If you’re going out, expect police at the party too. Themed Halloween events and other mass gatherings will see preventive checks and patrols at venues and meeting points. Part of the aim is to catch parties held without permits. Shopping centers, which draw families in costume on Halloween, are also on the patrol list.

If you’re driving, watch for the Caravana del Payaso, or Clown Caravan, a Halloween ride that draws hundreds of motorcyclists. Police will watch the route and the gathering points, and the ministry said highway patrols are meant to prevent crashes. Give riders room and allow extra time where the caravan passes.

Taking kids trick-or-treating? Police are asking parents to stay with their children and keep them in sight the whole time they go door to door. Before you head home, make sure the car you get into is the ride you actually booked. Lat night, the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) said it had detained four men suspected of drugging and robbing people outside bars and nightclubs in San José.

According to the OIJ, one of the suspects allegedly posed as the ride-hailing driver victims had requested, then offered them drinks laced with a sedative. Investigators said other members of the group then withdrew cash and moved money out of victims’ accounts and spent it on goods and services, including fuel.

Saturday is also Costa Rica’s National Masquerade Day, when towns celebrate with giant-headed mascareros, cimarrona bands and dancing in the streets. Police said those community events fall under the same security operation. In beach towns, Halloween runs all weekend. Tamarindo has costume surfing, parades and beach parties on the calendar. Big crowds also draw thieves, so keep valuables with you and out of parked cars, where a rental can be emptied in minutes. In an emergency, call 911.

Halloween has grown steadily in Costa Rica alongside our own masquerade tradition, blending a centuries-old holiday with local customs. Authorities are betting that a visible police presence will keep this year’s celebrations safe for everyone who takes part.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Cambronero Bridge to Reopen
World.content:
The Cambronero bridge on Route 1 is scheduled to reopen Tuesday, November 3, restoring traffic through a stretch of the Inter-American Highway closed since a truck damaged the structure in September. The reopening is planned for noon, nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. The bridge is at kilometer 71, on the road connecting San Ramón, Alajuela, with Esparza, Puntarenas.

The crossing has been closed since the night of September 7, when a tractor-trailer struck the modular steel bridge. Crews had to dismantle parts of the structure, replace damaged components and remove and reinstall the bridge deck. Before those repairs could begin, workers built a support tower to hold the bridge’s weight while damaged pieces were removed. Some parts of that temporary support had to be manufactured specifically for the work.

Additional work will continue after the bridge reopens, but those remaining tasks are not expected to interrupt traffic. Drivers should slow down and use caution around crews at the site. The reopening will restore passage through Cambronero while preparations continue for a permanent solution to the ground instability affecting this section of Route 1.

Bids for that project are under review, with construction expected to begin in early 2027. The planned work includes stabilizing the slope, removing the modular bridge and restoring the road’s two lanes. A possible third lane is also being studied, but it has not been approved for construction.

World.title: Tamarindo Celebrates Halloween Weekend With Costume Surfing, Parades and Beach Parties
World.content:
Tamarindo is getting ready for a Halloween weekend that promises everything from surfers riding waves in costumes to trick-or-treating, costume contests, live music and beach parties. The popular Guanacaste destination will host the fifth annual Tamarindo Halloween Fest, with its main celebrations taking place this Friday and Saturday.

Organized by the Tamarindo Development Association (ADIT), the festival brings together local families, tourists, businesses and community organizations for two days of activities designed to offer something for just about everyone. There will be events for children, contests for pets, a nighttime running race and plenty of entertainment for adults looking to celebrate Halloween at the beach.

The celebration has grown since it began in 2022, with Tamarindo’s hotels, restaurants and local businesses joining the festivities. Organizers hope the event will also bring more people to the community before Costa Rica’s busy tourism season gets underway. This year, Halloween falls on a Saturday, giving everyone a full weekend to enjoy the celebrations without having to rush home the next morning.

The main family activities begin Friday at 5 p.m. with a costume parade through downtown Tamarindo, starting near Hotel Tamarindo Diria and continuing toward Parque Oneida, where much of the evening’s entertainment will take place. Children and adults are encouraged to dress up, with costume competitions planned for kids and families. Even dogs will have their chance to compete, as organizers invite pet owners to bring their four-legged companions dressed in Halloween outfits.

The Friday celebration will feature a crazy hair competition, trick-or-treating, music and activities for younger children. The traditional Payasos Los Alegres will also join the parade, bringing a touch of Costa Rican entertainment to the festivities. For those who prefer something a little scarier, Journey School will operate a haunted house at Parque Oneida beginning at 6 p.m. Admission to the haunted house carries a fee, with proceeds supporting scholarships for students at the school.

Those looking for food will find local vendors participating in the Tama Market, offering a variety of dishes and refreshments throughout the evening. A dance competition will add another element to the celebration, with participants performing routines inspired by Halloween characters and popular horror-themed entertainment. Organizers are encouraging groups to put together their most creative performances for a chance to win prizes.

Friday will also feature a recreational 5-kilometer (3.1-mile) race organized by Tama Run. The event combines exercise with Halloween fun, rewarding runners who show up wearing the most creative costumes. After the family celebrations, Tamarindo’s nightlife will take over. Crazy Monkey will host its Haunted Paradise party on Friday beginning at 9 p.m., featuring several DJs and three stages with dancehall, reggaeton and electronic music.

The festivities continue Saturday morning with a free Halloween reading event at the Tamarindo Children’s Community Library. From 10:30 a.m. until 12:30 p.m., children can enjoy themed stories and collect candy. One of the weekend’s most unusual events takes place Saturday afternoon when surfers head into the Pacific Ocean wearing Halloween costumes.

The costume surfing event is scheduled from 3:30 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. in front of Witch’s Rock Surf Camp, bringing together local surfers, instructors, residents and visitors for an afternoon of waves, music and prizes. Participants will be judged in different categories, adding a playful twist to a sport that has helped make Tamarindo one of Costa Rica’s best-known surfing destinations.

Several local surfing organizations are participating, including the Tamarindo Surf Association, the Tamarindo Sports Committee and the North Pacific Surf Association. For anyone who would rather watch than paddle out, the beach will provide a chance to see surfers attempt to catch waves while dressed in costumes not normally associated with the ocean.

Saturday evening will bring another round of parties and competitions. Sharky’s is planning a Halloween celebration with $1,500 in costume prizes, while Iguana Surf and NAIA restaurant will hold a sunset gathering featuring music and additional costume contests. A pickleball tournament organized by 15 Love Tamarindo is also part of the festival’s activities, with prizes that include a two-night hotel stay for two people.

Beyond the entertainment, the festival is intended to support Tamarindo’s tourism businesses during a traditionally slower period of the year. Hotels including Pasatiempo, Mar Rey, Hideaway Costa Rica and Las Guapas are offering special accommodation promotions, with some deals extending into November.

Restaurants and shops are also participating, giving everyone more reasons to spend the weekend in town. Several beachwear and fashion retailers have announced discounts ranging from 10% to 70%. Elizabeth Cole, president of the Tamarindo Development Association, said the goal is to make the community a destination people associate with Halloween celebrations in Costa Rica.

The combination of beaches, restaurants, nightlife and family entertainment makes Tamarindo well suited for a festival that appeals to different age groups, while providing additional business for local merchants ahead of the high season. Although many of the community activities are free, some attractions, races and private parties may require advance registration or paid admission.

Anyone planning to attend should check individual event details, particularly for nighttime entertainment and competitions with limited participation. The main family celebration at Parque Oneida runs from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. Friday, while the Saturday program offers activities from the morning through late evening.

For travelers already visiting Guanacaste, Halloween weekend provides another reason to spend time in Tamarindo. And for those living in Costa Rica who want something different from the usual Halloween party, watching costumed surfers catch waves in the Pacific might be difficult to beat.

The complete schedule, registration details and any last-minute changes are available through the Tamarindo Development Association’s official website and its social media accounts.

World.title: Quadruple Murder: Police identify four victims of Coastal Plain Highway massacre, including 16-year-old boy; five men detained as investigators probe possible links to recent shootings
World.content:
Quadruple Murder: Police identify four victims of Coastal Plain Highway massacre, including 16-year-old boy; five men detained as investigators probe possible links to recent shootings

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have officially confirmed the identities of four persons murdered in Friday morning’s deadly shooting along the Coastal Plain Highway, including a 16-year-old boy, as new information obtained by Breaking Belize News raises questions about possible connections to Thursday’s murder of 19-year-old Dodrick Madrill and what sources suggest may be an internal gang conflict involving a struggle for leadership of the “Through The Park Gang”.

The victims have been identified as 16-year-old David Usher of Freedom Street, Belize City; 33-year-old Lloyd Leslie of Armadillo Street, Belize City; 23-year-old Robert Gladden of Freedom Street, Belize City; and 23-year-old Dayton Palacio, also of Freedom Street.

During Friday evening’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed that the Major Crimes Unit launched its investigation around 8:15 a.m. after receiving reports of a shooting between Miles 21 and 22 of the Coastal Plain Highway.

Responding officers discovered a red Ford Escape overturned with numerous apparent bullet holes. Three men were found unresponsive at the scene, while a fourth victim, identified as Palacio, was transported to the Southern Regional Hospital, where he was subsequently pronounced dead.

Police have since intercepted a vehicle of interest travelling toward Belize City and detained five Belize City men for questioning. No firearms were recovered from the intercepted vehicle.

However, a potentially significant connection has emerged between two of Friday’s murder victims and 19-year-old Dodrick Salvador Miguel Madrill, who was gunned down on Freedom Street in Belize City on Thursday morning.

Breaking Belize News has established that three of the five men murdered across the two incidents were jointly charged in the same firearms case in February 2025.

According to a Breaking Belize News court report published on February 1, 2025, Madrill was charged alongside Robert Lincoln Gladden, then 22, Dayton Daniel Palacio, then 21, and Emily Angelica Lopez, 49, following the discovery of an unlicensed 9mm pistol and 13 live rounds of ammunition inside a residence on Freedom Street.

Madrill, who was 18 at the time, pleaded guilty and accepted responsibility for the weapon, while Gladden, Palacio and Lopez pleaded not guilty. Madrill was subsequently remanded to prison pending sentencing.

The previous case establishes a documented association between Madrill, Gladden and Palacio, who have now been murdered in separate shootings occurring less than 24 hours apart.

The connection is particularly noteworthy amid growing concerns about possible retaliatory violence and divisions within criminal groups.

A source who spoke to Breaking Belize News suggests that the recent killings may be connected to an internal dispute involving persons associated with the same gang.

According to the source, the violence may stem from a struggle for power and leadership within the group rather than a conventional conflict between rival gangs. However, the source stressed that the information remains unconfirmed, and BBN has not independently established the motive behind the killings.

Interestingly, during Friday’s police briefing, Smith also raised the possibility of internal gang conflicts and leadership struggles while discussing the recent violence.

Asked whether the killings were retaliatory or connected to other recent shootings, Smith acknowledged that investigators had not established a definitive link but suggested that police were considering the broader pattern of violence.

“We are not so daft to think that there is no nexus between these incidents,” Smith remarked, while emphasizing that police could not officially confirm a connection.

She explained that gang violence is not always the result of rivalry between opposing groups and can sometimes originate from disputes among members of the same organization.

“When it reaches a situation where there is an internal conflict, or a struggle for leadership, or an implosion, that makes policing these incidents even more difficult,” Smith explained.

She noted that individuals involved in such internal disputes are often familiar with one another’s movements, territories and methods of operation, making it easier for them to target each other.

While Smith did not confirm that an internal leadership dispute was responsible for the latest killings, her remarks are consistent with one of the possible explanations being examined in connection with the recent bloodshed.

The developments also follow Wednesday’s shooting at a Belmopan residence reportedly associated with paralyzed street figure Ronlee Petillo, which left a 19-year-old woman injured.

When questioned directly about a possible connection between that shooting and Friday’s quadruple murder, Smith acknowledged that police had taken note of the incidents and the individuals involved, but said investigators had not established a motive or confirmed any connection.

Investigators are also reviewing surveillance footage from cameras positioned at the La Democracia junction and another junction connecting the Coastal Plain Highway to southern Belize.

Meanwhile, police have already implemented strategic changes to their deployment and are considering additional measures to prevent further violence.

Smith said the department intends to use every available resource and legal mechanism to pursue those responsible for the recent killings, including individuals who may have assisted the perpetrators before or after the crimes.

The latest murders bring renewed attention to the possibility of an escalating internal conflict among criminal elements, although police have yet to officially determine whether the shootings are connected.

Investigations remain ongoing.

World.title: Belize joins Global initiative to strengthen women’s leadership in Ocean Conservation
World.content:
Belize joins Global initiative to strengthen women’s leadership in Ocean Conservation

By Zoila Palma: Belize has joined Madagascar and 14 other countries in pledging to strengthen women’s leadership in marine conservation and blue economy development through the Women Ocean Guardians Initiative.

The commitment was announced at the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (CBD CoP17), adding Belize to a growing coalition focused on placing women at the forefront of ocean governance and the sustainable management of marine resources.

Minister of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, Orlando Habet, highlighted the important role Belizean women play in protecting the country’s marine environment. “Belize has always punched above its weight in marine conservation,” Habet said. “But our success has never been an accident of geography—it is the result of the dedication, wisdom, and leadership of our women on the coast.”

The latest commitments bring the initiative’s support to more than 50 signed pledges, including 16 governments and over 30 partner organizations. The coalition’s progress is credited to the collective leadership of 75 women ocean guardians from 33 countries.

The initiative seeks to address gaps in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, particularly Target 23, which focuses on gender equality, and Target 3, which aims to protect 30 percent of the world’s land and ocean areas by 2030. Reports indicate that gender-responsive approaches remain among the least advanced areas of the global biodiversity commitments, while inclusive governance and effective management continue to pose challenges to the 30×30 target.

The Women Ocean Guardians Initiative was convened by the Wildlife Conservation Society, Conservation International and the Global Environment Facility (GEF) to create opportunities for women working on the frontlines of conservation to influence decisions and lead marine protection efforts.

GEF CEO Diego Mesa Puyo said the initiative demonstrates the importance of bringing together financing, policy and community leadership. Wildlife Conservation Society Marine 30×30 Director Pamela Castillo also emphasized that women’s participation is essential to achieving global ocean conservation goals, stating, “We cannot protect the ocean without the women ocean guardians.”

The initiative has established three regional hubs covering Southeast Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Africa.

World.title: Mayor Wagner takes Belize City’s voice to the Commonwealth
World.content:
Mayor Wagner takes Belize City’s voice to the Commonwealth

By Zoila Palma: Belize City Mayor Bernard Wagner has called for greater authority, financial resources, and climate resilience for local governments while representing Belize at the Wilton Park Dialogue on Sustainable Urbanisation in Georgetown, Guyana.

The event brought together Commonwealth leaders, policymakers, and urban development experts ahead of the 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

Mayor Wagner who also chairs the Commonwealth Local Government Forum (CLGF), challenged governments to reconsider how cities are financed and empowered to respond to rapid urbanisation and climate change.

Drawing on Belize City’s experiences with flooding, informal settlements, and infrastructure challenges, he emphasized the importance of stronger partnerships between national and municipal governments.

Wagner also highlighted Belize City’s municipal bond initiative and its contribution to the development of Belize’s Municipal Securities Act, pointing to the initiative as an example of how local government innovation can influence national policy. He called for greater municipal autonomy and innovative financing mechanisms to ensure cities have the resources needed to address their development challenges.

Mayor Wagner met with several regional and international urban development leaders, including Guyana’s Minister of Culture, Youth and Sport, Charles Ramson Jr.; Beth Chitekwe-Biti of Slum Dwellers International; urban economist Astrid Haas; Montego Bay Mayor Richard Vernon; and Professor Clyde Phillip of Trinidad and Tobago.

World.title: International News: Flavio Bolsonaro ally blames ChatGPT for deleted ‘President-Elect’ claim
World.content:
International News: Flavio Bolsonaro ally blames ChatGPT for deleted ‘President-Elect’ claim

By Zoila Palma: A close ally of Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro is blaming ChatGPT for language in a now-deleted social media letter in which the right-wing politician described himself as Brazil’s rightful “president-elect.”

The explanation came after Bolsonaro sparked controversy by questioning the legitimacy of the country’s recent presidential election, despite losing to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes.

Bolsonaro initially shared the letter on Wednesday, alleging without evidence that the election had been marred by fraud and presenting himself as the country’s legitimate president-elect.

About an hour later, he deleted the document and posted a revised version, replacing the phrase “president-elect” with “leader of Brazil,” prompting speculation about the sudden change, Reuters report.

Paulo Figueiredo, a right-wing influencer and podcast host who serves as an unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family in the United States, said the wording was mistakenly included during the document’s preparation.

According to Figueiredo, Eduardo Bolsonaro, Flavio’s younger brother and a former congressman, had used ChatGPT to help finalize the letter. He claimed the chatbot incorporated an earlier draft containing the disputed wording, along with an outdated version of Brazil’s coat of arms.

Figueiredo said the errors were only noticed after the document had been distributed to journalists and described the revision as minor.

He maintained, however, that the senator’s position had not changed and that Bolsonaro continued to reject the election result.

World.title: Belize strengthens regional preparedness for El Niño 2026–2027
World.content:
Belize strengthens regional preparedness for El Niño 2026–2027

By Zoila Palma: On October 29, 2026, the Government of Belize, through the Ministry of Economic Transformation, participated in the regional workshops on the 2026–2027 El Niño phenomenon, held under the Regional Action Plan promoted by the General Secretariat of the Central American Integration System (SG-SICA), CEPREDENAC and the Regional Committee for Hydraulic Resources (CRRH), in collaboration with COSEFIN and with support from the World Bank.

The workshops brought together representatives from Ministries of Finance and Economy, regional institutions and development partners to discuss the potential impacts of El Niño, including drought, water shortages, agricultural losses, and the resulting pressures on economic activity and public finances.

Through the leadership of Dr. Osmond Martinez, Minister of Economic Transformation and Pro Tempore President of COSEFIN, Minister Martinez highlighted the importance of taking a coordinated and forward-looking approach to the potential impacts of El Niño, emphasizing that:

“Preparing for climate-related events requires us to look beyond the immediate impacts and consider the wider implications for our economies and public finances. By working together, sharing knowledge and strengthening our financial preparedness, we can better protect our communities, support vulnerable sectors and build resilience across the region,” Martinez said.
