World.title: Poland and UK sign Warsaw Defence Plan to “deter Russian threats”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and the United Kingdom have signed the Warsaw Defence Plan, an agreement to enhance their cooperation on security. The aim, says the British Ministry of Defence, is to “deter Russian threats”. The plan, which follows on from the two countries signing a strategic defence partnership earlier this year, will include joint development and production of defence technologies and military exercises in the Baltic Sea. The UK and Poland share a deep and historical defence partnership. Today, Defence Secretary @WesStreeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan to bring our two nations’ Armed Forces and industries closer together and help ensure collective security in Europe. 🇬🇧🤝🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/IP98D1Qs1L — Ministry of Defence 🇬🇧 (@DefenceHQ) October 27, 2026 “Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century,” said British defence secretary Wes Streeting on a visit to Warsaw. “The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” he added. His Polish counterpart, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, declared that “the Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is now”. Both he and Streeting also emphasised the importance of working together to support Ukraine. Among the aims listed for the plan are collaboration in the development and manufacture of next-generation air-defence missiles, as well as drones and counter-drone technologies. Earlier this year, Poland and the UK, along with Germany, France and Italy, agreed to jointly develop and procure air-defence systems, including missiles and drones. The Warsaw Defence Plan also pledges to “increase defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea”. The two countries will also seek to build upon existing cooperation between their defence industries, including Poland’s purchase of CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles and 100 launchers from MBDA and last year’s strategic partnership on ammunition production between Poland’s PGZ and Britain’s BAE Systems. Poland and the UK have signed a major new defence and security treaty. The agreement includes plans to jointly develop a new air-defence missile, hold large-scale military exercises, and cooperate on countering Russian hybrid attacks https://t.co/cXeYT2u1lw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026 This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security. Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year. In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway. In November, Poland will host the first military exercises organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing. Thousands of personnel from the UK, Poland, France and Germany will test operational readiness for a multinational force to secure a potential future Ukraine peace deal. World.title: Prague to Begin Winter Maintenance of Roads and Sidewalks on November 1
World.content:
Prague will begin its annual winter road maintenance programme on November 1.

Until the end of March, the Technical Administration of Communications (TSK) will be responsible for keeping roads, sidewalks and other public routes accessible to vehicles and pedestrians.

Maintenance priorities are determined by the importance of individual routes for traffic and local residents. Roads and pedestrian areas are divided into several categories, each with specific deadlines for snow and ice clearance.



Residents can check the designated maintenance routes and the type of work planned for each area through the city’s online Winter Maintenance application (Zimní údržba).

Road maintenance is divided into three priority categories. The first covers 1,399 kilometres of the city’s busiest roads, which must be treated within two to four hours of maintenance crews being deployed.

The second category includes 519 kilometres of roads, with a clearance deadline of 12 hours. The third covers another 346 kilometres, where maintenance must be completed within 48 hours after the first- and second-priority routes have been treated.

Sidewalks, cycle paths and other pedestrian routes follow a separate schedule. The first category includes 1,063 kilometres, which must be serviced within 12 hours. The second covers a further 693 kilometres, with work required by 5 p.m. on the day after maintenance of the first category has been completed.

Altogether, Prague’s winter maintenance programme covers 2,264 kilometres of roads and 1,756 kilometres of sidewalks and other pedestrian routes.

From December 1 to March 31, temporary workers will help clear sidewalks in parts of Prague 6 that are more difficult to reach with standard maintenance equipment.

These include Hanspaulka, Baba, Sedlec, the Šárecké Valley and parts of Ořechovka.

World.title: Prague Appears in Apple’s Latest MacBook Pro Commercial
World.content:
Prague has once again provided the backdrop for an Apple advertising campaign.

The American technology company has released a new commercial promoting its latest MacBook Pro, featuring several recognisable locations across the Czech capital.

The two-minute video centres on the Prague Congress Centre, with additional scenes filmed around Vyšehrad and Karlovo náměstí. Although Apple does not identify the locations in the commercial, viewers familiar with Prague will recognise several of the city’s landmarks.



The Congress Centre plays the largest role in the production. Its glass-walled entrance hall, with views of the Nusle Bridge, features in several sequences.

The commercial also shows people working on laptops at long rows of tables on an upper floor, alongside an overhead view of the building’s spiral staircase and its metal sculpture The Sun, created by Czech artist Vladimír Procházka.

The production also moved outdoors, using the historic fortifications of Vyšehrad as a setting. Another location is the park at Karlovo náměstí, where the monument to Czech physician and naturalist Jan Evangelista Purkyně can be seen.

Not all the Prague scenery in the  is entirely authentic. In some sequences, Apple has used computer-generated imagery to modify the views through the Congress Centre’s windows, replacing the familiar city panorama with skyscrapers and mountain landscapes.

The latest production continues Apple’s history of filming s in the Czech Republic.

Two years ago, the company also used Prague locations for an iPhone 16 Pro campaign, which featured the roof of the Prague Congress Centre and the Vyšehrad area, alongside the sandstone formations of the Prachov Rocks in the Bohemian Paradise region.

The new MacBook Pro introduces a touchscreen for the first time in Apple’s laptop range. The device is powered by the company’s M5 Pro and M5 Max processors. In the Czech Republic, prices start at CZK 84,990, with sales scheduled to begin on November 6.

World.title: Guitar Legend Carlos Santana to Return to Czech Republic in 2027
World.content:
Legendary guitarist Carlos Santana will return to the Czech Republic on July 22, 2027, for an outdoor concert in the Castle Gardens of Slavkov u Brna, near Brno.

The ten-time Grammy Award winner will perform as part of his Planet of Free Will Global Tour 2027, bringing more than five decades of music to the Czech audience.

Known for blending rock, blues, jazz and Latin rhythms, Santana has built a distinctive sound that has influenced generations of musicians and listeners.



His performance at the 1969 Woodstock festival helped establish him as an international star, while early albums such as Santana*(1969) and Abraxas (1970) produced classics including “Evil Ways,” “Black Magic Woman” and “Oye Como Va.”

Santana reached another career milestone with the 1999 album Supernatural, which featured collaborations with artists including Rob Thomas. The record became a global hit, spawning the singles “Smooth” and “Maria Maria” and winning nine Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year.

Over his career, Santana has received ten Grammy Awards and three Latin Grammy Awards. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1998, received the Kennedy Center Honors and was ranked 11th on *Rolling Stone* magazine’s list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time.

Despite his long career, Santana continues to release new music and perform internationally. His live shows are known for extended guitar solos, Latin-inspired rhythms and a mix of classic hits and newer material.

Tickets will cost CZK 2,000, plus booking fees.

General ticket sales start on October 30, 2026, at noon, through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

World.title: Prague Metronome Lets People Donate to Charity for Just 50 CZK
World.content:
Prague’s Metronome is taking on a charitable role through a new initiative that allows people to pay for a minute of illumination while supporting one of six nonprofit organizations.

The project, called Puls města (City Pulse), was launched by real estate company PSN, which operates the landmark on Letná Hill. Donations start at 50 Czech crowns, and participants can choose which organization they want to support.



The new initiative connects its lighting system with fundraising, allowing members of the public to contribute through the project’s website.

Six Colors, Six Charitable Causes

Each participating organization is represented by a different color. Red supports the Tereza Maxová Foundation for Children, while light blue represents the Kapka naděje (Drop of Hope) Endowment Fund.

Yellow is associated with Díky, že můžem, an initiative focused on civic engagement and democratic values. Pink represents Pink Crocodile, dark blue supports the AutTalk Endowment Fund, founded by Kateřina Sokolová, and green is dedicated to the Fund for Endangered Children.

Visitors can select a cause and make a contribution directly through the project’s website.

Donations Start at 50 CZK

Contributions range from 50 to 9,999 CZK. Regardless of the amount donated, each payment purchases exactly one minute of illumination. A larger contribution therefore does not extend the lighting time.

The website also displays the amount raised for each organization, allowing donors to follow the campaign’s progress. A virtual queue shows when each participant’s turn is scheduled, with the expected time provided after payment.

World.title: Prague’s Golden Eye to Host Japanese Brunch With Live Chef Demonstrations
World.content:
Prague’s Golden Eye bar at Fairmont Hotel is hosting a Japanese-inspired brunch combining traditional ceremonies, live sushi preparation, premium food and signature cocktails.

The afternoon will begin with Kagami Biraki, a traditional Japanese sake barrel-opening ceremony often associated with celebrations and new beginnings.



Guests will then be able to watch a live tuna carving, one of the event’s main attractions.

The programme will also include omakase bites, with chefs preparing sushi at a live station. Guests can pair the food with signature cocktails and a curated selection of wines throughout the afternoon.

A live DJ will provide the soundtrack, adding music to the Japanese-inspired dining experience.

The event is designed exclusively for adults, with tickets priced at CZK 7,900 per person. Full prepayment is required to secure a booking.

Reservations can be made through Golden Eye’s online booking page.

World.title: Hip-Hop Star Xzibit Coming to Prague’s Roxy on November 17
World.content:
West Coast rap legend Xzibit will perform at Prague’s ROXY on November 17, bringing his show featuring tracks from his latest album and some of his best-known hits.

Presented by Gotobeat and Enjoy Events, the show will feature music from *Kingmaker*, alongside career highlights including “X,” “Multiply,” “Paparazzi” and “What’s the Difference.”



Xzibit returns with new album Kingmaker

A major name in West Coast hip-hop since the 1990s, Xzibit built his reputation through his distinctive deep voice, forceful delivery and collaborations with some of the genre’s biggest artists.

His albums Restless, Man vs. Machine and Weapons of Mass Destruction helped establish him as one of the defining rappers of his generation. His work with Dr. Dre, Eminem, Snoop Dogg and Ice Cube further cemented his place in hip-hop, while his television career brought him to a wider audience as the host of MTV’s Pimp My Ride.

Released on May 16, 2025, Kingmaker marked Xzibit’s first solo studio album since 2012.

The 20-track record brings together established names and newer voices, with guest appearances from Dr. Dre, Ice Cube, Busta Rhymes, Ty Dolla $ign, Royce da 5’9”, Redman and B-Real.

The album combines the sound that made Xzibit famous with a more contemporary production style, reflecting on his decades in the music industry while introducing his work to a new generation of listeners.

– Venue: ROXY, Dlouhá 33, Prague 1

– Show: 8 p.m.

World.title: From Takumi to Gonta, a New Chapter for Japanese Food in Prague
World.content:
For those craving a taste of Japan without leaving Prague, Takumi offers a chance to explore Japanese cuisine in the heart of the city.

Located behind Quadrio, near the moving head sculpture of Franz Kafka, the restaurant recently celebrated its first anniversary this September.

We spoke with co-owner Euntaek Kim about the restaurant’s history, his journey to Prague, and his latest project, Gonta, a Japanese tonkatsu restaurant.



From Korea to Prague

The Takumi franchise was founded in Düsseldorf, Germany, in 2007 by Haruhiko Saeki and Kenjiro Komatsubara. Kim and his business partner, Viet Hung Phung, later partnered with the founders to bring Takumi Ramen to Prague, opening their first branch on Senovážné náměstí in 2019.

Kim’s connection to the restaurant business began long before that. Before he moved to Prague, his uncle owned several Hanil restaurants in Vienna and planned to expand into the Czech market. This led Kim’s family to move to Prague in 2000, when he was just 12 years old.

Later, Kim and his sister took over the Hanil restaurant their parents had run. He eventually sold it to a Korean chef he had worked with for several years.

Over time, Prague became much more than a place to do business.

“Prague has become like my second home. After having lived here for almost 26 years, I feel connected to its culture as well as my own Korean culture. In business settings and everyday life, I always try to find a balance between both,” Kim says.

His decision to open a Japanese restaurant was driven by what he saw as a gap in Prague’s dining scene.

“I felt like something was missing in Prague. Previously, Asian cuisine was close to nonexistent here. I wanted to make a change,” he explains.

Since moving to Prague, Kim has noticed growing interest in Asian food and culture among local residents, reflecting the city’s changing culinary landscape.

Introducing Gonta, a Japanese Tonkatsu Restaurant

Kim’s latest project, Gonta, brings another Japanese specialty to Prague. Located at Jungmannova 750/34, near Můstek metro station, the restaurant focuses on tonkatsu, a Japanese dish made with breaded, deep-fried pork cutlets, typically served with rice and a tangy sauce.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gonta Prague (@tonkatsugonta.prague)

“When people think about Japanese cuisine, most people tend to think of sushi or ramen. Tonkatsu is a delicious dish that has not yet reached Prague. I craved it a lot,” Kim says, explaining what inspired him to launch Gonta.

The restaurant is scheduled to open in October 2026, adding another option to Prague’s growing selection of Japanese dining spots.

World.title: Why October 28 Is a National Holiday in the Czech Republic
World.content:
October 28th is Czechoslovak Independence Day, marking the establishment of Czechoslovakia in 1918.

Although Czechoslovakia peacefully split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, October 28 remains one of the most important dates in Czech history.

It commemorates the struggle for independence and the emergence of modern Czech statehood. It should not be confused with Czech Statehood Day, celebrated on September 28.



Why Czechoslovakia Declared Independence in 1918

Before 1918, the Czech lands and present-day Slovakia were part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia belonged to the Austrian half of the monarchy, while Slovakia was part of Hungary. For decades, Czech and Slovak political leaders had sought greater autonomy and the right to determine their own future.

World War I, which began in 1914, weakened the empire and intensified nationalist movements. Food shortages, economic difficulties and growing public discontent increased support for an independent state.

Politicians working abroad played a crucial role in the independence movement. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, Edvard Beneš and Milan Rastislav Štefánik coordinated diplomatic efforts to win support from the Allied powers. France, Great Britain and the United States recognised the Czechoslovak National Council as a provisional government in 1918.

Czechoslovak legions also fought on several fronts during the war, including in France, Italy and Russia, helping draw international attention to the independence movement.

How Independence Was Declared

On October 18, 1918, Masaryk issued the Declaration of Independence of Czechoslovakia in the United States, known as the Washington Declaration. It outlined the ambition to establish a democratic state based on the right of the Czechs and Slovaks to self-determination.

The decisive events took place in Prague on October 28, as news spread that Austria-Hungary had agreed to armistice terms. Many people interpreted the reports as a sign that the empire was collapsing and gathered in public squares to celebrate.

The Czech National Committee took control and issued the first law establishing an independent Czechoslovak state. October 28 subsequently became the official date of its founding.

Who Founded the New State?

Masaryk became Czechoslovakia’s first president after independence. A philosopher, educator and politician, he had spent years persuading foreign governments to support the creation of a new state.

Beneš was instrumental in diplomatic negotiations and later served as foreign minister and president. Štefánik, a Slovak politician, astronomer and military officer, helped organise the Czechoslovak legions and strengthen cooperation between the Czech and Slovak independence movements.

Politicians working in Prague, including Alois Rašín, Karel Kramář and Antonín Švehla, also helped organise the transfer of power.

What Happened After 1918?

During the interwar period, Czechoslovakia became a parliamentary republic with one of Central Europe’s most developed industrial economies. However, tensions between its different national communities presented ongoing challenges.

In 1938, the Munich Agreement led to the loss of the Sudetenland. Nazi Germany occupied the Czech lands in March 1939, while Slovakia became a separate state aligned with Berlin. Czechoslovakia was restored after World War II but later came under communist rule.

The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in 1989. On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia peacefully split into two independent countries.

World.title: Leading Czech magazine portrays Viktor Orbán in handcuffs
World.content:
A leading Czech political magazine has depicted former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in handcuffs next to Péter Magyar on its latest cover as it examines Hungary’s political transformation following his departure from power.

Popular magazine depicts Viktor Orbán handcuffed

The cover of Reflex, a popular Czech public affairs weekly, features Orbán handcuffed alongside Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar. The issue contains extensive coverage of the new government’s efforts to dismantle the political structures established under Orbán and restore the rule of law.

Magyar bought a copy of the magazine during a brief visit to Prague, where he also met Oliver Adámek, a journalist specialising in Hungarian politics. Adámek presented the prime minister with a copy of his newly published book, Világoš, which examines the collapse of Orbán’s political system after 16 years in power.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Book explores Orbán’s electoral defeat

Founded in 1990, Reflex is widely regarded as a right-wing libertarian publication. Adámek is among the Czech media’s best-known experts on Hungarian domestic politics and speaks Hungarian fluently.

An extract from his book appears in the latest issue, recounting the final days of the election campaign, including US Vice-President JD Vance’s visit and Orbán’s closing rally in Budapest. Adámek recalls sensing that the election had been decided when a large crowd gathered to welcome Magyar in Ráckeve early on the morning of 7 April, coinciding with Vance’s arrival.

The book’s title is a play on the Czech expression dostat világoš, meaning to suffer a beating or a heavy defeat. The phrase is believed to derive from the Hungarian surrender at Világos in 1849 and is used here to refer to Fidesz’s electoral defeat.

Stay up-to-date: Viktor Orbán reported to police over controversial speech about ‘handing out appropriate tools’

Questions over Hungary’s democratic reforms

A second major article by Adámek examines the Magyar government’s record in dismantling the former ruling party’s political structures. It discusses changes to state institutions, efforts to replace officials appointed under Orbán, and plans to introduce an age limit for Constitutional Court judges.

However, the journalist also questions whether the government’s reforms risk concentrating power rather than restoring democratic checks and balances. He asks whether voters gave Magyar a mandate for such far-reaching constitutional changes.

Adámek argues that Magyar must now demonstrate tangible improvements in people’s lives and prove that the political transition represents more than symbolic revenge against his predecessors. The Reflex coverage reflects wider Czech media interest in Hungary’s political direction, with other publications also examining the government’s reforms and the future of Hungarian democracy.

World.title: Egyptian president visits Budapest: Railway deal struck, new economic partnerships on the table
World.content:
Hungary has reached an agreement with Egypt to complete the delivery of 44 outstanding railway carriages, resolving a long-running and financially sensitive deal inherited from the previous government. The agreement also covers warranty repairs to 31 carriages already delivered and the settlement of related financial obligations and loan contracts.

David Vitézy, Hungary’s Minister for Transport and Investment, announced the breakthrough following bilateral talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and his ministers in Budapest on Friday. The negotiations were led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar and involved representatives of both governments.

Under the agreement, the remaining carriages will be manufactured and delivered by the Dunakeszi Railway Vehicle Repair and Manufacturing Company, which is now owned by Hungarian state railway company MÁV.

Vitézy said the parties had managed to find a solution that would serve Egyptian passengers while also protecting Hungarian taxpayers’ interests and remaining acceptable to Egypt.

Hungary to complete the remaining 44 railway carriages

The agreement brings an end to a complicated situation involving a major railway contract that had stalled before the current government took office.

The original deliveries were halted, while the Dunakeszi facility underwent a turnaround and was brought back under MÁV ownership in recent months. According to Vitézy, the unresolved deal had posed serious financial, diplomatic and operational risks for Hungary’s railway sector.

The minister said preparations for manufacturing the remaining 44 carriages would begin immediately. Hungary will also carry out warranty repairs on the 31 vehicles already delivered to Egypt. The financial aspects of the agreement and the associated loan contracts will be settled in a way acceptable to both sides.

Vitézy said he had worked extensively on the issue, holding negotiations with Egyptian Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir in Cairo, Berlin and, most recently, Budapest. He described the outcome as a significant achievement, saying the complicated dispute had been resolved in the interests of both countries in just over six months.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Hungary and Egypt seek closer economic cooperation

The railway agreement was among the key topics discussed during Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s visit to Budapest. However, the two governments also explored opportunities for future cooperation in several other sectors, including transport, railways, energy, water management and wastewater treatment.

Hungarian President András Baka received el-Sisi at the Sándor Palace, where both leaders highlighted the stability of bilateral relations and their commitment to strengthening cooperation.

Baka noted that diplomatic relations between the two countries date back almost a century, with their centenary set to be celebrated in 2028. He also pointed to the strategic partnership agreement signed in 2023 as an important foundation for closer ties.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. Photo: MTI

The discussions also covered major international challenges, including the Middle East situation, the conflict in Gaza, counter-terrorism and illegal migration. Baka stressed the importance of strengthening the strategic partnership between the European Union and Egypt to address these shared challenges.

El-Sisi, making his fourth visit to Hungary, described bilateral relations as strong and stable. He thanked Hungary for its support regarding the Palestinian issue, emphasising the need to prevent further military operations, ensure humanitarian aid reaches those in need and begin reconstruction in Palestine.

The Egyptian president also invited his Hungarian counterpart to visit Egypt, signalling both sides’ intention to deepen their partnership further.

World.title: Hungary’s political shake-up offers Serbia a blueprint – but the hardest part may still lie ahead
World.content:
Political changes in Hungary could offer valuable lessons for Serbia, as the country prepares for a new government following an election victory by the Student List. A Serbian news portal has drawn parallels between the two countries, highlighting efforts to overhaul public media, investigate the previous administration and reform state institutions.

In an analysis published on Friday, Serbian news outlet Nova.rs argued that Hungary’s experience over the past six months also shows the challenges that Serbia’s incoming political forces could face.

Public media faces major shake-ups in both countries

Nova.rs identified the transformation of public service broadcasting as one of the most striking similarities.

In Hungary, news broadcasting on M1 was suspended on 7 July, Hirado.hu stopped operating, and Kossuth Radio switched to music programming. Viewers and listeners were greeted with a message apologising for the previous operation of the public media.

The revamped M1 news service returned on 20 August, with opposition parties’ positions already featuring in its very first broadcast.

Serbia has also seen major personnel changes in its public media. Manja Grčić, director-general of Serbian public broadcaster RTS, resigned on the third day after the election. Her departure had been demanded by the Student List, as well as some public media employees and trade union representatives. Before stepping down, she had also dismissed Bojana Mladenović, editor-in-chief of news programmes.

Calls for a review of previous reporting practices have also emerged at Radio Television of Vojvodina. A group of employees said on Monday that the broadcaster owed viewers an apology for years of one-sided coverage, insufficient criticism of those in power and the suppression of certain issues. On Friday, the institution’s director-general, Goran Karadžić, also resigned.

Investigating public spending and previous government deals

Another area of common ground is the scrutiny of public money and state contracts. Nova.rs referred to a Telex article examining the first 100 days of Hungary’s new government. According to the report, the cabinet ordered reviews of ministries and state-owned companies, suspended several contracts and payments, and filed criminal complaints.

Among the cases mentioned were matters involving a concession agreement for a section of the M6 motorway and the operations of Eximbank.

Serbia’s incoming political forces have also promised similar measures. In an interview with weekly magazine NIN, published on Thursday, academician Radomir Šačić, a candidate on the Student List, outlined plans to reorganise state operations, introduce professional standards into public administration and make contracts publicly accessible.

He also pledged to freeze assets suspected of having been acquired illegally and confiscate them once the relevant legal proceedings had concluded.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Authorities move to protect official documents

The preservation of official records has already become an issue ahead of the transfer of power in Serbia.

On Thursday, Serbian Chief Public Prosecutor Zagorka Dolovac instructed heads of prosecution offices to work with the police to prevent the destruction of official documents. She cited reports that records were allegedly being destroyed in state institutions and other organisations.

EU relations and the rule of law remain key challenges

Nova.rs also highlighted the restoration of relations with European institutions as an important part of Hungary’s political changes, particularly negotiations over EU funding that had previously been withheld.

In Serbia, European Council President António Costa identified the rule of law, the fight against corruption and press freedom as central areas for reform on the country’s path towards EU integration. He made the remarks on Tuesday following a conversation with Ilija Srđanović, leader of the Student List.

However, the Serbian outlet warned that Hungary’s experience shows that winning an election is only the beginning. Transforming an institutional system built up under a previous administration is a much longer and more complicated task.

World.title: Hungary cuts EU defence loan request by two-thirds – could it also bring the euro closer?
World.content:
Hungary has secured European Commission approval for a EUR 5.4 billion defence investment plan, around one-third of the amount originally sought under Viktor Orbán’s government. The cheaper EU loan could help fund major infrastructure projects, ease pressure on the state budget and potentially make it easier for Hungary to meet the fiscal requirements for adopting the euro.

The European Commission approved the revised plan on 28 October, after raising concerns about Hungary’s original EUR 17.4 billion request, including issues related to procurement costs. The new proposal, worth around HUF 2,000 billion, is part of the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme.

The Commission’s approval is an important step, but the plan must still be considered by the Council of the European Union before Hungary can proceed with the next stages.

If you missed it: European Commission approves Hungary’s EUR multi-billion defence plan

What can Hungary spend the SAFE loan on?

The SAFE programme provides EU member states with access to favourable, long-term loans to strengthen defence capabilities and military readiness. Funding can also cover certain dual-use infrastructure, meaning projects that serve both civilian and military purposes.

According to G7, in Hungary, this could potentially include railway developments, the new Danube bridge at Mohács and improvements to the expressway network, alongside defence-related investments.

The government will still need to decide whether to use the loan for projects already planned or to finance new investments, as well as how quickly to draw down the funds.

Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said in September that Hungary should take its economic capacity into account when deciding how much to borrow, since the money will eventually have to be repaid. He also suggested that the loan could cover existing defence contracts or bring forward investments originally scheduled for later years.

A smaller loan after concerns over the original plan

The revised request follows concerns raised by the European Commission and Péter Magyar, whose Tisza Party reconsidered the plans after winning the April 2026 election.

Under the original proposal, the funds could potentially have benefited companies linked to major Hungarian business figures, including Jászai Gellért’s 4iG group, which has interests in the defence industry, and construction companies associated with Lőrinc Mészáros and László Szíjj. The concerns centred partly on corruption risks and procurement costs.

Hungary initially sought one of the largest loans among participating countries. With the revised EUR 5.4 billion request, it moves towards the middle of the field.

Poland is the largest prospective borrower, with EUR 43.7 billion, accounting for nearly a third of the programme’s EUR 150 billion lending capacity.

Eight EU member states – Austria, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Sweden – have decided not to take up loans under the scheme. This partly reflects differences in countries’ financing options: governments that can borrow cheaply on financial markets may find the SAFE terms less attractive.

Following the Commission’s latest announcement, just over EUR 21 billion remains unallocated. The Commission is expected to offer the unused funds to member states in another application round.

Could the loan ease pressure on Hungary’s budget?

The EUR 5.4 billion loan is equivalent to roughly a year of Hungary’s defence spending, illustrating the scale of the financing compared with the country’s public finances.

Hungary’s planned central budget deficit for 2026 stands at HUF 7,110 billion. Although SAFE funding can be used over several years, it represents a substantial source of financing relative to the state budget.

The loan could help reduce pressure on public finances if the government uses it to fund investments that would otherwise have been financed through more expensive market borrowing. Lower interest costs could, in turn, help reduce the budget deficit.

However, the effect will depend on how the money is used. The loan does not eliminate the cost of investment or the obligation to repay the borrowed funds.

Why the euro could enter the picture

The potential budgetary savings matter because Hungary would need to bring its deficit down significantly to meet the fiscal criteria for adopting the euro.

At the same time, NATO members are expected to increase defence and defence-related spending towards 5% of GDP by 2035, compared with levels of around 2% today.

This creates a challenge for Hungary: it must strengthen its defence capabilities while also putting public finances on a more sustainable footing if it wants to move towards euro adoption.

By providing access to cheaper financing for eligible investments, the SAFE loan could make both objectives easier to pursue. It remains to be seen, however, how the government will allocate the funds and whether the resulting savings will be sufficient to make a meaningful difference to the budget deficit and Hungary’s path towards the euro.

World.title: Hungary lands another potential world record as angler catches enormous 52kg carp – VIDEO
World.content:
An enormous 52kg common carp has been caught at a Hungarian fishing lake, potentially setting a new world record. However, the extraordinary catch has already sparked heated debate among anglers over whether it should officially count as one.

Ash Hegarty landed the giant fish on 28 October at Euro Aqua Lake, near Balatonederics, a private fishing venue that has become internationally famous for its record-breaking carp. The fish weighed an astonishing 114lb 10oz (approximately 52kg), making it one of the largest carp ever caught.

The news was reported by Totally Carp Baits, while Hegarty himself also shared the achievement on Facebook, describing himself as a world record holder.

“Words genuinely cannot describe the emotions I’m feeling right now,” he wrote, adding that there was a huge story behind the catch. He also thanked the Euro Aqua team, saying that without their help, his dream would not have come true.

Hungary’s Euro Aqua Lake has a history of record-breaking catches

This is far from the first time Euro Aqua Lake has attracted international attention. Located between Balatonederics and Nemesvita, the private venue has been the setting for several extraordinary carp catches over the years.

In November 2018, Michel Schoenmakers caught a 51.2kg mirror carp at the same lake. For a long time, the fish was regarded as the world’s largest carp.

The venue has also repeatedly broken records in the common carp category. In May 2025, David Knock caught a 47.8kg specimen, setting a new benchmark for common carp.

Then, in May 2026, Richard Ince raised the bar again with a 49.5kg common carp, also at Euro Aqua Lake. Hegarty’s latest catch surpasses that figure by 2.5kg.

The new 52kg fish is even 800g heavier than Schoenmakers’ famous 2018 mirror carp. However, common carp and mirror carp are not always treated as the same category in record listings, and there has been no confirmed information about formal international verification of Hegarty’s catch.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

VIDEO: See the enormous 52kg carp caught in Hungary

Reel Fishing News has also shared footage of the remarkable catch. The video shows the enormous common carp being held in the water by the angler, giving viewers a good impression of its extraordinary size.

Why are anglers questioning the potential world record?

Although Hegarty’s announcement attracted hundreds of congratulatory messages, it also triggered considerable criticism and debate on social media.

Some anglers questioned the significance of a record caught at an intensively managed, paid fishing venue. They argued that catches made in private lakes should not necessarily be compared directly with those achieved in natural waters.

Others raised questions about the weighing procedure and the circumstances in which the fish’s weight was established. However, these comments do not in themselves provide evidence of any irregularities.

Hungarian angling personality Gábor Döme also shared the news on Facebook, where reactions were similarly divided. While many users celebrated the extraordinary size of the fish and Hungary’s prominent position in international carp fishing, others questioned the role of private fishing lakes in establishing world records.

Whatever the outcome of the debate, one thing is certain: Euro Aqua Lake has once again put Hungary on the international carp fishing map.

World.title: Breaking: Former Fidesz MP István Boldog sentenced to 5 years in prison
World.content:
A Budapest court has sentenced former Fidesz MP István Boldog to five years in prison for his role in a corruption scheme involving EU-funded projects in Hungary. The former politician was also banned from public affairs for five years, fined and ordered to forfeit HUF 6.6 million (approximately EUR 18,000).

The Budapest Metropolitan Court handed down the first-instance verdict on Friday, finding Boldog guilty as an accomplice in several offences, including accepting bribes and agreements restricting competition in public procurement procedures, Telex reported.

According to the ruling, he may be released after serving two-thirds of his sentence at the earliest. The decision is not final, and Boldog had already indicated before the verdict that he would appeal if convicted.

István Boldog. Photo: MTI

How the corruption scheme worked

The court found that an unlawful kickback system operated in Boldog’s former parliamentary constituency in Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok County. Using his political influence, the former MP helped municipalities with connections to him secure EU funding while favouring certain businesses in public procurement contracts.

According to the judge, this was not an isolated incident but a system operating across the constituency. Unlike more conventional corruption schemes involving inflated contracts and documented kickbacks, money was returned in cash to Boldog and people working with him.

The investigation focused primarily on three projects in Cserkeszőlő: the construction of a nursery, the renovation of the Baghy-Szinyei Merse Mansion and energy-efficiency improvements to municipal buildings. However, investigators found indications that other municipalities and contractors could also have been involved.

István Boldog. Photo: MTI

The court also highlighted evidence that a contractor handed HUF 20 million to one of Boldog’s associates, identified as Péter K. The defence argued that the associate had kept the money for himself without Boldog’s knowledge, but the court said other evidence contradicted this explanation.

The judge added that witnesses’ testimonies and intercepted conversations suggested municipalities believed Boldog had decisive influence over which localities would receive EU funding. This influence extended beyond the main regional development programme to other funding schemes, including the Hungarian Village Programme.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Other defendants also receive prison sentences

Boldog was not the only defendant convicted in the case. Petra Fehér, a former Fidesz municipal and county representative who was widely known as one of Boldog’s closest associates, also received a five-year prison sentence. Her time spent in pre-trial detention will count towards her sentence.

Another associate, Péter K., was sentenced to three years in prison and fined. The court found the other defendants guilty as well, with the exception of the ninth defendant, who was acquitted.

István Boldog. Photo: MTI

Boldog denies wrongdoing and plans to fight the verdict

The former MP has consistently denied the accusations, insisting that he never interfered unlawfully in funding decisions or participated in bribery. Before Friday’s ruling, he told Telex that he expected to be acquitted and promised to appeal if the court found him guilty.

At an earlier hearing in February, Boldog again rejected the allegations, claiming that he had spent his entire life fighting corruption. He also questioned the credibility of witnesses, particularly former Kengyel mayor Szilárd Nagy, whose testimony helped launch the investigation.

The case first came to public attention in October 2019, and prosecutors filed charges against Boldog and eight others in 2020. The preparatory hearing took place in June 2021, meaning more than five years passed before the court delivered its first-instance verdict.

Fidesz replaced Boldog as its candidate ahead of the 2022 parliamentary election, after which he withdrew from active politics. He has remained active on social media, describing himself as a national-minded commentator and food blogger.

World.title: Budapest drivers to face weeks of disruption as major junction undergoes renovations
World.content:
Motorists in Budapest should prepare for traffic jams and road restrictions in November, as maintenance work at one of the capital’s busiest junctions is set to disrupt traffic for almost four weeks.

Busy Budapest junction will undergo repairs

Track repairs will take place at the junction of Bocskai Road and Bartók Béla Road, around Kosztolányi Dezső Square, from 7 AM on Monday, 2 November, until 27 November, according to Budapest Közút. During the works, a construction site will occupy the centre of the junction, forcing vehicles to pass around it.

On Bocskai Road, two narrowed lanes will remain open in each direction, while traffic on Bartók Béla Road will be restricted to one lane in each direction. The temporary layout is expected to slow traffic, particularly on Bocskai Road and around Kosztolányi Dezső Square. Drivers heading towards the city centre will also face a change to their usual routes.

Left turns temporarily prohibited

Motorists travelling towards the centre on Bocskai Road will not be able to turn left onto Bartók Béla Road in the middle of the junction. Instead, they must continue straight across Bartók Béla Road and use a temporary left-turn facility near the service road at Kosztolányi Dezső Square. They can then reach Bartók Béla Road via the service road.

Budapest Közút has urged drivers to approach the junction with extra care and use alternative routes where possible.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Tram services and replacement buses

The repairs will also affect public transport. Between 2 and 27 November, trams 19 and 49 will run on shortened routes, terminating at Móricz Zsigmond Square instead of continuing to Kelenföld Railway Station. Replacement buses operating under route number 19 will serve the section between Kelenföld railway station and Móricz Zsigmond Square.

For journeys towards central Budapest, the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) recommends using metro line M4 or buses 7, 58, 114, 213 and 214. Passengers are advised to check timetables and plan their journeys in advance, using the BudapestGO app for route planning and real-time travel information. The works are scheduled to finish on 27 November, with delays expected in the surrounding area throughout the construction period.

World.title: Hungary raises public transport fines – what passengers need to know
World.content:
Passengers travelling by train, bus and HÉV services in Hungary will face higher penalties from 2 November. The standard surcharge for travelling without a valid ticket will rise by HUF 5,000, while reduced fines for early payment are also going up.

Higher fines on trains, buses and HÉV services from November

Hungary’s MÁV Group has announced an increase in surcharges across intercity trains, buses and HÉV suburban railway services from 2 November.

The standard penalty for travelling without a valid ticket will increase from HUF 25,000 (approximately EUR 68) to HUF 30,000 (approximately EUR 82). The same higher surcharge will apply to various breaches of passenger rules, including smoking on trains or at stations, dirtying vehicles and using discounts without being entitled to them.

Passengers who pay their fine promptly can still benefit from reduced rates. However, these will also increase: on buses, passengers paying on the spot or within three working days will have to pay HUF 15,000 (EUR 41) instead of HUF 12,000 (EUR 33). The same reduced rate will apply on HÉV services for payments made within two working days.

The HUF 50,000 (EUR 137) surcharge for payments made more than 30 days after the penalty is issued will remain unchanged.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Budapest commuters: remember to buy your train ticket before boarding

The MÁV Group is particularly reminding passengers about the mandatory advance ticket purchase zones introduced around Budapest two years ago.

At all stations and stops along the affected railway sections, passengers must have a valid ticket before boarding any train. Buying one from the ticket inspector after getting on is not sufficient to avoid the higher penalty.

The affected routes include connections between Budapest and:

Győr

Esztergom

Székesfehérvár

Pusztaszabolcs

Szob

Veresegyház and Vác

Hatvan

Cegléd and Szolnok

Nagykáta

Pestszentimre

The rule applies to all stations and stops along the listed sections, not just their final destinations.

Passengers should also check whether they need a seat reservation and whether their tickets are valid for the correct train, departure time and entire journey.

If there is no working ticket machine or open ticket office at the station, tickets can be purchased online through the MÁVPlusz mobile app or the official MÁV ticket website. However, the purchase must still be completed before boarding.

Other penalties are changing too

The increase is not limited to passengers travelling without tickets in the mandatory advance-purchase zones.

From 2 November, the HUF 30,000 (EUR 82) surcharge will also apply across intercity trains, buses and HÉV services in cases such as the unauthorised use of travel discounts and breaches of passenger regulations.

On HÉV services, the fee for subsequently presenting a travel pass purchased on the day the penalty was issued will also increase, from HUF 6,500 (EUR 18) to HUF 7,500 (EUR 20.5).

There is, however, one way to reduce certain penalties considerably. Passengers who can prove within 15 days that they already held a valid ticket, pass or travel entitlement at the time of inspection can have the surcharge reduced to an administration fee. This is HUF 2,600 (EUR 7.1) on trains and HUF 2,500 (EUR 6.8) on buses.

Fines on tram-train services will not change.

Thousands of penalties already issued this year

According to MÁV Group data, inspectors issued 5,300 penalties on HÉV services during the first nine months of this year, generating almost HUF 53.5 million in revenue.

The figures were even higher on other services. Nearly 14,700 penalty cases were recorded on trains, generating HUF 88.5 million, while buses accounted for more than 14,500 cases and HUF 97 million in penalty revenue.

The most common reasons included travelling without a valid ticket or pass, failing to provide proof of eligibility for a discount, and being unable to demonstrate that the ticket or pass belonged to the passenger.

MÁV Group says many of these situations can easily be avoided by checking travel documents before departure. From November, that small precaution could save passengers an additional HUF 5,000.

World.title: Tragedy that Led to Change: Serbia Marks Two Years Since Canopy Collapse
World.content:
Novi Sad, Serbia’s second city, was in shock and mourning on November 1, 2024.

Since Sunday, the grief and anger once so palpable in this Danube city and the country as a whole has given way to hope for a better future and talk of ‘liberation’ following a bruising election defeat suffered by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, at the hands of a student-led protest movement.

On November 1, 2024, Serbia and Novi Sad were firmly under the rule of the SNS and its founder, then President Aleksandar Vucic. At 11.52 that morning, everything changed.

That was the moment the outdoor canopy of Novi Sad’s newly renovated railway station collapsed. Fourteen people, including children, were killed instantly, buried under tonnes of concrete. Three others fought to stay alive, but ultimately only one did not succumb to their injuries, taking the death toll to 16.

World.title: The Anatomy of Forging Freedom: Lessons from Serbia’s Students
World.content:
An avalanche of small acts

Through the same painstaking, often exhausting practice of direct democracy, faculty assemblies distributed quotas to select 250 parliamentary candidates, ensuring representation across the country. Every name then underwent nationwide scrutiny, with faculties able to challenge and collectively veto one another’s choices. Finally, they chose a parliamentary list reflecting the breadth of Serbian life they had encountered on foot, from workers and farmers to academics, doctors and judges: Student List – Students Are Winning.

On September 9, 492 days after the students first called for early elections, Aleksandar Vucic finally yielded and called the vote. Eighteen days later, he resigned the presidency to run for prime minister.

From that moment, the fruits of the students’ long democratic struggle began to show. Student working groups, established months earlier, launched the campaign, backed by a formidable infrastructure of civic self-organisation, with millions of citizens contributing whatever time, skills and resources they could. Recognising the circumstances, most opposition parties stepped aside. By election day, there was hardly a corner of Serbia where students and citizens had not organised to safeguard the vote against fraud and manipulation.

Turnout reached a historic high. The Student List secured 52.71 per cent of the vote against 39.17 per cent for the then-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, winning an outright parliamentary majority. So decisive was the victory that even a regime determined to hold on to power at any cost had no choice but to concede defeat.

At the beginning, these young people had little more than imagination and the stubborn hope that their country could be different. Through two years of determined work, courage and sacrifice, they brought millions alongside them. Most had wanted nothing more than a democratic Serbia, a country where they might finally imagine a future of their own.

And yet, by bringing down a regime that had long fuelled tensions across the Western Balkans, maintained close ties with Putin’s Russia and presented itself to Europe as a guarantor of stability, they accomplished something far beyond a change of government.

They loosened the grip of a politics that had held the region’s future hostage for far too long, inviting the Western Balkans and the EU to finally begin building the future they had spent so many years waiting for.

Milan Vujić currently works at the Erste Foundation in Vienna, and is also a lawyer and former student activist from Novi Sad in Serbia.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Week in Review: Big Changes, Bigger Challenges
World.content:
Many in Serbia are still pinching themselves after Sunday’s parliamentary elections. Not only did Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party lose the election, they did so in a landslide. Contrary to many expectations, they also quickly conceded defeat.

The extent of the swing away from the long-time ruling party surprised many observers. Our analysis takes stock of the elections and their outcome as both Serbia and the region digest the results.

World.title: New Exhibition Features Italian Photojournalist’s Work from Wartime Sarajevo
World.content:
Mario Boccia was among the many journalists and photojournalists that covered the siege of Sarajevo. “Many were better than me,” he said, humbly.

But few others, he believes, held their first exhibition of Sarajevo photos in the city itself while it was still under siege.

In September 1994 he took some photos of a class in Ciglane, a neighbourhood in Sarajevo, where instructors were teaching children how to use a computer. “In January 1995 I brought those pictures back, glued them on cardboard and hung them on the wall and the children came to see them,” he said. “It was something quite unique.”

World.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Race Heads to Runoff as Russia Divides the Two Candidates
World.content:
On Sunday, Bulgarian voters head to the polls again for the second round of geopolitically charged presidential elections.

In the first round on October 25, current acting President Iliana Iotova won 34.7 per cent to opposition candidate and former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov’s 31.9 per cent.

The elections were marked by record low turnout. The Central Election Committee reported that only 22.98 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot.

Iotova and Gyurov are both running as independents, but they are supported by opposing factions and represent opposing foreign policy approaches and political alignments.

Iotova has been endorsed by the ruling party Progressive Bulgaria, the Bulgarian Socialist Party (which she is a former member of) and the nationalist party VMRO. Her potential victory would represent a consolidation of power by Progressive Bulgaria and Prime Minister Rumen Radev, whom Iotova served as vice president when he was president from 2017 to early 2026.

Gyurov has been supported by the pro-EU opposition parties Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change, of which he was formerly a member. However, his campaign has tried to present him as independent of party dynamics.

During a TV debate on October 29, Iotova positioned herself as the candidate who can guarantee peace in the region and maintain more balanced diplomatic relations with Russia.

Among her criticisms of her opponent is that as interim Prime Minister, Gyurov signed a 10-year agreement with Ukrainian President Zelensky. She also disapproves of his past association with the party We Continue the Change, particularly the party’s work on gas diversification in 2022 after Russia’s Gazprom cut off supplies to Bulgaria.

The opposition has recently criticised Iotova for pardoning five people sentenced for drug dealing since 2022, at least one of whom was later arrested again for the same crime.

For both candidates 2026 brought major changes. Iotova became acting president after Rumen Radev stepped down and ran successfully in the April snap elections with his Progressive Bulgaria party. Before Radev took over as prime minister, Gyurov led the caretaker cabinet.

The presidential campaign coincided with increased drone attacks in the Black Sea which stoked public debate and divisions over the government’s reluctance to name Russia as the aggressor. Both Radev and Iotova remain elusive about Russia’s potential role in the security risks in the Black Sea region.

Shortly after the first round, the government was criticised for using official communication channels to promote Iotova and for domineering language directed at journalists who cover the elections. On October 30, the government issued a statement saying that the Central Election Committee found no wrongdoing but has deleted the Iotova-related posts if Gyurov’s team is “so sure this would help them in their campaign”, in an atypically ironic tone for an official statement.

Opposition figures have also accused Radev’s government of meddling with social media. Three popular satirical social media pages – often targeting political figures through memes and jokes but occasionally appearing supportive of Gyurov and the pro-EU opposition parties – were taken down and restored repeatedly.

World.title: Mourning Day Declared in Bosnia’s Brcko Following Deadly EUFOR Helicopter Crash
World.content:
The mayor of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s semi-autonomous administrative unit Brcko District, Sinisa Milic, declared a day of mourning on Friday following the deaths of four EUFOR personnel from the Italian armed forces.

The deaths occurred when a helicopter operated by the European Union Force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, EUFOR, crashed on Thursday during a routine operation near Brcko in northeastern Bosnia.

Milic said the victims were members of the force deployed to maintain peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

“This is a symbolic way of expressing solidarity with the victims’ families and the entire Italian people,” Milic said.

He emphasised that special recognition should go to the helicopter pilots, who tried to keep the aircraft airborne and prevent it from crashing into populated areas, thereby avoiding civilian casualties.

EUFOR confirmed on Thursday night that two of the four people killed in the helicopter crash were members of the Italian armed forces, while the other two belonged to the Italian Red Cross Military Corps.

Another 11 people were injured, all of whom are in stable condition, according to EUFOR. Two were transferred to the Tuzla Clinical Centre for treatment, while the remaining nine are receiving medical care in Brcko.

“EUFOR is deeply saddened by this tragic loss of life and extends its deepest condolences to the friends and family of those who lost their lives in the service of peace,” a EUFOR statement said.

Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto announced on Thursday that those killed in the crash were Sergeants Simone Ruggia and Claudio Marchesi of the Italian armed forces, and Lieutenant Franco Adriano Zecchillo and Sergeant Laura Procacci of the Italian Red Cross Volunteer Military Corps.

EUFOR reiterated its appeal to the public not to spread disinformation or speculate about the circumstances of the crash, urging the public to rely exclusively on official sources for information.

They reported that no civilian infrastructure, property or vehicles were damaged in the incident and that no civilians were injured, adding that the investigation into the accident is currently ongoing.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her condolences, saying the news had caused deep sorrow.

“The news of the tragic crash of an Italian EUFOR helicopter in Bosnia and Herzegovina is a cause of deep sorrow. My thoughts are with the victims, their families and everyone involved in the mission to maintain peace and stability in the region who are now going through hours of uncertainty,” Meloni said.

The European Union Force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, EUFOR Althea, is an EU-led military operation established in 2004 to help maintain a safe and secure environment in the country.

Operating under a United Nations mandate, EUFOR supports the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement and is headquartered at Camp Butmir in Sarajevo. A total of 24 countries take part in the mission, including some non-EU countries, with the commanding structure rotating on an annual basis.

World.title: Moldova Steps Up Border Security Amid ‘Unprecedented’ Threats
World.content:
From airspace violations to cyber attacks, Russia’s war in Ukraine has confronted Moldova with “unprecedented” threats, forcing the country to upgrade its defences with new surveillance systems, drones and anti-drone technology, border police chief Ruslan Galusca has told BIRN.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Moldova has registered more than 100 drone incursions, 65 of which occurred this year.

In recent weeks, Russia has targeted border crossings between Ukraine and Moldova that it claims are being used to resupply the Ukrainian military despite Moldovan denials.

On October 5, one of Galusca’s officers was wounded in Russian drone strikes near the Palanca-Maiaki-Udobnoe crossing.

“The risk is real,” Galusca said in an interview.

World.title: New Ultra-Fast Chargers Put Into Operation on Croatian Motorways
World.content:
October the 31st, 2026 – New ultra-fast electric vehicle chargers have been put into operation on the Croatian motorways A1 and A3, with some having power as strong as 400 kW.

Petrol has put into operation 18 new ultra-fast charging points for electric vehicles on the Croatian motorways A1 and A3, among which are six charging points with a power of 400 kW intended for heavy electric trucks. Poslovni reports that the new connections have been installed at the Janjče west, Dragalić south, Dragalić north and Desinec north rest areas, the company announced. This therefore expands the network of charging stations on important transport routes towards the Adriatic and on the motorway that connects Slavonia with Zagreb.

there are now 70+ ultra-fast connections across croatia

During the summer, Petrol already opened new ultra-fast charging stations at the Vrata Jadrana north and south and Dragalić north rest areas, and the latest investment also includes infrastructure for electric freight vehicles. The company now has more than 300 charging points for electric vehicles dotted all over Croatia, of which more than 70 are ultra-fast. At the regional level its network covers approximately 1,300 connections. Particularly significant is the installation of 400 kW charging points for electric trucks, which due to the large capacity of their batteries require more powerful infrastructure than passenger cars.

Nevertheless, the actual charging speed depends on the capabilities of the vehicle, the state of charge of the battery and other conditions, so the nominal power of the charger does not mean that every vehicle will be able to charge the battery at a power of 400 kW.

eu cash helped to expand the network

The new charging stations are part of Petrol’s OneCharge network and the European CROSS-E project, which is co-financed with European Union funds through the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF). The project includes the development of infrastructure for ultra-fast charging of passenger cars and electric trucks on important transport routes in Croatia and in neighbouring Slovenia. Within the scope of this particular project, Petrol plans to install a total of 98 charging points at 22 locations in the two countries. Part of the infrastructure will be intended for electric freight vehicles.

These considerable investments are also linked to the European Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), with which the European Union is gradually introducing requirements for the availability of charging stations on the main transport corridors. The overarching goal is to facilitate travel by electric cars on longer routes, reduce the need for detours for charging and enable the development of electric freight traffic.

World.title: Croatian Railway Projects Totalling €1.7 Billion Are Now Underway
World.content:
October the 31st, 2026 – Croatian railway projects totalling €1.7 billion are currently underway as part of a major investment cycle.

The Croatian railway network is currently in the middle of a major investment cycle. Index reports that large projects worth €1.7 billion are underway, and by 2035 additional investments of around six billion euros are planned. The goal of the modernisation is to ensure faster, safer and more reliable transport of passengers and freight and to strengthen the competitiveness of Croatian ports.

State Secretary in the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure Žarko Tušek, member of the Management Board of HŽ Infrastructure Marijan Ćužić and professor from the Faculty of Transport and Traffic Sciences Mladen Nikšić spoke on HRT about the current projects, traffic safety and the deadlines for the first results. State Secretary Žarko Tušek emphasised that the modernisation of the railway is a continuation of major investments in transport infrastructure, after road, maritime and air transport. “It is the turn of the railway, without which there is no development of the economy, port capacities, logistics, rural areas and regional transport,” Tušek said.

a lowland railway to rijeka

He noted that projects worth more than a billion euros have been completed, and almost 700 million euros have been invested in the maintenance of the sector in the last eight years alone. “The value of active, contracted projects currently amounts to €1.7 billion,” he said. Among the largest projects are the reconstruction of the Dugo Selo – Novska railway, worth 900 million euros, and the Hrvatski Leskovac – Karlovac section of 350 million euros. Investments are also being made in the Podravina and Istrian railways and the Zadar – Knin railway, while the Vukovar – Vinkovci section has been completed. Long-term plans envisage investment of another around six billion euros by 2035, and the modernisation of the entire 2,600-kilometre network will continue after that as well. As a key future project Tušek singled out the lowland railway towards Rijeka, estimated at around five billion euros.

the dugo selo-novska railway is becoming double-track

“Just yesterday we selected international consultants who will accompany us in the negotiation procedure so that within a year we can reach the conclusion of an Alliance contract for the construction of that major project,” he announced. Member of the Management Board of HŽ Infrastructure Marijan Ćužić said that the reconstruction of the Dugo Selo – Novska railway, worth almost 900 million euros, will bring a significant step forward in the development of transport. “That section is the only one on the former tenth international corridor that has remained single-track. With the completion of the works we will have a double-track electrified railway from the border with Slovenia to the border with Serbia, with speeds of up to 160 kilometres per hour,” Ćužić explained. He compared the importance of the second track with road traffic, where an additional lane increases throughput. He emphasised that this will enable Croatia to reach the standards of modern European railways and ensure faster and safer travel.

croatia will need to wait a decade before it notices a difference

Professor Mladen Nikšić from the Faculty of Transport and Traffic Sciences believes that the current investments will bring significant improvements, especially after the completion of all projects. “I believe that we will have higher-quality railway traffic, shorter journey times and greater track capacity for the transport of passengers and freight. This will also make our ports more prominent,” Nikšić said. He assessed that the modernisation should significantly shorten journeys. “I believe that when those projects are completed, we will be able to reach Slavonski Brod or Vinkovci in two to two and a half hours, and we will travel faster towards Rijeka and the Adriatic cities as well.

That takes time, but I think the full effects will be visible in about ten years,” he said. Nikšić added that investments in infrastructure must be accompanied by better quality of transport, especially the punctuality and reliability of trains. “Work needs to be done on the quality of transport, punctuality and reliability. We also have new vehicles, and all of that together with a quality timetable must form a complete whole,” he said.

Professor Nikšić also commented on recent railway accidents in Croatia. He pointed out that the causes can be divided into two groups: non-compliance with procedures and problems in communication, and shortcomings in vehicle maintenance. “The number of freight train accidents on the Rijeka railway is particularly worrying.

With the liberalisation of freight traffic the state has lost part of its influence on the maintenance and control of vehicles,” he warned. He believes that the Railway Traffic Safety Agency should intensify extraordinary and unannounced inspections, and that for the prevention of human errors the key are the education of employees and compliance with procedures. “Administratively everything can be in order, but vehicles can be better or worse maintained. Work must certainly be done on that,” he emphasised. Marijan Ćužić from HŽ Infrastructure said that preliminary checks of recent accidents have not shown irregularities on the infrastructure, but that investigations are still ongoing.

the rijeka railway can’t deal with all the freight

“Our first preliminary investigations have shown that there was no error on the infrastructure. The railway systems, including tracks and switches, are correct,” Ćužić said. He added that the education and communication of all participants in railway traffic need to be improved in order to reduce the risk of accidents. Žarko Tušek emphasised that investments in the railway have a key role in strengthening the competitiveness of Croatian ports. As an example he cited Rijeka, whose traffic is growing, but the existing railway cannot accept all the freight, so it ends up on the roads. Marijan Ćužić continued and explained that the construction of the second track will enable significantly greater freight transport. “We calculate that with the new railway we will be able to transport to Europe all the additional quantities of freight that the Port of Rijeka plans in the next ten years or so,” he stated.

could rijeka become a bigger logistics centre than trieste and koper?

Mladen Nikšić believes that along with Rijeka it is also necessary to develop the Dalmatian ports, modernise the Lika railway and better connect Zadar, Šibenik and Split. He also warned that the future lowland railway towards Rijeka will require additional port capacities.

“When the lowland railway is built, its capacity will be 30 million tonnes, which Rijeka alone will not be able to generate. That is why we already need to think about a new port on Krk, a railway connection and a new bridge that would connect the island with the mainland,” Nikšić said. Tušek confirmed that the lowland railway, a new terminal on Krk and a large freight centre in Zagreb are part of the Government’s strategic plans. “Krk is not any fantasy, but a project that needs to start being elaborated urgently. Its potential is such that Rijeka could become a stronger logistics centre than Koper and Trieste together,” Tušek concluded.

When asked when the general public and the economy will feel concrete benefits, Marijan Ćužić replied that the first results will be visible in two to three years, and that the Croatian railway in the next decade should reach the European level. “The first advances will be seen on the section from Zagreb to the Hungarian border, but also on the railways in Istria, in the Knin and Zadar area and on the Podravina main line. Already in a relatively short time our users will be able to use the advantages of a modern railway,” he concluded.

World.title: Meet The Croatian City With a Monument Not to a King, But to a Frog
World.content:
October the 31st, 2026 – There’s a central Croatian city which was once home to a monument dedicated not to a nobleman or a king, but to a frog.

Rulers and historical warriors are the most common monuments you’ll see dotted all over Croatia. A contemplative artist, statesman, writer or philosopher is also not a rarity. Nor is the one and only Nikola Tesla. Women are also found across the country, including the legendary Mila Gojsalić high in the mountains above Omiš. As Lana Mindoljevic writes for Putni kofer, however, you won’t often notice monuments to animals. That is, of course, unless they’re being ridden by some hero into battle. In Karlovac, one of the best-known monuments was for a long time the one dedicated not to a brave horse or dog, but to a frog. The small bronze resident of the city on four rivers stood for years at the entrance to the city’s so-called Promenade.

croatia’s only frog monument

The frog monument was unveiled in March 2008 and until 2024 stood at the intersection of Stjepan Radić Street and Dr. Franjo Tuđman Promenade, better known as the Promenade. Until 2022 it was the only frog monument in Croatia, but then one was also placed in Zmijavci near Imotski. Unfortunately, you cannot see the Karlovac frog anymore. It was removed during the renovation of Radić Street, when it was taken for safekeeping to the warehouse of the Public Fire Brigade of Karlovac. It never returned to its old location. When relocating it, the city announced that it would find a new location for it, because the old one had proved non-functional; it obstructed, they say, the passage and the organisation of events on that Promenade. But the works have been completed, and the Karlovac frog has still not received a new place.

The monument to the frog was unveiled on the 31st of March 2008, and it was made by the academic sculptor Stjepan Gračan. It was donated to Karlovac by the City of Zagreb on the initiative of Zvonimir Bešker, a Karlovac native who worked in the Zagreb city administration. It arrived in the city two years before it was placed, and in the meantime the best place for it was being sought; even placement on the wall of the city magistrate was considered. In the end a location accessible to passers-by and children was chosen, for whom it was believed they would rejoice most in the new attraction.

a monument to the frog catchers of karlovac

The Karlovac frog was chosen because of the old nickname of the people of Karlovac: the inhabitants of the city on four rivers were once, namely, called frog-catchers (žabari). What was once a pejorative name, some of the inhabitants over time accepted as part of their identity. While the frog was still standing in its place, a story also appeared that it brings luck: one was supposed to, allegedly, rub it behind the left eye and make a wish. Whether the firefighters today whisper their wishes to the frog or have already become so used to it that they don’t even notice it, we don’t know, but we believe that many more people would rejoice in it on some public surface.
