“We learned only in 1981 that a forced-labor camp had operated inside the museum during the final months of the occupation,” says Valentyna Avramenko, head of the Tarasova Svitlytsia section.

She recalls a visitor from Moscow who wandered through the galleries as if he knew every corner of the building. It turned out that he was a native of the area who, as a teenager, had been caught in a roundup.

Young people were deported to the Reich for forced labor, while children as young as 13 or 14 were made to dig trenches and build fortifications. Several hundred schoolchildren were held inside the building, half-starved, sleeping on damp, rotting straw alongside horses. A toilet had been hacked directly into the parquet floor. Armed guards marched the children to the banks of the Dnipro with shovels and forced them to work under gunpoint. If one escaped, the others were beaten almost to death.

Staff at the reserve began tracking down the former child prisoners and recording their testimonies. Those who had survived long enough were later helped to submit applications for compensation from Germany. Why had no one spoken about the camp sooner?

The author found the answer herself in an archival leaflet issued by the Taras Shevchenko partisan unit, which operated in the forests of the Cherkasy region:

“We will find and kill everyone who helps the Germans build defensive lines along the Dnipro!”

Makohon’s bust: From Kaniv to Volodarka

In Davidzon’s second photograph, Shevchenko’s bust has a bullet hole in its forehead. The resemblance to the monument in Borodianka, shot up by Russian forces in 2022, is chilling.

The author was told that Ivan Makohon, a prominent Soviet Ukrainian sculptor, had created the plaster bust in 1937 specifically for the opening of the museum in Kaniv. But the work’s fate after World War II remains unknown. It is held neither in the museum’s exhibition nor in the collection of Ukraine’s National Art Museum.

The sculptor’s son, Ihor Makohon, himself a painter, sculptor and graphic artist, is now 90 and lives in Italy. He was surprised to hear the story of the wounded, missing Kobzar.

“There must be some misunderstanding! I visited Kaniv in the mid-1950s and took photographs. The bust was on the second-floor balcony, completely undamaged.

“In 1961, my father decided to modify the composition slightly, adding shoulders. The new version was more monumental. Two plaster casts were made in the workshop at the Kyiv Art Institute, where Professor Makohon taught, and the mold was preserved.”

More than 60 years passed. In 2024, Ihor Makohon received a request from Volodarka, a district center in the Kyiv region. Local residents wanted to install a “historic” Shevchenko monument by Makohon and asked for his permission.

Ihor Ivanovych not only found the original mold but also arranged for the bust to be produced.

“We cast the bust in concrete with the lads and took it to Volodarka. There was enormous interest, and a lot of people gathered,” he recalls.

The unveiling took place on the Feast of the Intercession of the Holy Mother of God, which Ukraine also celebrates as the Day of Defenders and Defendresses. The project fulfilled an idea conceived by Oleksandr Ushynskyi, a local resident, environmentalist, researcher of the Holodomor, Maidan protester and war veteran.

In 2014, Ushynskyi volunteered for the front, defended Donetsk airport and later established a community museum dedicated to the Russian-Ukrainian war in his hometown. The monument in Volodarka became the 1,385th monument to Shevchenko in Ukraine and around the world.

The nazis, the communists and Russian propaganda

“Both the Nazis during World War II and the Soviets used Shevchenko to manipulate Ukrainians’ minds for propaganda purposes,” says Ihor Solovey, head of the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security under Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture.

“The Nazis tried to exploit our national sentiments under the guise of ‘friendship.’

“They took passages from Kobzar and amplified them to turn people against Soviet rule. The message was supposedly about resistance to Russian oppression, mixed with all sorts of vile nonsense about ‘Jewish Bolshevism.’ They even put Taras’s words on posters – the familiar line: ‘Muscovites are strangers; they bring you harm.’

“To present themselves as benefactors, the Nazis deliberately published his poetry and prose during the occupation and ran articles about Shevchenko that served their purposes. They wanted people to believe that Ukrainian culture was free and flourishing under the Reich.”

“The Communists did exactly the same thing. They just dressed it up differently to persuade Ukrainians to fight the Germans. Think of the famous rallying cry: ‘Drench freedom in the enemy’s blood!’” Solovey continues.

Eighty years have passed. In June 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service announced that a 57-year-old woman from Kaniv had been formally notified of suspicion over the dissemination of “materials justifying and denying the Russian Federation’s armed aggression against Ukraine.”

The woman reportedly referred to the invasion as a “special military operation,” urged support for the Russian army and openly promoted pro-Kremlin narratives among acquaintances and colleagues. According to investigators, she was one of the deputy heads of the Shevchenko National Reserve.

Modern Russian propaganda reproduces methods first used under the Russian Empire and later adopted by the Soviet Union. One is to present Shevchenko primarily as part of Russian culture, pointing to the fact that he wrote his diaries and prose in Russian.

Another is to portray him as a “pan-Russian poet,” downplaying the importance of his work in shaping Ukrainian national identity.

But those carrying out Russia’s full-scale war on Ukrainian soil increasingly see Shevchenko, his monuments and his museums not as shared cultural heritage, but as an adversary and a source of resistance.

World.title: Mayor and entrepreneur: Transparency International calls for dismissal of Georgian officials over business ties
World.content:
TI identifies 24 officials heading private companies

Transparency International Georgia (TI) has identified 24 serving public officials who simultaneously hold directorships at 30 private companies, in violation of anti-corruption legislation.

The officials include mayors, deputy mayors, heads of municipal councils and representatives of state agencies.

Georgian law prohibits public officials from simultaneously engaging in business activities. TI says officials whose violations are confirmed must be dismissed.

Under the law, newly appointed officials have 10 days to relinquish their positions as directors of commercial organisations. Failure to comply requires them to leave public service.

What the law says

Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest.

At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director.

Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

World.title: Council of Europe chief: Ban on opposition parties in Georgia could be challenged in Strasbourg court
World.content:
Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset has said that legal issues surrounding the initiative to ban opposition parties in Georgia could come before the European Court of Human Rights.

On 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began hearing a case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition groups: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. The lawsuit alleges that these parties violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits parties whose aim is to overthrow or forcibly change the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments is that the parties refuse to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. All five parties deny the allegations. Hearings are scheduled to continue until 30 October. The court must deliver its final ruling by 24 June 2027. A simple majority is required to uphold the claim, meaning four of the seven judges must vote in favour.

Berset made the statement at a meeting of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg on 27 October.

He described the deterioration of democratic processes in Georgia as alarming and urged the authorities to protect political pluralism.

Berset commented on Georgia’s political situation after Nadine Pittfield, a British politician and head of Derby City Council, asked about developments in the country and the Constitutional Court case seeking to ban five pro-Western opposition parties.

Berset said the deterioration of democratic processes in Georgia, new laws restricting civic space and pressure on the opposition were causes for serious concern.

“All of this undermines political pluralism and the country’s commitments as a member of the Council of Europe,” Berset said.

He noted that Council of Europe member states must respect the European Convention on Human Rights and the case law of the European Court of Human Rights.

Berset stressed that any decision to ban a political party must have a strong legal basis and strictly comply with the principles of necessity and proportionality.

He said he would refrain from predicting the outcome of the ongoing constitutional dispute in Georgia, but did not rule out the possibility that important legal aspects of the case could eventually come before the Strasbourg court.

He urged Georgia’s ruling majority to protect political pluralism and stressed that his statement was not intended to influence the Constitutional Court’s decision.

The Secretary General noted that he had always sought to take an active role in the work of the Council of Europe delegation in Georgia and maintain close contact with the authorities.

“In September, during a meeting with Prime Minister Kobakhidze in New York, I discussed the decline of democratic processes in Georgia and stressed the importance of honouring the country’s commitments. I would also like to mention the Venice Commission’s recent recommendations on restrictive legislation in Georgia.

“The situation is quite difficult at the moment. Membership of the Council of Europe means more than joining a club of countries. It entails accepting high-level commitments based on the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as an obligation to comply with court rulings,” Alain Berset said.

He noted that he regularly meets representatives of the Georgian government because Georgia is one of the Council of Europe’s 46 member states.

World.title: Azerbaijani, Georgian PMs attend inauguration of ART Riverfront Hotel Tbilisi (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Prime Ministers Ali Asadov of Azerbaijan and Irakli Kobakhidze of Georgia attended the inauguration of ART Riverfront Hotel Tbilisi.

Located on the banks of the Kura River in the Georgian capital, the hotel combines modern design with an artistic concept. It offers 152 rooms, a restaurant, conference halls and a range of other amenities.

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva attend official opening of Art Weekend (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. The official opening of the Fly to Baku. Art Weekend. Sense the Future NOW festival was held at the Heydar Aliyev Center on October 30.

Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Founder of IDEA Public Union, together with Alena Aliyeva, attended the opening ceremony of the festival.

The Heydar Aliyev Center presented several exhibitions as part of the "Art Weekend" opening.

Addressing the opening ceremony, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Founder of IDEA Public Union, said that renowned artists from various countries joined the event. “And over the next few days, you will discover many paintings, installations, sculptures, and performances. All to show the beauty of nature and also its strength and its rigidity.

In 2012, we have established a Caucasus "Big Five" that include endangered species of animals, which are the brown bear, grey wolf, the Caucasian leopard, the imperial eagle, and the gazelle. And since then, we have worked together with local departments and international organizations to preserve these endangered species of animals and to reintroduce them into the wild and also to increase their habitat. And it has been quite successful.

In order to understand nature and to love it, the best way is to spend more time in the nature. Then you can really connect to it. And also, we want to make sure that everybody remembers that they can make a huge difference by themselves, even with very small actions. So, this is what the Sense the Future NOW festival means to us,” Leyla Aliyeva added.

The event also featured the national dances performed by Azerbaijan State Children's Philharmonic

Expressing his gratitude to Leyla Aliyeva on behalf of international art representatives, who have come to Baku to participate in the festival Fly to Baku. Art Weekend. Sense the Future NOW, Art curator Simon de Pury said: “Back in 2012, I had the great pleasure to meet you there in London. And I remember you said there are two things that I'm really very, very interested in. One is, I really want the artists from Azerbaijan to get a wide acknowledgement, to get widely seen around the world and to get a lot of international exposure. And so we discussed and did do an exhibition in 2012, Fly to Baku, which incorporated some of the greatest and most interesting living artists of Azerbaijan.

We did the first exhibition in London. It was a huge success and subsequently, that exhibition travelled to many cities. It went to Paris, it went to Moscow, it went to several cities around the world.

Then, in 2016, we did a great retrospective dedicated to the American artist George Condo. And that exhibition was a big success here in the Heydar Aliyev Centre. And that is when I discovered this incredible building Zaha Hadid was one of the greatest architects of our time. And I think that the building in which we are now is her magnus opus. In my view, it's her best work in a brilliant career.”

The event featured the immersive theatrical performance authored and directed by Parviz Mammadrzayev, with the visual atmosphere created for "Art Weekend" by Laman Yusifli. Through choreography, music, and visual storytelling, the play embodies a poetic journey that explores the fragile relationship between humanity and nature.

Following the ceremony, the Azerbaijan State Dance Ensemble performed "Jangi" and "Yalli," dances showcasing the country’s ancient dance traditions.

Held for the second consecutive year at the initiative of Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Head of the IDEA Public Union, the festival's exhibition program brings together diverse artistic approaches, generations, and geographies, offering audiences an opportunity to reflect on themes such as memory, cultural heritage, nature, biodiversity, identity, and the future.

The “Big Five of the Caucasus” is one of the key themes of this year’s “Art Weekend,” exploring the region’s biodiversity and the role of animals in cultural memory, mythology and collective identity.

Another project presented in the Heydar Aliyev Center is “Legendary Creatures: An Azerbaijani Bestiary”. Connecting the “Big Five” with mythological creatures from Azerbaijani folklore, it highlights the importance of preserving wildlife and cultural heritage.

The exhibition features six works by six artists, including carpet art, sculpture, photography, metalwork and mixed media.

All the works are presented to the public for the first time as part of “Art Weekend.”

A contemporary art exhibition “When Nature Speaks. Heirs” features the Caucasian leopard, brown bear, grey wolf, golden eagle and goitered gazelle, exploring the relationship between humanity and nature, highlighting heritage, responsibility and the natural world we leave to future generations. It brings together artists working in installation, sculpture, ceramics, textiles and mixed media.

Attendees then toured an exhibition titled “The Skin of Truth” by Chinese artist Zhang Ji feature works from the artist’s “The Skin of Truth” and “Ultima” series, blending architectural motifs from different religious and cultural traditions with contemporary painting. Inspired by landmarks such as the Great Mosque of Córdoba and the Alhambra Palace, Zhang Ji uses a syringe instead of a brush to create raised surfaces reminiscent of bas-relief sculpture. His works have been exhibited in the United States, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, China, France, Spain, Switzerland, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and other countries, and included in collections worldwide.

The Heydar Aliyev Center also presents “What If Women Ruled the World?” by renowned American artist Judy Chicago and Italian artist Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Mirror of Eternity.

Since 2022, the What If Women Ruled the World?” project has developed a global archive spanning several countries. Visitors in Baku will be able to contribute to its next chapter by answering questions in an interactive recording booth.

Italian artist Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Mirror of Eternity project employs artificial intelligence to combine human portraits, generating new faces that have never existed before. Participants upload their portraits to the system, which then merges them with another person’s portrait to create a new image. Each portrait thus exists not as a fixed record of memory, but as an evolving digital entity transformed through successive encounters. The project explores the relationship between humanity, memory, technology, and the ever-changing nature of life.

The Fly to Baku. Art Weekend. Sense the Future NOW festival will run until November 1.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s average monthly wages rise 18%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Uzbekistan’s average monthly nominal accrued wage reached 7.27 million soums (about $606) in January-September 2026, up 18% year over year, according to data from the country’s Statistics Agency. The figures exclude agricultural enterprises and small businesses.

Tashkent recorded the highest average monthly wage, at 12.3 million soums (around $1,026), an increase of 18.3% compared with the same period in 2025. The figure was about 69% above the national average.

Navoi region ranked second, with an average monthly wage of 8.82 million soums (approx. $736), followed by Tashkent region at 6.89 million soums (about $574). Bukhara region recorded an average of 5.84 million soums (around $487), while wages in Samarkand region reached 5.37 million soums (approx. $448).

Qashqadaryo region reported the lowest average monthly wage, at approximately 4.97 million soums (about $414), followed by Surkhandarya region at 4.99 million soums (around $416). Namangan region recorded an average of 5.40 million soums (approx. $450).

In terms of annual growth, Namangan region led the country, with average wages increasing by 20.3%. Jizzakh region followed at 19.8%, while Tashkent region recorded 19.1% growth. Samarkand region posted the slowest increase, at 11.5%.

According to Trend’s calculations, the national average monthly wage increased by approximately 1.11 million soums (about $92.60) compared with the same period last year. Tashkent’s average was about 2.48 times the wage recorded in Qashqadaryo region, highlighting substantial regional differences in nominal earnings.

The longer-term trend also shows sustained wage growth. The national average rose from 3.73 million soums (around $311) in January-September 2022 to 7.27 million soums (approx. $606) in the same period of 2026, an increase of approximately 94.8% over four years.

However, nominal wage growth does not necessarily translate into an equivalent increase in purchasing power. The real improvement in workers’ living standards depends on inflation, while differences in regional economic activity, employment structure and the composition of surveyed businesses may also affect average wage figures.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s broad money supply rises 16.7% to $32.95B year over year
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. As of October 1 of this year, the broad money supply (M3) in Azerbaijan stood at 56.008 billion manat ($32.95 billion).

According to Trend’s calculations based on the statistical bulletin of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), the M3 money supply increased by 8.022 billion manat ($4.72 billion), or 16.7%, compared to October 1, 2025.

During the reporting period, the manat money supply (M2) totaled 45.118 billion manat ($26.539 billion). This figure increased by 7.929 billion manat ($4.67 billion), or 21.3%, compared to the same date last year. As of October 1, 2025, the M2 money supply stood at 37.188 billion manat ($21.88 billion).

As of October 1 of this year, the M1 money supply, which includes demand deposits and non-bank currency in circulation, amounted to 34.484 billion manat ($20.29 billion). This represents an increase of 5.016 billion manat ($2.95 billion), or 17%, year-over-year. As of October 1 of last year, the M1 monetary aggregate stood at 29.468 billion manat ($17.34 billion).

At the same time, the volume of cash outside banks (monetary aggregate M0) amounted to 19.126 billion manat ($11.25 billion). Compared to the same period in 2025, the volume of M0 increased by 2.115 billion manat ($1.25 billion), or 12.4%. As of October 1 of last year, this figure stood at 17.011 billion manat ($10.01 billion).

According to the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), as of October 1, 2026, the ratio of monetary aggregate M3 to monetary aggregate M2 was 2.09, and the ratio of monetary aggregate M2 to monetary aggregate M1 was 1.82.

The M3 monetary aggregate encompasses the broad money supply; M2 represents demand deposits; and M1 consists of demand deposits and cash in circulation.

World.title: Iranian banks' agricultural lending surges 87% to $1.66B in six months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Loans extended by Iranian banks to the agricultural sector rose 87% in the first six months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through September 22, 2026), compared with the same period last year (March 21 through September 22, 2025).

According to Trend’s calculations based on statistics from the Central Bank of Iran, loans to the agricultural sector totaled 3.09 quadrillion rials (around $1.66 billion) during the six-month period, compared with 1.65 quadrillion rials (approximately $885 million) in the same period last year.

Loans worth 2.36 quadrillion rials (around $1.27 billion) were provided to the agricultural sector for working capital.

During the six months, banks extended 458 trillion rials (approximately $245 million) in loans to establish agricultural enterprises and develop orchards and cultivated land.

Another 97.1 trillion rials (around $52 million) in loans were allocated to agricultural sector development.

The statistics also show that loans worth 72 trillion rials (approximately $38.5 million) were provided to the agricultural sector on a non-repayable basis, while 65.7 trillion rials (around $35 million) went toward the purchase of personal equipment, 38.7 trillion rials (approximately $20.7 million) toward self-employment, and 197 billion rials (around $105,000) toward repairs.

Overall, banks and financial institutions in Iran extended loans worth 55.3 quadrillion rials (approximately $29.6 billion) across various sectors during the first six months of the current Iranian year. Total lending increased by 57.3% compared with the same period last year.

Meanwhile, in Iran, the year is called the "true solar year." The current year in Iran is 1405. The Iranian year begins on March 20 or 21. The first 6 months of the year have 31 days, the next 6 months have 30 days, and the last month has 29 days in 3-year cycles and 30 days in 4-year cycles. Thus, the months of the Iranian year begin on the 21st, 22nd, or 23rd of the Gregorian calendar.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 31, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 35th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to the German ARD TV channel on October 28.

- The territory of Tartar, Aghdam, and Agjabadi districts came under artillery fire.

- The Defense Ministry has announced the latest situation on the frontline as of October 31. The list of destroyed military equipment of Armenian troops has been announced. In response to the artillery fire at Gubadli district, a return fire was opened at Armenian troops.

- Qiyameddinli village of Agjabadi districts was fired upon. Armenian Armed Forces tried to lay the groundwork for future provocations by bringing phosphorus-laden cargo in the direction of Khojavend.

- A video of the destruction of equipment and manpower of Armenian troops has been released.

- Fighting continued in the direction of Aghdara, Khojavend, Gubadli.

- The reconnaissance and sabotage group of the Armenian Armed Forces was destroyed, and a video of the destruction of two military vehicles was released.

World.title: Creator's monster Halloween display proves 'people aren't so scary'
World.content:
With its webs, witches and werewolves, Halloween draws Zoe McKavanagh further out of her shell every year.

The 30-year-old Gold Coast resident lives with autism and has, for the past six years, slowly collected a monster haul of pumpkins, spiders and skulls of different shapes and sizes.

Zoe McKavanagh is considering a competition to name the giant spider, which is her favourite decoration. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"I love Halloween because of how happy it makes everyone," Ms McKavanagh said.

"People often call Christmas the giving holiday but with that you only do family and friends — this way you can do it for everyone."

Speaking with people outside her family hasn't always been easy for Ms McKavanagh.

"I did a lot of her talking for her when she was growing up," her mum and full-time carer, Colleen Millard, said.

"She would whisper in my ear because she was scared of talking to people, she wouldn't go around people, or she would hide from them."

Colleen Millard (left) says her daughter used to hide from the trick-or-treaters who would come to visit their home. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

She said in the first few years of creating Halloween displays, her daughter would do all the work but then hide in the house when trick-or-treaters arrived.

"Slowly, over the years she's started to stay out … and now it's got to the point where she'll talk to people without me doing it for her," Ms Millard said.

" It brings tears to your eyes … that's such a big, big step. "

Despite the ghoulish and often dark themes of Halloween, Ms McKavanagh said she saw light in the community's love of the occasion.

Zoe McKavanagh's collection of pumpkins grows larger after every Halloween. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"Everyone's so nice, they're so excited about the decorations, so kind about the treats and everything," she said.

" It's made me realise that people aren't so scary. "

Retailers use spooks as signpost for spending

Griffith University business analyst and retail expert Graeme Hughes said the national consumer spend on Halloween had increased year-on-year for the past decade.

Research from the National Retail Association and Roy Morgan predicts Australians will spend more than $500 million on Halloween this year.

"If we go back 10 years, very few consumers would celebrate this tradition but now, 10 years on, we're seeing all sorts of people really buying into it," Mr Hughes said.

Some Halloween decorations incorporate movement sensors and electronics, driving up the cost. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

He said once people started spending, retailers were quick to encourage them to keep it up.

"It's critical for business now to signal that something's happening, to get everybody, young and old, involved in that retail spend cycle," he said.

"We know that this really does have a knock-on effect for those Christmas sales … and we're seeing retailers trying to get as much as they can when we know that consumers are doing it tough."

Little rest for the wicked or the whimsical

Halloween display creator Ian Kane draws on his experience as a DJ and lighting technician to put on an annual show in the front yard of his Gold Coast home.

Ian Kane says Halloween allows him to be more creative than he can with Christmas lights. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Mr Kane said he'd been doing a Christmas display for the past 20 years, but first decided to "take on" Halloween five years ago.

"I've always loved Christmas, but I find Halloween's a bit more exciting," Mr Kane said.

" There's a lot more stuff you can do with Halloween, so it makes it more interesting. "

Mr Kane's display incorporates dozens of creepy characters, smoke machines, lasers, lights, and even motion sensors connected to pneumatic relays and an air compressor.

Ian Kane's favourite Halloween decoration is an animatronic dragon to which he's added a smoke machine. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

"With all the pneumatics, you can get some really powerful effects and some good jump scares," he said.

"It's just great seeing all the kids happy."

After Halloween, Mr Kane spends days dismantling his display — almost as long as he spends putting it up.

Ian Kane's Burleigh home is transformed every Halloween. (ABC Gold Coast: Mark Rigby)

Then his attention turns to his Christmas lights.

"Come Boxing Day I turn everything off for Christmas and then get to have a bit of a break," he said.

"I'll get a week off work if I'm lucky."

World.title: Council proposes road extension through protected wildlife sanctuary
World.content:
Since it was established nearly a decade ago, the Wandiyali-Environa Wildlife Sanctuary has become an ecological haven.

It is home to a variety of native plants and animals, many of them rare or endangered.

Box-gum grassy woodland, gang-gang cockatoos and pink-tailed worm lizards are all there, and a koala was sighted earlier this year — a rare species in the ACT region.

Carolyn Larkham opposes council's proposal to build a road through the sanctuary. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

"We've seen an amazing response here," Carolyn Larkham, Wandiyali's environmental coordinator and landowner said.

"We're still getting new sightings of plants and animals … There are these species that we know are regionally very rare, and they're all represented here in this one place."

The natural ecosystem is near the growing Googong and Jerrabomberra region, where residents have hoped for decades for better road infrastructure to connect the area to Canberra and the ACT.

Wandiyali-Environa Wildlife Sanctuary is home to several threatened animals and plants. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

The Queanbeyan-Palerang council endorsed its preferred road route last week, after ongoing debate and a consultant's report into the various development options.

Known as option five, the road will cut through the wildlife sanctuary.

Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council Mayor Kenrick Winchester said it was the only viable choice.

Kenrick Winchester says putting the road through the sanctuary is the right choice. (ABC News: Ruby Thomas)

"We will now be proceeding with getting the studies done to try to prove to the New South Wales Minister for Environment that the road must and should only go via that option five," he said.

The council's preferred option is more expensive than several others, but the consultant report showed it had a higher cost-benefit ratio.

Ms Larkham said the choice was disappointing, given there were alternative routes available and other recommendations made.

Conservation Council ACT biodiversity working group chair Matt Whitting said he understood residents' commuting needs, but there had been 25 years of conservation work at the protected sanctuary.

Matt Whitting is concerned about the future of the sanctuary. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

"We've got a lot of sympathy with the residents of Googong, who've been told for decades that this might be possible and that might be possible," he said.

" But this place has been set aside securely, legally protected, and we can't afford to just keep squandering opportunities to protect really high conservation value places like this one. "

Cr Winchester said council wanted to limit damage to the stewardship site, and it was a "delicate balance between the environment and the needs of the population.

The sanctuary is home to a variety of native plants and animals. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

He said that all the options for the road route were "problematic", but council would not support a route through existing suburban development.

"The council made it very clear that they do not want the road to impact on houses and on people and where they live," he said.

" We would much prefer to have a small impact on that sanctuary site than potentially have to knock down, compulsorily acquire houses that people have spent generations growing up in. "

The Queanbeyan-Palerang council will take its case to the New South Wales government.

The government is not expected to decide on the proposal until at least mid-next year.

It is a decision that Ms Larkham said must be made in the interests of the natural environment.

"We have community programs with Jerrabomberra High School and University of Canberra, and we have community engagement through our wildflower walks," she said.

"Habitat fragmentation is such a death of a thousand cuts to these sorts of areas."

World.title: Etsy cracks down on AI-copying issues but some users still sceptical
World.content:
Global online marketplace Etsy has updated its artificial intelligence policies following widespread criticism from users faced with AI-generated products.

Etsy recently sent an email to sellers, informing them of the changes, and published the new policy online.

"We recognise we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted," it said.

" AI is threatening [buyer] trust, and we have a responsibility to protect it. "

The statement provided a list of policy updates to set clearer restrictions on AI use.

Lucy Cooper checks out Etsy's new policy on AI-generated art. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

One requires sellers to include at least one unedited photo of their item against a real background, with exceptions for some products.

"Some digital items, like audio files, don't have visual elements. For those listings, you may use representative imagery, including AI-generated images, as long as it doesn't mislead buyers about what they're purchasing," it said.

Photo-editing tools, such as exposure, crop and background adjustments, including AI, are still allowed for other listing images "as long as those edits don't make the item appear different".

Etsy said that if the item received by buyers is "materially different" from the listing images, the seller may be responsible for a refund.

Lucy Cooper is sceptical that the platform is taking AI-generated copies seriously. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Another update banned AI-generated functional guides like recipes and crochet patterns.

Listings for these items that aren't AI-generated must also provide an image of a real result.

New features are also being introduced, such as a specific "misleading AI-generated images" reporting option and guidance for listing photos.

However, at this stage, the reports are only to help Etsy "better understand how members perceive potential AI misuse and won't result in immediate enforcement action".

It's unclear if the guidance for listing photos has been implemented.

AI-generated art, like prints, are still permitted "when sellers play a clear creative role in what they create and are transparent about their process".

'Bit of a laugh', seller says

Earlier this month the ABC spoke with Lucy Cooper, a Hobart-based crochet artist known for her 90s-surf-wear-inspired spiral beanie design.

Ms Cooper said she had discovered an Etsy store selling an AI-generated version of her crochet beanie pattern, with AI-generated images.

Lucy Cooper's small business started gaining traction in March with her "spiral beanie" design. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Etsy's new AI policy changes suggest it will prevent experiences like hers from occurring.

However, it has since happened again.

Ms Cooper found another Etsy store selling an AI-generated version of her beanie pattern, and all eight product images were generated by AI.

Lucy Cooper has been crocheting since she was 15. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

The listing was published on October 28, six days after Etsy announced its policy update.

"It's good that they're actually doing something, but I think that it's a little bit of a laugh," Ms Cooper said.

" They're addressing the problem, but they're not actually really doing anything about it. "

Ms Cooper said she felt the changes relied too heavily on sellers doing the right thing.

"The problem is people aren't being honest," she said.

"If you're the platform owner, you have to do something to make it so that this can't happen."

Lucy Cooper recently discovered a US-based Etsy store was selling a copy of her spiral beanie with AI-generated images. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Etsy's community has mixed feelings

Following Etsy's announcement, users across the globe took to social media to voice their opinions on the changes.

In an Instagram post, Jade, a seamstress, said, "It seemed like [Etsy] didn't want to demonise AI usage, but I think that's going to alienate a large part of their database — buyers and sellers alike — who are truly anti-AI."

In the comments, one user said: "They are trying to serve a larger group of people and shops. Banning AI entirely would mean a lot of shops would close.

"I am a visual and web designer, photographer and … wood artisan. I create physical and digital crafts. There is a place for AI, and banning it would really make some parts of the design process unnecessarily slow.

" Just because so many create AI slop does not mean the entire use of AI should be banned. It just needs more guidance. "

In another post, Molly, a crochet artist, asked, "is Etsy going to take a proactive approach to finding [AI-generated pattern listings]? I think that these are positive changes … I'll believe it when I see it."

Etsy has acknowledged it failed to address AI issues as quickly as users may have wanted. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Some are frustrated by Etsy's decision to not immediately remove listings that are reported for AI misuse.

"I think [the new reporting feature is] really good. But if you're not going to do anything about it, what's the point of it being there?" Ms Cooper said.

"When you report an item, and you say it's AI-generated or this pattern doesn't work or it's copyright or it's plagiarism, it should immediately get taken down, or they should notify you what's happening with it."

Changes just a 'starting point', Etsy says

Etsy says it is aware there is more to address as AI continues to evolve, and that it will keep making improvements as it listens to its community and learns what it needs.

"We recognise we haven't always addressed the topic of AI as directly or as quickly as you may have wanted," the company said.

"It's changing fast, and like many of you, we're thinking seriously about what it means for Etsy, what's allowed on our marketplace, and how it impacts running a creative business.

"We are closely monitoring developments in this rapidly evolving area, listening to feedback from our community, and periodically re-evaluating our policies.

"These changes are our starting point, not the finish line."

World.title: Triple premiership coach Chris Fagan joins Carlton as director of football
World.content:
Chris Fagan has made the next step in his football career, with the triple premiership coach joining Carlton as director of coaching.

The newly created role will see Fagan, who announced his departure from Brisbane after the team's third consecutive grand final win, join the Blues to provide support to coach Josh Fraser.

The move reunites Fagan with Blues chief executive Graham Wright. The pair worked together at Hawthorn when Fagan was head of coaching and development and then general manager of football operations as the Hawks won three flags in a row between 2013 and 2015.

Fagan steps down from Brisbane Lions AFL premiership-winning coach Chris Fagan has stepped down from the club days after securing a third-straight grand final victory.

In a club statement Fagan said the chance to join the Blues was "an opportunity too good to pass up".

"While I loved my 10 years as a senior coach, this is a role I am passionate about and where I know I can have a real impact in this next phase of my football career," Fagan said.

"Supporting people to get the absolute best out of themselves is what I love most about football, so the chance to now be able to do that on a full-time basis is incredibly exciting.

"I can't wait to connect with each person in the football department, and in particular work closely with Josh to help every coach and player be the best Carlton person they can possibly be."

After four finals in 2023 and 2024 combined, Carlton missed finals in 2025 before coach Michael Voss was sacked after a 1-8 start to 2026.

Interim coach (now permanent) Fraser then led the Blues to 11 wins and a draw from the final 14 games to get Carlton to the finals. The Blues beat Melbourne in a wild card game before an elimination final loss to Geelong.

ABC

World.title: G20 foreign ministers skip 'family' photo amid objections over Russia
World.content:
Foreign ministers from the G20 have skipped a traditional group photo ahead of their meeting after European and Australian representatives objected to the presence of Russia.

A US official said the State Department had taken the family photo off the official agenda on Friday, US time, because Washington did not want it to become a spectacle or distraction.

A third of the participants, including Australia and Canada, made clear they opposed the idea of being photographed alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.

A spokesperson for Foreign Minister Penny Wong said they support the decision of the United States as G20 host to cancel the photograph.

"Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia's brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine," the statement said.

"Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy."

The 2026 G20 Summit is taking place at the Trump National Doral Miami. (Reuters: Megan Varner/Pool)

European G20 members also back Ukraine, which has objected to US President Donald Trump's recent decisions over Russia, including a deal to buy diesel and waive some sanctions.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband explicitly called out Mr Lavrov, saying that "if we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine".

"An assault not only on Ukraine but on us all — trampling international law, sovereignty and self determination — core principles on which we all depend," he said.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters in Atlanta that, "I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov."

Consensus looks elusive

Secretary of State Marco Rubio opened the talks with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.

"We are in a critical moment," Mr Rubio told his colleagues.

" We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises. "

Mr Rubio pointed to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation and said many are posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for unity, saying the world is in "a critical moment". (Reuters: Megan Varner/Pool)

Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they faced.

Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the US-Israeli war against Iran, US tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.

Australia bids for UN Security Council seat Anthony Albanese plans to trade on Australia's good name and international reputation as he officially launches the campaign for a two-year term on the powerful United Nations Security Council.

Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia's position on Ukraine was unyielding — as was its opposition to Poland's membership in the G20.

Those disagreements, which also cover the Trump administration's not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will likely prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.

Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month's G20 leaders summit hosted by Mr Trump in Florida a success.

AP/Reuters

World.title: The visually impaired triathlete preparing to take on a half marathon
World.content:
When Mathew Kent is competing in the first leg of a triathlon or half ironman event, things can feel a little dicey.

"I get very paranoid when I feel a splash around me swimming," says the 37-year-old visually impaired athlete.

"I hope it's a person, not a shark."

Kent has retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic eye disorder that causes vision loss including night blindness and tunnel vision, with his vision currently limited to 0-5 degrees.

"It's almost like putting a hole through a piece of paper and you look through that hole … you just see what's in front of you," he says.

During the swim leg of a triathlon, Kent is connected to a guide via a tether around both of their waists.

The pair stay out wide of the pack to avoid thrashing arms and potential collisions.

The pair share a laugh while competing in the Barwon Heads Triathlon. (Supplied: Beckworth Racing)

"Because [the guide] is on my left, I breathe a lot to my left. So I try and find him while I'm swimming," Kent says.

"If the tether gets really tight, I know I'm going the wrong way — then I try and push back into him.

"Every now and then I swim over the top of him," he laughs.

Kent, who lives in Albury, is training for the Ironman 70.3 Melbourne on November 8, which he will tackle with guide Brad Manczak.

The 70.3 represents the number of miles covered, which equates to 113 kilometres, accounting for the 1.8-kilometre swim, 90-kilometre ride and 21.1-kilometre run.

The pair has already competed in other events together including the half marathon in the recent Geelong Running Festival, along with the Ironman 70.3 Geelong in March and the Barwon Heads Triathlon.

Kent (left) and Manczak compete in the half marathon at the Geelong Running Festival in September. (Supplied)

A sport-loving teen who began losing his vision

Kent was fully sighted until he was 15, after which he gradually began losing his vision.

He could still get his car licence, as long as he didn't drive at night.

However, by age 20, Kent says he had lost most of his sight — and as a result, that car licence and much of his freedom.

"You have to sort of change everything you do," he says.

" You can't just go out and do what you want, when you want. "

Having been a sporty teen who loved water polo, Kent found himself limited in the sporting activities he could do.

That was until his brother Jeremy "dragged" him into triathlon about three years ago, becoming his first guide.

Mathew Kent's brother Jeremy (right) encouraged him to give triathlons a go. (Supplied)

Last year, the brothers attempted a full ironman in Busselton, Western Australia.

They had completed the 3.8-kilometre swim, and were about 20 kilometres off finishing the 180-kilometre bike leg when they had to pull out due to illness.

The ups and downs of competing in a pair

Kent now mostly trains with the help of a local support worker, and then teams up with Manczak, who lives in Jan Juc, for race days.

Manczak, an experienced triathlete and ironman, says being a guide is a very different experience to racing solo.

"You've got to try to navigate a tandem bike," he says.

"But also just that communication and being aware of everything around you really."

Four legs are better than two — until it comes to going uphill. (Supplied: Beckworth Racing)

From his perspective, the swim leg is the easiest part of a triathlon because there is not much to do in terms of communicating with Kent.

"He'll just keep a feel of where I am, and I'll just make sure he's OK," Manczak says.

From there, they will reach a specially allocated section of the transition area and switch to Kent's custom-made tandem bike — imported from the Czech Republic.

And while the pair does not always stand out in the swim and run legs, Kent's extra-long bike is a show stopper.

"They do notice a tandem bike," Manczak says, noting that four legs rather than two can equate to a fair bit of speed.

" When you're flying past somebody and they turn around and there's a longer tandem bike, it does raise an eyebrow. "

While Kent says it is great fun smashing the field on the downhill sections, with the pair reaching up to 70 kilometres an hour, inclines are another story.

"We're like a truck going up a hill because we're double the weight on the bike."

'Enjoying the moment' as next challenge nears

By the time they reach the run leg of a triathlon, the field has thankfully usually spread out.

Kent and Manczak use the same tether they did in the swim, again fixed around their waists.

If it is a consistently flat section, Manczak says his offsider will just jog normally.

However, Kent may sometimes rest his hand on his arm for some extra support.

"Where the guide comes into most importance is during the run because any change in gradient or surface or anything around, you kind of have to talk Matt through it," Manczak says.

Competing in a triathlon or half ironman together is one way to forge a fast bond. (Supplied)

Manczak says triathlon can be a selfish sport, especially over longer distances.

"Unless you're training with a group, it's a lot of time on your own and it can be quite isolating," he says.

"So to help Matty out has been rewarding for myself. But it's great to see him achieve and be happy with the races as well."

As the November Melbourne half ironman nears, Kent says he does not have an exact time in mind but wouldn't mind finishing in about six hours.

It is a long time to be exercising intensely for.

"Oh it is, but we're done by lunchtime, and we can have a beer at 1 o'clock," Kent says.

And while he enjoys the challenge of such events, it's not really about winning, even if he and Manczak are likely to do very well in their category due to a dearth of other visually impaired competitors.

"You can't take life too seriously, with what I've been through," says Kent.

"Now I'm just having a bit of fun and just enjoying the moment."

World.title: Victorian town loses last LPG servo as demand for the fuel falls
World.content:
When Barry Nuttal's truck runs low on fuel, he has two options: drive a 120-kilometre round trip to the nearest LPG bowser, or fill up with petrol, which is more expensive.

Mr Nuttal lives in Horsham, a town of about 20,000 people on the Western Highway in the Wimmera region of western Victoria, about 300 kilometres from Melbourne.

The last service station in town selling LPG went into receivership this week, leaving drivers with nowhere to fill up.

Mr Nuttal's dual-fuel truck runs on both LPG and petrol, but he said driving to Warracknabeal, almost 60 kilometres away, to fill up was not economical.

"By the time you go up there you're running low, and by the time you come back, you're running low," he said.

" It's a sad indictment on the town. "

The BP on Baillie Street in Horsham was the last service station in town providing LPG gas for vehicles. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

LPG sales in Victoria have suffered a steep decline in recent years, dropping from 1.9 billion litres in 2011 to 242 million litres in 2025.

Mr Nuttal said friends had recently paid "a couple of thousand dollars" to convert their vehicles to gas to save money, and now "they can't fill up with gas at all in Horsham".

"It was a saving, that's why it was done, now they take it away," he said.

LPG cars disappearing from Australia's roads LPG vehicle owners are experiencing range anxiety as fewer service stations offer the cheaper alternative to petrol.

Dale Pickering, whose car relies solely on LPG, said once he had driven to Warracknabeal and back, gas would cost him the same as petrol.

"It seems ridiculous that we have over 20,000 people in the surrounding area and plenty of cars on gas," he said.

Kylie Holliday said she had not realised there was no LPG in town.

"I've got to go out of town now and I didn't realise that and I've got quarter of a tank of gas and I don't know whether I can make it to the next town," she said.

"I was thinking of getting my best friend to follow me to Stawell, so I could get gas just in case I run out."

BP Australia has been contacted for comment.

The last petrol station in Horsham that provided LPG has gone into receivership. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

Falling demand for LPG

The number of LPG vehicles in Australia has fallen from about 500,000 in 2013 to 200,000, according to ELGAS.

Australasian Convenience and Petroleum Marketers Association CEO, Rowan Lee, said demand for LPG had fallen as LPG cars left the fleet, and service station owners were generally not replacing tanks when they wore out.

"What they're replacing them with is car parks and so on, which will probably return the greater profit, because people come in and buy goods from the store" he said.

Rowan Lee says the demand for LPG has dropped and replacing infrastructure is expensive. (ABC News: Ed Gannon)

Mr Lee said it was "highly unlikely" the situation would be fixed in Horsham.

"It's really unfortunate for those people who are using LPG, and generally it's elderly people running older cars," he said.

Wimmera mechanic David Hateley, who has been a licensed LPG fitter for more than 30 years, said low-income drivers would be hit hardest.

Mechanic Dave Hateley says those already it tough would be feel the greatest brunt from the situation. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

"There's a lot of people out there with good old cars that have still got plenty of life left in them but you're going to see them get put off the road now because there's no LPG," he said.

Mr Hateley said drivers of dedicated LPG cars would arrive expecting a town the size of Horsham to have LPG.

"And when they get here they're going to need a tow truck to get into the next town," he said.

Federal member for the Mallee Anne Webster said she understood Horsham residents' frustration.

She said individual service stations were entitled to make commercial decisions about the fuel they provided.

Horsham Rural City Council said the situation had not been raised with it.

World.title: Who was behind the largest crypto heist in history?
World.content:
Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency has been hacked from exchange company Binance in the largest cyber attack in the cryptocurrency sector's history.

The bulk of the heist unfolded in about 20 minutes, blockchain records show, and 30 or 40 different tokens were affected, including Ethereum, Bitcoin, and stablecoins, according to crypto watchers.

So who did it and where has the money gone?

Who did it and how?

The exact culprit behind the heist isn't known, but many analysts have been quick to point the finger at a cyber unit in North Korea, which has previously orchestrated similar hacks.

US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs said the attack mirrored a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed to North Korea.

During the attack, hackers manipulated Binance's virtual wallets to empty into hack-controlled ones and from there move the money.

Bitcoins and cryptocurrencies issued by the Trump-family owned World Financial Liberty were affected by the hack. (Unsplash: Executium)

"TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence," the company said on its website.

"We make this judgement with high confidence."

Blockchain analysis company, Chainalysis, agreed with TRM's assessment.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a compromised laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.

Later, the company added it had uncovered additional points of breach.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has previously warned of the threat TraderTraitor posed, saying they had been targeting cryptocurrency companies since 2020.

"These actors will likely continue exploiting vulnerabilities of cryptocurrency technology firms, gaming companies, and exchanges to generate and launder funds to support the North Korean regime," it said in 2022.

Where is the money?

Binance has said customer funds are safe and it is working to recover $4.2 billion of funds it froze following the attack.

"[We have] begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," it said.

Binance CEO and founder Zhao Changpeng is the richest Canadian and 17th-richest person in the world, according to Forbes. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

"The company has already publicly committed to cover losses through company funds in the prior announcement."

Binance said it had enough money to "cover this incident" and much of it was in the same type of tokens that were stolen.

North Korean hackers steal millions posting fake job ads A North Korean hacking group infiltrated 30,000 devices stealing millions of dollars worth of cryptocurrency from people in more than 100 countries.

These include a variety of different cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin and stablecoin.

Cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin, are a type of digital asset, which can be bought, sold and transferred online. Most are not issued by a government or central bank, and their value can fluctuate.

The Bank of England describes stablecoin as a cryptocurrency backed by a specified asset or collection of assets, which their creator uses to maintain their value.

Coin value can be pegged to currencies, such as USD.

Roughly half of the stolen coins have been frozen by issuers, but TRM estimated roughly $3.4 billion worth of crypto is out of reach.

Chainalysis's investigators have traced funds stolen from Binance being laundered and shuffled around in an automated process from different destinations to obscure the trail.

"The investigation remains ongoing and we expect the stolen funds to continue moving in the coming days," it said.

What is Binance?

Binance is like a virtual stock exchange crossed with a bank, but for crypto.

There, people can buy, sell and swap coins, as well as make deposits and withdrawals.

It was founded in 2017 and is the largest exchange in the cryptocurrency space by volume.

October 31, 2026 — 9:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Is Australian rugby making the same mistake it made with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii with Zac Lomax? The Western Force utility back has been named at No.13 in the Australia A side to take on the United States in New Jersey at 11am on Saturday, AEDT, but he’s not realistically going to be the Wallabies’ No.13 at the Rugby World Cup. Former NRL stars turned rugby converts Zac Lomax and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii. Getty Images Despite this column’s oft-stated scepticism at how NRL players can improve the Wallabies, it happily recognised how impressive Lomax was when he made his entry into Super Rugby this year from round 9 onwards. But that assessment was based on his performances as a winger, due in part to his outstanding skill set under the high ball.



Lomax also showed great work rate, athletic capability and capacity to learn, but really it was his superpower under the high ball that marked him down as a Test prospect on the wing. Yes, there is a necessity to pick him in the midfield for Australia A after David Feliuai’s red card last week, but there is a strong argument that Lomax should not be in the United States at all. Loading Rather, Lomax and his Force teammate Dylan Pietsch, who formed the best Australian wing combination in Super Rugby last season, should count themselves very unlucky not to be part of the Wallabies’ touring squad for the Nations Championship northern series. Lomax and Pietsch will again be the best Australian combination in Super Rugby next year, if the Force can resist the temptation to play Lomax at No.13, and their absence feels like a wasted opportunity with Harry Potter and Filipo Daugunu picked ahead of them.



Perhaps Lomax has been his own worst enemy by signing for the PNG Chiefs from 2028 onwards. But at least that bit of business has been concluded early and there will be no tiresome “will he, won’t he” distractions going on to suck up all the oxygen. Besides, the quality of Lomax’s work for the Force suggests he is a task-focused athlete who is very capable of blocking out noise. You give him a target – the Rugby World Cup – and just let him go. Zac Lomax made a promising start to his rugby career at the Western Force. Getty Images That aerial ability is also far too good to waste an on a near-impossible project of making him a better midfield candidate than Len Ikitau, Hunter Paisami or Isaac Henry will be next year. As for Pietsch, who scored two tries for Australia A last weekend, he comes with some priceless guarantees.



For example, there is no way that some of the soft defending on the edges against the All Blacks during the Bledisloe series would have happened on Pietsch’s watch. He tackles like a loose forward and it is close to mystifying that he isn’t in Les Kiss’ squad. No doubt injuries and a lack of recent rugby have played a part, in both the cases of Pietsch and Lomax, but they look like obvious picks. A window of opportunity is hopefully still open for them. The Wallabies’ touring party currently stands at 35, with James Ramm and Kalani Thomas added and Kurtley Beale named to replace Hunter Paisami. That is one shy of the 36 the All Blacks are taking, and the Wallabies squad will fall to 34 when Tate McDermott returns to Australia on fatherhood duties.



Beale’s late inclusion, deemed a shock, is understandable. Not only did Kiss name-check him in recent weeks, but his form for the Force in Super Rugby and Super Rugby AUS was good. Related Article Wallabies ‘I have created my own legacy’: McReight wins first John Eales Medal His 37-year-old legs won’t carry him through 80 minutes of Test rugby, but he would be a more sensible starter in the No.12 jersey than Suaalii in the No.13 if it means than Ikitau plays at No.13, with Suaalii now clearly more impactful as a Wallabies winger. Beale at No.12 would also mean he can babysit the Wallabies’ still-developing trio at No.10 without feeling like a threat to their places. But the inclusion of Lomax and Pietsch feels like a more pressing matter.



Could Lomax make a genuine difference at Test level? Can Pietsch make a genuine difference at Test level? The answer to both is yes. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

Stefano Utoikamanu has little recollection of his debut for Tonga last year after a regulation hit-up resulted in him being knocked out inside the opening minute by Samoan front-rower Francis Molo. Molo was placed on report for his dangerous tackle in the Pacific Nations Championships match, but the Storm enforcer’s day ended immediately. The tackle that ended Stefano Utoikamanu’s Tongan debut last year. NINE “It was pretty crazy because I was so excited to play for Tonga,” Utoikamanu, 26, said. “I got a high shot. But it’s how the game is. They miss some of them, unfortunately that was one they missed. I was angry after that. But it’s a year on, it’s in the past, I’m just excited to go up against them again.”



Molo and Utoikamanu will renew their rivalry on Sunday night when Tonga and Samoa clash in a highly anticipated World Cup match at a sold out CommBank Stadium in Parramatta. It will be a chance for Utoikamanu, who has been named on the bench, to get one back at Molo who will start. Stefano Utoikamanu rips into training at Wentworth Park on Tuesday. KATE GERAGHTY “I’ll go out and do what I do best, which is run hard and try to get at someone,” Utoikamanu said when asked if he would give Molo some special treatment. “Whoever is in front of me, I’ll do what I can to try and get over them.



Related Article Rugby League World Cup Why you’re wrong about Leniu’s ‘character’ as star reveals why he snubbed Kiwis “I’ve been watching the Samoans, they like to play a bit of footy, they’ve got a very strong pack, like ours, so I’m excited for that battle.” Utoikamanu previously represented Samoa to honour his mother, Esther, but always wanted to make his Tongan father, Kava, proud. “I spoke to ‘Woolfy’ [Tonga coach Kristian Woolf] when I first came into the NRL, he asked me to train with the team, or listed me in their extended squads, so I’ve always had that kind of relationship with them before I played,” Utoikamanu said. “I loved watching their games out at Penrith and Campbelltown when they used to play. I’m just happy to wear this red jersey.



“Mum will support me on Sunday no matter what, but she’ll probably also support the Samoans. She knows I always wanted to play for the Tongan team, especially at a World Cup where you get the chance to upset some big teams. “We didn’t have much success in clubland this year, so a big motivation for me was trying to get into this team because I know when we’re at our best, we can beat any team.” The winner of Sunday’s all-Pacific clash is likely to play New Zealand in a semi-final in Newcastle next Saturday, with the loser to remain in Sydney for Australia next Sunday.

World.title: Concerns for welfare of two Australians after Spanish train crash
World.content:
WorldEuropeAustralians abroad Concerns for welfare of two Australians after Spanish train crash David Crowe and Jack Gramenz Updated October 31, 2026 — 6:06am ,first published 8:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Australian authorities are working to confirm the welfare of two Australians linked to this week’s deadly train crash in Spain, amid fears for at least 14 foreign nationals who are listed as missing. A high-speed train on Wednesday smashed into the rear of another on the line running south from Madrid, killing at least 69 people and injuring almost 200. Loading Australian diplomats are supporting the family of two Australians in connection with the collision, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said on Friday. The department expressed its “heartfelt condolences” for all affected by the train crash, but made no comment on the fate of the Australians involved in the tragedy.



“Owing to our privacy obligations, we are unable to provide further comment,” a spokesperson said in a statement. The Spanish foreign ministry initially said that 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, but it outlined new details on Friday afternoon in Madrid – about 2am on Saturday, AEDT – about the countries involved. A crane operates at the site of wrecked train carriages in Spain on Friday. AP Photo/Bernat Armangue The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said there were 51 individuals of 23 different nationalities caught up in the crash, including two confirmed fatalities, but authorities are still working to find missing passengers and identify the dead. Some foreign nationals emerged from the two trains unharmed, Spanish media outlet Heraldo reported on Friday. It cited government sources to report that there were nine injured foreign nationals, two fatalities and 22 whose status was yet to be determined.



The foreign nationals yet to be accounted for come from countries including Argentina, Australia, Canada, Czechia, France, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, Tunisia, the United States and Venezuela, according to multiple reports in Spanish media. Healthcare workers and officials are facing major challenges in establishing the facts and treating the injured. The president of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed the death toll of 69 on Friday, but he cautioned that this depended on further work. “We cannot rule out the possibility of more deaths,” he said. The foreign nationals reported dead include one passenger from Portugal and one from Argentina, according to Spanish media.



In a sign of the horrific nature of the crash, emergency workers have been recovering partial remains in the wreckage from the carriages. Officials from the Castilla-La Mancha government said it would take time to identify the dead. “Testing ​is proceeding slowly, although families will be contacted throughout the day so that they can come ⁠and collect their results,” said Esther Padilla, a government spokesperson, on state television network TVE. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente blamed the disaster on human error, with a control centre in Madrid failing to tell the driver of a high-speed Renfe AVE service that another train, run by private operator Iryo, was stationary on the tracks ahead. But the minister’s comments provoked a furore, with rail unions accusing him of “scapegoating” the rail control workers and demanding his resignation, while the train operators offered different accounts of what drivers had been told.



Related Article Analysis

Tragedy Leaked recordings reveal final moments before the Spanish train disaster The Renfe AVE train had 397 passengers, while the Iryo train was carrying 147. The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies. The Spanish accident authority issued a preliminary report estimating the Renfe train ​was travelling at ⁠a speed of between 160km/h and 200km/h when the collision occurred. The public debate about the crash has focused on whether the controller at the Atocha railway station in Madrid told the Renfe driver to “resume normal operations” rather than telling the driver to keep to 40km/h because there was a stationary train ahead.



Related Article Tragedy ‘Inexplicable’: How the catastrophic train crash in Spain unfolded “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers,” said the report from the Independent ​Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents. The rail centre operator who authorised the Renfe AVE train to resume its journey with normal operation, and therefore reach speeds of 160km/h or more, was questioned by authorities on Thursday. Spanish newspaper El País said he invoked his right to remain silent before the Civil Guard. With Reuters Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.
