The department expressed its “heartfelt condolences” for all affected by the train crash, but made no comment on the fate of the Australians involved in the tragedy.



“Owing to our privacy obligations, we are unable to provide further comment,” a spokesperson said in a statement. The Spanish foreign ministry initially said that 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, but it outlined new details on Friday afternoon in Madrid – about 2am on Saturday, AEDT – about the countries involved. A crane operates at the site of wrecked train carriages in Spain on Friday. AP Photo/Bernat Armangue The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said there were 51 individuals of 23 different nationalities caught up in the crash, including two confirmed fatalities, but authorities are still working to find missing passengers and identify the dead. Some foreign nationals emerged from the two trains unharmed, Spanish media outlet Heraldo reported on Friday. It cited government sources to report that there were nine injured foreign nationals, two fatalities and 22 whose status was yet to be determined.



The foreign nationals yet to be accounted for come from countries including Argentina, Australia, Canada, Czechia, France, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, Tunisia, the United States and Venezuela, according to multiple reports in Spanish media. Healthcare workers and officials are facing major challenges in establishing the facts and treating the injured. The president of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed the death toll of 69 on Friday, but he cautioned that this depended on further work. “We cannot rule out the possibility of more deaths,” he said. The foreign nationals reported dead include one passenger from Portugal and one from Argentina, according to Spanish media.



In a sign of the horrific nature of the crash, emergency workers have been recovering partial remains in the wreckage from the carriages. Officials from the Castilla-La Mancha government said it would take time to identify the dead. “Testing ​is proceeding slowly, although families will be contacted throughout the day so that they can come ⁠and collect their results,” said Esther Padilla, a government spokesperson, on state television network TVE. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente blamed the disaster on human error, with a control centre in Madrid failing to tell the driver of a high-speed Renfe AVE service that another train, run by private operator Iryo, was stationary on the tracks ahead. But the minister’s comments provoked a furore, with rail unions accusing him of “scapegoating” the rail control workers and demanding his resignation, while the train operators offered different accounts of what drivers had been told.



Related Article Analysis

Tragedy Leaked recordings reveal final moments before the Spanish train disaster The Renfe AVE train had 397 passengers, while the Iryo train was carrying 147. The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies. The Spanish accident authority issued a preliminary report estimating the Renfe train ​was travelling at ⁠a speed of between 160km/h and 200km/h when the collision occurred. The public debate about the crash has focused on whether the controller at the Atocha railway station in Madrid told the Renfe driver to “resume normal operations” rather than telling the driver to keep to 40km/h because there was a stationary train ahead.



Related Article Tragedy ‘Inexplicable’: How the catastrophic train crash in Spain unfolded “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers,” said the report from the Independent ​Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents. The rail centre operator who authorised the Renfe AVE train to resume its journey with normal operation, and therefore reach speeds of 160km/h or more, was questioned by authorities on Thursday. Spanish newspaper El País said he invoked his right to remain silent before the Civil Guard. With Reuters Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: New vaccine turning the body's immune system against cancer, expert says
World.content: "And this vaccine that we've been working on with a global team around the world, what it does is we take someone's tumor and then we take their normal DNA and we send it to Moderna in the States. And what they're doing there is they're mapping 34 different areas in the tumor DNA and comparing it to someone's normal DNA - and those areas are where the tumor might make weird-looking proteins on the outside of these cancer cells, and your immune system would come along and say, 'Hey, that's not one of our proteins, we need to attack the cell'.

World.title: Fire crews keep blazes clear of billionaire Graeme Hart's Auckland estate
World.content:
Firefighters tackled two blazes near the clifftop estate of billionaire Graeme Hart in Glendowie, Auckland, on Friday.

Fire and Emergency was alerted to the first blaze, above Gentleman's Bay Beach, at 3.18pm on Friday by a person on a vessel, shift manager Josh Pennefather said.

Three fire crews and a helicopter using a monsoon bucket fought the vegetation fire, which covered an area 100 metres by 50 metres, he said.

The fire was extinguished by 7.40pm, then a 111 call alerted FENZ to a second fire about 10.50pm, Pennefather said.

Four fire crews went to the second fire, just east of the first, which they accessed from Waitara Road, he said.

With the helicopter not able to operate overnight, firefighters attacked the blaze from the ground and it was out by 1.40am Saturday, he said.

Crews stayed on site overnight to monitor for flare-ups before leaving the scene around 6am.

A fire investigator was looking into its cause, Pennefather said.

World.title: Four parties sign pledge to tackle youth homelessness if elected
World.content:
Four political parties have signed a set of commitments aimed at preventing and ending youth homelessness, following the country's first Youth Homelessness Summit in Tāmaki Makaurau, Auckland.

Representatives from Labour, the Green Party, Te Pāti Māori and the Opportunity Party signed the commitments at Friday's summit, which brought together more than 100 housing and youth advocates and rangatahi with lived experience.

New Zealand First also attended, but its representative Vicky Hau was invited to take the commitments back for further discussion.

National and ACT were not represented, although invited.

Political parties from the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, Labour, The Opportunity Party and New Zealand First attended the country's first Youth Homeless Summit: From Crisis to Collective Action. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Manaaki Rangatahi chief executive Bianca Johanson said the summit was being held ahead of the election to ensure youth homelessness remained on the political agenda.

"Right now, Aotearoa, they do not have a youth strategy. We do not have a plan to get out of youth homelessness," she said.

She said a 16-year-old experiencing homelessness that night would not necessarily know where to go or how to access support.

"And that is a shameful fact. So whānau, we're here today to do something about that."

Rangatahi, housing providers, advocates and political united together for the Youth Homeless Summit under the theme: From Crisis to Collective Action. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

The commitments were read aloud by rangatahi advocates Anaru Mihaere and Platinum during the political panel, and set out six areas of action for elected representatives and candidates.

They included backing a legally recognised right to safe, stable and affordable housing for every young person, and supporting legislation to prevent government agencies from releasing rangatahi from care, corrections or health services without somewhere safe to live.

Another commitment called for a national strategy to prevent and end youth homelessness, developed alongside rangatahi, Māori and Pacific communities.

The pledge also called for sustained funding for youth housing services, regular national data on youth homelessness, and further research involving Māori and indigenous researchers.

Youth Advocates Anaru (left) and Platinum say rangatahi voices must be at the heart of solutions to youth homelessness. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

A separate set of commitments focused on rangatahi Māori, including supporting a statutory duty to assist Māori young people who were homeless or at risk.

It also called for Māori-led youth housing providers to be recognised as Te Tiriti partners in the design, delivery and governance of services, and for rangatahi to have greater opportunities to lead decision-making.

Those signing the pledge also committed to meeting with Manaaki Rangatahi annually and reporting on progress.

Te Pāti Māori MP for Tāmaki Makaurau Oriini Kaipara had previously signed the pledge and recommitted to it at the summit.

Green Party's Ricardo Menéndez March shows off his signed set of commitments aimed at preventing and ending youth homelessness. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

[hl] Move-on orders divide parties

The controversial move-on orders were among one of the key kaupapa discussed during the political panel.

The Government's Summary Offences (Move-on Orders) Amendment Act, which came into effect in on 25 October, gave police the power to order people to move elsewhere if they were being disorderly, begging or rough sleeping.

Anyone disobeying the order would face a fine or possible jail sentence.

Green Party representative Ricardo Menéndez March said the legislation treated people experiencing homelessness as a problem, rather than addressing the causes of homelessness.

"We have a government that prioritises treating homeless people like they're a problem as opposed to creating solutions," he said.

The Green Party would repeal the legislation, he said, and focus on "approaches that worked" rather than making "emergency housing harder to access".

An art installation made by rangatahi from Kākano Youth Arts Collective depicts 'from a trap house to a home'. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Hau defended her party's support for the legislation.

"Unpopular opinion, but yes, my party, New Zealand First, did agree to the move-on orders. I have to state that it only affects 18 and over, so ... it doesn't really affect rangatahi under 18," she said, saying it was intended to address public safety concerns and antisocial behaviour affecting businesses and communities.

"I manage the Māngere Town Centre and we see a lot of disruptions and we get a lot of complaints for aggressive and antisocial behaviour, and also that leads people away, because it's not just happening in the CBD, it's happening in the suburbs as well.

"But the whole point is that they should be housed."

Labour's candidate for Tāmaki Max Harris signs a list of commitments to prevent and end youth homelessness in NZ. RNZ / ayla Bailey-McDowell

Labour representative and Tāmaki candidate Max Harris also pledged to reverse the legislation, saying existing laws already dealt with behaviour that genuinely threatened public safety.

"I absolutely reject that public safety is a good ground to justify the move-on orders," he said.

"This was completely unnecessary. It's appalling legislation. And what was also appalling was the rhetoric that was used to justify it."

Harris said rangatahi under the age of 18 were only excluded from the orders following advocacy - from many of the housing and youth advocates present - during the select committee process.

Kaipara said the orders risked pushing people experiencing homelessness into the justice system rather than helping them find housing.

Rangatahi and frontline workers came together to turn lived experience into action and find solutions to youth homelessness. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

"They're moving them on to jail, not to homes," she said.

Kaipara also raised concerns about the criminalisation of begging, saying people asking for food or money could end up with a criminal record.

"Absolutely we do not support that because most of them are Māori, and that's a fact."

National had consistently defended the bill saying it was not a criminilisation of homelessness.

"This is about reclaiming our streets and our city centres for the enjoyment of everybody who visits, works and lives there," Paul Goldsmith previously said.

Opportunity's Romea Tevaga and New Zealand First's Vicky Hau. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

The Opportunity Party candidate for Upper Harbour, Romea Tevaga, said the party would repeal the orders, arguing there was no evidence they produced effective outcomes.

"There's no evidence that shows that it actually gives any effective outcome, and that's what we are. We're [an] evidence-based party."

World.title: RealMe fraudster jailed for nearly 10 years
World.content:
A man has been sentenced to nine years and eight months in prison for serious fraud offending using the RealMe identity verification service.

Hayden Gobey was sentenced at Wellington District Court on Friday. Detective Inspector Stuart Mills said the offending involved the dishonest access and misuse of personal information, forgery and impersonation.

"Victims lost thousands of dollars and this will have caused an extreme amount of financial stress, both short and long term."

Mills wanted to acknowledge the assistance victims provided police throughout the investigation.

"The offending was deliberately deceptive in nature and is likely to have had a significant impact on victims, undermining their trust not only in individuals but also in a range of organisations and services."

World.title: Pooing in bushes, laundry in the lake: Calls for freedom camping ban at popular Wānaka lakeside spot
World.content:
Audio player for " Wanaka residents calling for freedom camping ban at lakeside " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/community/2257706%2Fpooing-in-bushes-laundry-in-the-lake-calls-for-freedom-camping-ban-at-popular-wanaka-lakeside-spot

Wanaka residents calling for freedom camping ban at lakeside Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Wānaka residents are calling for a freedom camping ban at a popular lakeside spot, saying some visitors are defecating in the bushes, doing laundry in the lake and dumping their rubbish.

There are just three spots designated for overnight camping on Beacon Point Road overlooking Lake Wānaka, with the site overwhelmed by campers fighting over them.

Nearby resident Sandy Hazeldine told Checkpoint the site was extremely busy, especially over the summer months.

He said it was a tricky spot to access, and despite the limit, he had just seen four camper vans there.

"It's down several hundred metres of single-lane road. It's a no-exit road, so whatever goes down there has to turn around and come back at some stage, and it's a major walking and cycling track. It's actually part of the the Te Araroa Trail.

"Especially over the summer months, towards the end of the day, any time after three or four o'clock, it's a real battle between the camper vans coming down to see if any of those three spots are still available, and the locals and visitors who are walking, cycling and doing their thing."

Hazeldine said his neighbour once counted over 50 camper vans going in one direction.

The council would sometimes put a sign up at the entrance saying it was full, but that didn't happen very often, he said.

"It doesn't actually stop all the freedom campers going down just to check it out for themselves," Hazeldine said.

"And of course, towards the end of the day, I guess they have to find somewhere to stay, and if it's towards the end of the afternoon, early evening, if they can't park there or it's full, they just sort of go around the corner and park somewhere else. "

Human waste, lake laundry and rubbish dumping

Hazeldine said some of the behaviour he had seen was concerning.

You could lump the whole problem under health and safety, he said.

"I suppose the major health one, and it's fairly unsavoury, is that some people, I'm sure they don't all do it, but some just go and have a crap in the bushes," Hazeldine said.

"And that's not hard to find, especially if you're walking a dog. We've all seen it down there, we've all cleaned a bit up.

"There are four or five homeowners down there that share that track as access. They have rubbish over the fence and people drying their clothing on their fence and all that sort of thing."

He said it was quite common to see people doing laundry in the lake.

Local councils can't use bylaws to completely ban freedom camping across their region, but they can regulate it.

Queenstown Lakes District Council has been hearing submissions on proposed changes to those bylaws.

'Fantastic' alternatives for campers

Hazeldine would like to see the camper vans concentrated in more suitable areas.

"Some years ago, the council opened up an area of wasteland just outside of Wānaka, just on the other side of the Luggate Bridge, and they built some loos there, and that can accommodate probably 50 or 60 vehicles without a problem. That's been operating for quite some time.

"Last summer, we had that as an option and four others in Wānaka that the council had designated for one reason or another, two of those have since dropped off the option list.

"And we're down to the recreation centre, and that can hold quite a few, and that's okay, because it's out of an urban area."

Hazeldine said there were more appropriate alternatives for the camper vans.

"We have three or four camping grounds, and some of those are in absolutely fantastic places, and for a small fee every night, you can go there and have a shower and you can use the loo and you can camp right by the river or right by the lake," he said.

"It's just an odd spot to put three camping sites in an area that was really popular with the public, and it's a walking track mainly, and a biking track, and they have to drive to get there.

"They're not meant to be there before 6pm at night. They had to be gone by 8am in the morning, but that doesn't work. It's just a free-for-all."

Hazeldine said they weren't paying anything and if they wanted to continue to do so, had to be in areas that didn't upset the locals, especially with traffic.

World.title: Meth dealer's 10-year sentence blow to drug trade: police
World.content:
The sentencing of a key player in a Wairarapa drug supply network is a blow to the distribution chain, police say.

Reuben Flutey, 34, received a 10-year, five-month sentence in the Wellington District Court last week after being convicted on 18 charges, including importing and supplying methamphetamine and participating in organised crime.

Police said Flutey was responsible for supplying millions of dollars' worth of methamphetamine across the country.

A Wairarapa CIB investigation ran from March 2023 to December 2024 and uncovered the network's operations.

Police seized nearly $200,000 worth of assets, including drugs, a classic car, motorbikes, jetskis and cash.

Four of Flutey's associates had also been sentenced, while another four were due to appear in court in November and December.

Detective Senior Sergeant Phil Skoglund said methamphetamine and organised crime contributed significant harm to communities and destroyed families.

World.title: Can the health system deliver parties' election promises?
World.content:
Hot on the heels of a hard-hitting flu season, healthcare has become one of the major election issues. As 7 November approaches, the parties are offering cheaper access, more medicines and new services - but can the health system actually deliver them? Health correspondent Kate Green reports.

Free visits to the doctor? Free dental care? Or a brand new cancer treatment centre?

Political parties have put forward a raft of ideas to improve the state of the system, from free care to funding boosts to new taxes ringfenced for health.

See a list of every political party's election policies on health here.

But according to Professor Frank Frizelle ONZM, surgeon and editor-in-chief of the New Zealand Medical Journal, policies and outcomes are not the same thing.

Free GP consultations would still require GPs, just as lowering the bowel screening age would require enough colonoscopy, pathology and treatment capacity, while funding more cancer drugs would require oncology capacity, he said.

He compared this year's election promises to patching holes rather than addressing the underlying problem.

"Everyone's thinking very short term with health and it's very hard to see how continuing to do minor adjustments is going to change the fundamental issue we have, which is that we've got an ageing population."

Professor Frank Frizelle. Michael Bradley

Health targets here to stay

The government's most recent health target results show the postcode lottery remains a barrier to care. Nationally, all five targets had improved on the year before, but in the Northland and Southern districts, more than 40 percent of patients were waiting longer than the target of four months for elective treatments.

Compared with the previous quarter, emergency department wait times improved in half of the country's health districts, while the other half went backwards.

Labour has said it would keep coalition government's health targets if elected.

Focus on primary care and early detection

Labour has promised three free doctor's appointments a year, funded by its new capital gains tax, as well as free prescriptions, maternity scans and cervical screening.

ACT has promised a $400 million funding boost aimed at retaining more GPs in New Zealand and attracting more from overseas.

The Greens want to provide free dental care.

NZ First is promising to focus on prevention by embedding good nutrition into the school curriculum, focusing on metabolic health to prevent chronic illness, funding research into how nutrition can prevent or treat mental illness and investing in hospital trials of how effective intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery is for treating infection.

And Opportunity wants to work across the aisle to establish a 10-year health plan, increase health spending from the current 7.4 percent of GDP to 9 percent, and increase the proportion going to primary care.

Grey Power NZ Federation national president David Marshall. Supplied / Grey Power

David Marshall, national president of Grey Power, said access to primary care was important for seniors.

"If people are seen early, you prevent deterioration and getting into hospital and clogging up the system and poorer outcomes," he said.

While some Grey Power members didn't believe they needed free GP visits, Marshall said cost was a real barrier for others. Delaying treatment could mean their condition worsened, eventually requiring hospital care and adding to pressure there.

But he raised the same question as Frizelle: "Do we have the GPs available to service that?"

He also wanted more commitment from parties to supporting aged care.

"We really don't want older people having to be in hospital, which once again is very expensive," Marshall said. "It would be far better that they could be cared for in home or in residential care. But of course, there's not enough beds at the moment."

Malcolm Mulholland, chair of Patient Voice Aotearoa, said the Greens' dental policy could help a large number of people and argued it could save the country millions of dollars.

A dentist in Timaru had told him he was performing a huge number of teeth extractions, and characterised the state of children's dental care as "a total disintegration of services".

Medicines and cancer care

The National Party wants to redirect foreign aid money into funding for new medicines, and would continue to pursue its health targets.

ACT wants to build New Zealand's first dedicated national cancer centre, as well as allowing pharmacists to treat and manage more conditions.

The National-led government has already boosted Pharmac's budget and funded a series of new cancer drugs.

Patient Voice Aotearoa chair Malcolm Mulholland. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But Mulholland described the increase as a "sugar hit".

"[The improvements] won't be obvious to the public, but they certainly will be by the end of next year, I would expect.

"The bit that we need the politicians to focus on is what they're responsible for, and that is the budget that Pharmac receives," he said. "Give us a plan by which we can catch up with the rest of the world, a plan that preferably would have multi-partisan support."

Frizelle said no matter who people normally voted for, health was a "significant issue" this election.

World.title: Ruthless Cats crush Bulldogs in AFLW finals statement
World.content:
Geelong star Jacqueline Parry has kicked five goals on return from injury to help the Cats ruthlessly cut down the Western Bulldogs by 68 points and lock in a top-two AFLW finish.

The Cats were simply a class above the Bulldogs on Friday night, piling on seven straight goals across the first half en route to a 13.10 (88) to 3.2 (20) triumph at Kardinia Park.

Geelong (11-1) can finish no lower than second on the ladder, with defending premiers North Melbourne — who boast the better percentage — to take on lowly Richmond on Saturday.

Rejuvenated by flag-winning coach Mick Stinear's arrival at the end of last year, the Cats will end their two-year absence from finals in red-hot form after extending their winning streak to 11 games.

The Bulldogs (8-4) have similarly enjoyed a change in fortunes in their third season under coach Tam Hyett, sitting sixth ahead of the weekend's games to earn their first finals berth since 2022.

But Friday's result will be a crude reminder of where the Bulldogs realistically sit in the premiership race.

The visitors could do little to contain Geelong's star on-ball brigade, with Georgie Prespakis controlling the tempo alongside Amy McDonald and Mikayla Bowen.

Parry's five majors on return from concussion saw her surpass Sydney star Chloe Molloy (24 goals) with a league-high 26 goals this season, while young gun Chantal Mason kicked three.

There was no hero to spark the comeback for the Bulldogs, with experienced midfielder Ellie Blackburn rested ahead of finals.

Co-captain Deanna Berry was playing in her first game since round two, but her lone goal in the third quarter — which was the final score for the Bulldogs — was not enough.

Berry had struggled to break back into the side after being sidelined for a month with a collarbone injury earlier this season.

Cats forward Parry wasted no time in making her return known and drew first blood within the opening minute.

The Bulldogs went coast-to-coast to find an immediate response through a Rylie Wilcox goal, only for the visitors to then lose their way.

Geelong soared to a 20-point lead at the first break after taking 86 disposals to the visitors' 41, and 11 forward entries to just two in the first quarter.

The gulf between the Cats and the Bulldogs became more apparent, with the hosts building to a 44-point lead at half-time en route to victory.

AAP

World.title: England's World Cup fate is resting on a miracle
World.content:
England's World Cup campaign may well be over but throwing themselves at the feet of the rugby league gods and praying for mercy is a fitting fate for a tournament that has seemed beyond their control from the start.

After their 34-12 win over Papua New Guinea in Wollongong on Friday night, the English need a Tongan win over Samoa by at least 46 points in order to fall backwards into a semi-final berth.

It's a byzantine tournament structure, one which has copped plenty of heat since it dawned on everyone that England's opener against Tonga was essentially a de facto elimination game.

England are standing on the outside looking in for the World Cup. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

That loss sent England off the road before they'd even started moving and they've spent the past two weeks in purgatory, hoping for a salvation they barely had a say in given they'd already lost control of their destiny.

Against the Kumuls they played like that knowledge caught up with them. There were moments of slick attack and individual brilliance in the first half as they ran out to a 22-0 lead in as many minutes.

Their spine combined nicely, especially for AJ Brimson and Dom Young's tries, and Matty Smith won't recieve a finer gift this Christmas than the offload Kai Pearce-Paul gave him for his try.

For a few minutes it looked as though they'd chew well into the points turnaround they'd need if they were to stumble into the knockout phase.

But then the errors came, thick and fast and often. They did not stop until Matty Ashton dropped it in contact inside the final minutes to record England's 20th mistake of the night.

By the end, England were limping home amid a spirited Kumul revival that threatened to turn the game into a genuine contest.

The gap was just 24-12 with 12 minutes left and only some good England scrambling defence stopped it from being even tighter.

It was spearheaded by ripping winger Dudley Dutoi and five-eighth Gairo Voro, who started out as a diamond in the rough but is looking brighter every time he's exposed to the top level.

The Kumuls won the second half 12-10, and while last week's loss to Samoa was a poor one, it's easy to see better days ahead for them.

Dutoi and Voro are proof the pathways from local football can produce capable and exciting players, and there's the potential for plenty more of them with the looming arrival of the PNG Chiefs.

As they splash around in their rivers of gold some of it is bound to trickle down to the national side.

There is money and talent in Papua New Guinea, and if you smash enough of that together, you're cooking with gas.

Up and coming stars like Gairo Voro are the future for Papua New Guinea. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

For England, the future is less certain and not just over the next few days as they pray for a Tongan massacre.

Their run through the tournament has been dogged with constant debate on the future of the sport in its birthplace, and the rise of the international game in the Pacific has spotlighted how rugby league in Europe, and England especially, is standing still at best.

Barring a succession of miracle results, this game will be the only win by a northern hemisphere team over a southern hemisphere side in the entire tournament.

England or Great Britain have not beaten Australia since 2006. Fiji scored more points against the Kangaroos last week than England managed in all of last year's Ashes series.

Samoa and Tonga's rivalry turns fans into heroes Ahead of the latest instalment of their timeless rivalry, a new generation of Samoan and Tongan stars have transformed from fans into the new heroes of their nation.

They have not beaten New Zealand since 2018. Their loss to Tonga was their heaviest ever defeat to a Tier 2 nation.

As the gap threatens to widen, there's no shortage of opinions on how to close it and all anybody can seem to agree on is what has to happen, even if nobody can agree on how it will.

The English game needs a silver bullet that will raise the standard in Super League and thus ensure more consistent and quality matches for the league's best players and teams.

It needs more players in NRL systems, because that will make them better players, but not so many that their own competition is devoid of homegrown stars, a conundrum that is a very fine balance.

It needs things that are easy to want but hard to find, like money to invest in itself and the time to let that investment grow, and it needs more patience from a fanbase that is as desperate for success as it is accustomed to failure.

Everybody knows where they want to go but they're all shouting out different directions and, as a result, the wheels keep spinning but nothing really moves.

The English game finds itself at a crossroads. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Perhaps the changes that can bring about such a transformation are looming.

The undercurrent of England's campaign has been the ongoing negotiations between the NRL and the Rugby Football League about the Australians taking partial or total control of the game in the UK.

If it does go through, in whatever form it can, perhaps it will be the shock to the system the game is after. The injection of capital could bring about the kind of structural transformations rugby league so often struggles to implement.

But England enters that deal at the NRL's mercy, just like they're at the mercy of the fates in the days to come.

They're not fighting for a future as much as they are hoping for one, as sure as they're hoping for a Tonga win by 46 points on Sunday.

World.title: Series set for epic finale as Aussie batters must stand up
World.content:
Although doubts have been expressed in the last few days that the Cape Town speed gun is operating with flawless accuracy, late on day four of the third Test there appeared to be some validity to its claim that Mitchell Starc had breached the 150km/h barrier.

Soon after, one couldn't help thinking of that speedometer figure — illegal in a car, faintly alarming in a sporting arena — and wince. One of Starc's typically brutish bouncers had spat up off the Newlands pitch and was rearing towards a Proteas batsman.

In the split second it took him to realise his gloves would soon be in the ball's path, and having prized his wicket all day, Ryan Rickelton got his hands out of the way on the understanding the ball would cannon into his ribs with that horrifying thud only a rare breed of cricketer accepts as his duty. And boy did it thud.

There was a time not long ago when the done thing in such situations was to grit one's teeth and pretend it hadn't happened. Think David Boon's thousand-yard stare, or Justin Langer grinning sans tooth. Not Rickelton.

Mitchell Starc may not have taken many wickets on day four, but he made Ryan Rickelton pay for his runs. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Grant Pitcher)

He was on 92 by that point, hours into a game-turning innings, and knew that if a nasty bruise was blossoming, there was no point in pretending it wasn't so. Up came his shirt and sure enough, the mark was already ranking high on the Brian Close scale.

Rickelton showed it off to Travis Head at short leg, either for confirmation or possibly approval of its nastiness. Head seemed to offer both.

Quick hits from Australia vs South Africa day four Here are the quick hits from day four of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

It is one of those unspoken paradoxes of Test cricket: the more two teams respect each other, the more they try to hurt each other, and vice versa. As they had the previous evening, and for the telling first two-thirds of the fourth day, Australia's bowlers had been throwing everything at Rickelton and none of it was working.

In the end, it took a run-out to remove him — moments after he brought up a century that slowly but surely ruined Australia's hopes of a quick kill. Rickelton already has a Test double century to his name.

When Ryan Rickelton finally got out, it was due to a mix-up and run-out, but he had put South Africa back in the game. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Grant Pitcher)

He is a world champion. But here was the sort of high-stakes, backs-to-the-wall performance that can define a career.

As a result, from 4-140 at the start of the day, South Africa piled on 387 to convincingly rebut suggestions they'd roll over. For the third time in the series, a Test between these two proud cricket nations will go down to the fifth day.

The pressure is now all on Australia, who will need to chase down 288 runs to win and retain the status of world number one, with Kagiso Rabada, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer licking their lips at the prospect of series-winning wickets.

That Australia's task is so onerous is mostly a result of Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder's 154-run partnership for the sixth wicket, which stretched across 53 overs after Matthew Breetzke's dismissal for a spiky, counterpunching 43 in the morning.

Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder both made centuries on day four, and made life a lot tougher for the tourists. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Grant Pitcher)

Mulder was no second fiddle. After Rickelton departed for a brave and controlled 101 from 219 deliveries, Mulder carried on with a faltering tail, scattering fielders and clubbing sixes to reach a superb 115 of his own.

The above numbers should not give the impression the Australian attack misfired, per se, nor that Australia lacked intent. Until the last minute of the day, they fielded with great gusto to create pressure and affect run-outs to make up for the lack of help from the pitch.

All day, Nathan Lyon bowled with guile and control, jagging the ball at right angles.

It was just that for almost as long, Rickelton and Mulder defied him with the disciplined application of a solid plan: put your ego to one side, get back and across, don't hit against the spin, concede Lyon's end in the knowledge that the quicks at the other end would not get as much help from the surface.

Of the latter, Starc, in particular, gave everything of himself and more, and as late as the final half-hour of play was literally bowling himself off his feet to try and take South Africa's final wicket.

His nine dismissals for the game on a pitch that has offered him little represented a superhuman endeavour.

Where Australia can be faulted, perhaps, is for squandering the second new ball. South Africa was 5-222 when it arrived and there was no repeat of Starc's first-innings clean-up job.

In a day of thankless toil, skipper Pat Cummins broke his wicket drought but otherwise rarely threatened, only claiming his second when Mulder holed out in the final over of the day.

Again, there were industrial quantities of interpersonal drama, although nothing that crossed the line. Hyped up and a little uncoordinated between the wickets, Breetzke tangled with Lyon and spoiled for battles with every other bowler, including a prolonged one-way conversation with Starc.

After taking the bails to run out Rickelton, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted down the pitch like a terrier in the Crufts dog show to let Mulder know it was his fault.

Of course, Labuschagne and others will need their bats to do the talking on the final day, and there is a sense that Rabada will not miss out twice in one game, even without his muse Steve Smith around to get his blood boiling.

A week ago, one might have asked: who will be Australia's Rickelton and Mulder? But all of a sudden, there are a few more convincing answers.

So, a gripping Test series — worthy in every way of its billing as a de facto world title — will now get its fitting conclusion.

World.title: Quick hits: Mix-up ends schoolmates' mammoth stand, Breetzke brings the fight
World.content:
Ryan Rickelton was left fuming after a mix-up ended a mammoth partnership with schoolmate Wiaan Mulder, as Matthew Breetzke didn't back down on a day of toil for the Aussies.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Breetzke's tongue takes the fight to Australia

After a simmering, tempestuous end to day three, the chat continued as the Proteas looked to fight back on day four.

Matthew Breetzke and Mitchell Starc drew the battlelines early, with the pair sharing a few tense words and Starc providing a mixture of death stares and wry smiles.

And Breetzke, who had provided Marnus Labuschagne with a remarkable leaping send-off on day one, was never likely to back down.

With him and Starc a couple overs into their stoush, the quick had the South African ducking underneath a bouncer.

Rising from his haunches, Breetzke cocked his head and poked out his tongue in Starc's direction, before grabbing his box and holding the pose.

It was quite the statement from Matthew Breetzke. (Fox Cricket)

Things were heating up — but the chat began to dissipate when Breetzke fell, before almost completely disappearing as Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder got stuck into their work.

2. Cummins's breakthrough wicket

At the start of South Africa's second innings, Pat Cummins had gone 314 balls without a Test dismissal, with his last wicket coming in the second innings in Durban.

For a man who averages a scalp just about every 22 balls in Test cricket, that's a fair drought.

The Australian captain ran in hard late on day three, and came close to breaking through with a line-ball LBW call, but started day four at Newlands still in search of a pole.

It took over an hour of play, but finally, he broke through.

Bowling back of a length and to a leg-side field, Cummins had the well-set Breetzke (43) out hooking to Mitchell Starc at backward square leg in.

Pat Cummins gave Australia the breakthrough in the opening session, with the wicket his first since the first Test of the series. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

After 372 wicketless deliveries, Cummins had broken the longest dismissal drought of his Test career, and the Proteas were five down with just an 81-run lead.

3. Schoolmates Rickelton and Mulder break Australia

Rickelton was enormous on day four.

The wicketkeeper-batter played with supreme confidence and hardly presented an opportunity to the Aussie attack, managing the ebbs and flows of his innings to perfection.

Up the other end, Mulder was just as impressive, grinding the Australians into the dirt as he and Rickelton batted for the majority of the day in a mammoth 134-run, 319-ball partnership.

The pair looked completely at home together in the middle, and so they should — Rickelton and Mulder attended secondary school together at Johannesburg's St Stithians College.

Ryan Rickelton's gritty century on day four helped bat South Africa into a potential position of victory. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher)

After 218 balls and a whopping 12 overs in the 90s, Rickelton pushed the leg-side single that brought up his second Test ton, which he celebrated by embracing his old buddy on a red-letter day for St Stithians.

4. Rickelton fumes after being barbecued

With Cummins seemingly long out of ideas, Rickelton having just brought up his century, and Labuschagne into his fourth over of the day, Australia was not even threatening to take a wicket.

Centurion Ryan Rickelton was burnt by partner Wiaan Mulder. (Fox Cricket)

But there was trouble brewing for the old friends in the middle.

Mulder had nailed his reverse sweep to backward point, where Josh Inglis made a fantastic stop and followed it with a quick release.

From the non-striker's end, Rickelton had raced out of the blocks and found himself all the way up the other end of the pitch.

Unfortunately for the centurion, Mulder was ball watching and completely unmoved, with Rickelton unable to get home as Labuschagne broke the stumps.

Loading Instagram content

Speaking to ABC Sport at stumps, Rickelton was far from impressed — if not overly surprised — by his old schoolmate.

"Wiaan, he grates me sometimes because he drifts away in exactly that moment," Mulder said.

"He hit the shot and he just kind of ball-watched and it was an easy one, but sometimes he isn't really present and he can drift away.

"So it does frustrate me and I'm really irritated about that because we could have got a lot more tonight."

We hadn't seen a run-out all series before day four, but only a matter of minutes after the first, we were treated to a second.

Again, it was Labuschagne at the heart of it, brilliantly throwing down the stumps to have Gerald Coetzee on his way.

5. Mulder puts on a show late

With South Africa having lost 4-16 and No.11 Kagiso Rabada joining Mulder at the crease, the start of the Australian run chase loomed large.

But Mulder had other ideas.

Test cricket live South Africa sets Australia a target of 288 to win the third Test and the series after an thrilling comeback on day four in Cape Town.

The all-rounder farmed the strike smartly, and after batting within himself for the majority of the day, began to take the game to the Australians.

After becoming the day's second St Stithians alumnus to cross three figures, he battered the Aussies, taking Cummins and then Nathan Lyon for massive leg-side sixes in consecutive overs.

With Temba Bavuma opting against a late declaration, Mulder and Rabada extended South Africa's lead by a further 36 runs before the centurion holed out on the final ball of the day.

Australia will begin its fourth innings at the start of the series' deciding day, requiring 288 runs for victory.

World.title: New tennis number one as Zverev finally reaches the top
World.content:
Alexander Zverev, who spent years waiting for his moment to reach the summit of ​his sport only for a new golden generation to surge past him, has finally climbed to the top of tennis' world rankings.

Zverev had long been one of the brightest talents to emerge in the 2010s, but his path, like that of his peers, was largely blocked by the enduring dominance of Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray.

Despite ​winning two ATP Finals titles on either side of ‌an Olympic gold medal in 2021, Zverev struggled to make a similar impact at the grand slams as Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz formed a new roadblock when the greats began to decline.

All that changed this year, however, as Zverev, 29, capitalised on injuries to his major rivals and found another level to claim the French Open and US Open ‌titles.

"It's incredibly special," said Zverev, who will take over from Sinner on Monday and become the 30th man to top the world rankings since they were introduced ⁠in 1973.

"It's something I've worked towards for years and you have to show great tennis the whole ‌year to be in this position."

Zverev will become only the second world ​number one, after Daniil Medvedev, from the crop ‌of players now largely in their late 20s and early 30s who emerged during the "Big Four" era but never displaced them.

The summit had been within Zverev's reach before, but a serious ankle injury at the 2022 French Open derailed his push, and Grand Slam success continued to elude him on his return as Sinner and Alcaraz accumulated 12 majors between them.

Zverev wins US Open final Alexander Zverev wins his second grand slam title of the year with a dominant victory over American Ben Shelton in the men's US Open final.

With Alcaraz's season stalled by a wrist injury and Sinner suffering a knee injury, Zverev's consistency and ​durability ‌were decisive this year as he triumphed at Roland Garros and Flushing Meadows and reached the Wimbledon final.

"I've had a lot of difficult moments in my career: the lost grand slam finals, the injury in 2022," Zverev said.

"But I always somehow kept believing, kept going. This year I also took the ⁠step of changing my game a little and rebuilding it, at 29. The way ‌this season has gone is a dream."

Zverev's path to ‌the top has also included turbulence away from the court, with allegations of domestic abuse, which he has repeatedly denied.

A German court closed a case involving his former partner ‌Brenda Patea after a 2024 settlement without a finding of guilt, and the ATP ended a separate investigation into allegations by Olga Sharypova in 2023, citing insufficient evidence.

Zverev's 3-8 record against top-10 opponents this season may leave room for debate over whether the top ‌ranking makes him ​the best player, but noted coach Patrick ⁠Mouratoglou said staying fit and sustaining excellence were skills in themselves.

For Zverev, who has managed type 1 diabetes since childhood, durability has been a constant issue.

"A player is not only performing on court, it's also being healthy, managing your body," Mouratoglou said.

"If someone is never injured and others are often injured, the one that's not injured will probably end up having a higher ranking … staying healthy when you're a professional athlete ⁠is a real skill."

Zverev said reaching number one late in his career had left him better prepared for the responsibility that accompanies the ranking, both as the face of the sport and the player everyone ‌wants to beat.

"The number one position ‌brings a lot with it," said Zverev, Germany's second men's world number one after Boris Becker in 1991.

"You have to ​be a good role model, do a lot of things right and on court that means more than returning and serving well. I still have Carlos and Jannik. Hopefully, I can keep competing with them over the next few years."

Reuters

World.title: Joint's promising run in Japan ends with QF exit
World.content:
Maya Joint's encouraging run at the Pan Pacific Open in Japan has ended with a three-set quarterfinal loss on a day when world number one Elena Rybakina pulled out with an injury.

The Australian, ranked 94 in the world, had been impressive in earlier wins over sixth-seeded Romanian Sorana Cirstea and Spain's Cristina Bucsa to book her spot in the quarterfinals at the WTA 500 event against Kamilla Rakhimova.

The Uzbekistani won a tight first set 7-5, before Joint rebounded to claim the second by the same scoreline.

However, Rakhimova romped away in the final set to win 7-5, 5-7, 6-1 in Tokyo on Friday, local time.

Joint took the honours in first serves, landing 66 per cent compared with her opponent's 59 per cent, and serving five aces to Rakhimova's one.

However, the world number 66 was much more effective on her return, converting six of the 12 break points she set up, compared with the three Joint managed.

Despite the loss, the late-season Asian swing has been a welcome confidence boost for Joint.

Ranked a career-high number 28 in February, the Australian's year had been underwhelming until she made the final at last month's Korea Open in Seoul, where she lost to compatriot Kim Birrell.

The signs are certainly promising for the 20-year-old as she plans her assault on the Australian Open in January.

Rakhimova's victory set up a semifinal against Leylah Fernandez.

The Canadian had an armchair ride to the semis when world number one and reigning Australian and US Open champion Rybakina withdrew from their quarterfinal because of injury.

Rybakina said she could not play because of an undisclosed injury. She stepped onto the court in Tokyo and delivered the news to fans and ended by saying, "I hope to see you all next year."

She said she had been struggling for several days "with a little injury" and needs to be ready for next month's WTA Finals in Indian Wells, California.

AAP

World.title: Australia facing monster chase to win series after Mulder, Rickelton tons
World.content:
Australia will require 288 runs to win the third Test in Cape Town after centuries from Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder put South Africa back in favour.

After beginning day four at 4-140, Rickelton (101) and Mulder (115) combined to help South Africa post 387 in its second innings.

Mitchell Starc was once again Australia's best bowler, finishing with figures of 3-61 off 22 overs, while Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon added two wickets apiece.

If successful on day five, Australia will have recorded the second-highest successful run chase at Newlands behind their predecessors, who mowed down 334 with six wickets down in 2002.

Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder combined for a 154-run partnership to turn the tables on Australia on day four in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher)

South Africa began the day with a lead of just 40 runs with six wickets in hand having lost their skipper minutes before stumps yesterday.

Rickelton and Matthew Breetzke, two players who have shown an ability to score at rapid rates in other forms of the game, needed to curb their natural aggression.

They did so superbly, fending off vicious short deliveries from Australia's pacemen and snaking spinners from Nathan Lyon for much of the morning session.

Breetzke notched 43 off 121 deliveries before being the latest South African to be sucked into taking on a short delivery as he holed out, giving Pat Cummins his first wicket since the first Test.

Nathan Lyon could not reap the rewards of spin-friendly conditions on a frustrating day for Australia's bowlers. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

Breetzke's dismissal came prior to the second new ball and gave Australia fresh hope of wrapping up the Proteas innings in a hurry, as they did on day one.

However, it was not to be as Wiaan Mulder joined Rickelton at the crease and put on a partnership for the ages.

Mulder initially looked shaky, scoring just five off his first 30 deliveries while fending off the second new ball before he expanded his game after lunch.

The pair took the shine of the new ball through the middle session while simultaneously adding to South Africa's lead, adding 92 priceless runs.

Pat Cummins gave Australia the breakthrough in the opening session, with the wicket his first since the first Test of the series. (AP Photo: Halden Krog)

With the ball getting softer, Australia turned to spin later in the day with Travis Head, Matt Renshaw and Marnus Labuschagne all getting a chance at the bowling crease.

After seemingly spending an eternity toiling through the 90s while being peppered by short-pitched deliveries, Rickelton brought up his century with a classy flick to the leg side off Josh Hazlewood, sparking a raucous applause around Newlands.

However, his excitement was short-lived after being run out by Mulder in the very next over following a horrible mix-up, ending a sensational 154- run partnership between the pair.

Rickelton's dismissal brought a host of wickets, with Marco Jansen holing out in the deep before Simon Harmer was bowled by Lyon after leaving a big-spinning delivery that pitched well outside the off stump.

Mulder looked set to be stranded when Gerald Coetzee was run out late in the day, but he farmed the strike expertly with South Africa's No.11, Kagiso Rabada, to register his fourth Test century in the dying overs of the day.

Mulder hit out after reaching his milestone and was caught in the deep going for his fifth six of the innings in the final over of the day.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from day four as it happened.

World.title: Retiring Swan Rampe 'hurt' over Pullman Hotel saga
World.content:
Sydney stalwart Dane Rampe "selfishly" grappled with putting off retirement, feeling hurt and upset that the Pullman Hotel saga had derailed his final AFL season.

The 36-year-old defender, who has confirmed his playing career is over, had quietly settled on making this season his last and seemed on track to have one last crack at an elusive premiership after the Swans finished second on the ladder ahead of the finals.

But Sydney's premiership bid — as Swans chairman Andrew Pridham put it — was "torpedoed" after vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down.

The five were suspended from round 24 and the club's two finals for what the Swans termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

Those AFL-endorsed club bans were separate from a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, which is ongoing. No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Riley Bice were among the Swans players suspended by the club. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Rampe, who played in four losing grand finals (2014, '16, '22 and '24) across 289 games, confessed to his personal hurt at what happened.

The former Swans co-captain was emotional and held back tears as he announced his retirement on Friday in front of family, teammates and media.

"Deep down, I probably knew at this time last year, this was going to be my last year," Rampe said on Friday.

"Everything was going swimmingly … and then, I'm not going to lie, the events that happened at the back end of the season really muddied those waters.

"It really threw into disarray what I was thinking, what I hadn't probably admitted to myself yet.

"Selfishly, there was part of me that felt a little bit upset and hurt by what had happened.

"I was struggling to accept whether this was the way I was going to bow out.

"And then, coupled with that, was the place in which the club found itself. It didn't feel right. It didn't feel right leaving with where things are at."

Rampe said conversations with coach Dean Cox and football Leon Cameron had helped him achieve "clarity" surrounding his retirement.

He was re-drafted as a rookie this season alongside fellow defender Jake Lloyd, who has signed on for a 15th season.

Dane Rampe captained the Swans in a Grand Final defeat to Brisbane in 2024. (AAP: James Ross)

Cox "delicately" suggested that Rampe was struggling to meet the physical demands after 14 seasons in the system.

"I couldn't quite give the 100 per cent that made me Dane Rampe, the Swans player," Rampe said.

"I'm grateful for the way he [Cox] delicately posed that to me, because it was something I needed to hear.

"Given the emotions of the back end of the season, it was hard for me to see the forest for the trees."

A Swans fan who sprinted onto the SCG in 1999 after Tony Lockett broke the league's goal-kicking record, Rampe has been a heart-and-soul player since he was drafted as a rookie in 2012, aged 22.

He made his debut in 2013 and went on to co-captain the Swans with Josh Kennedy and Luke Parker from 2019 to 2023.

Rampe is a Bob Skilton Medallist (2019) as the club best and fairest and an All-Australian ('16), making him one of the club's greatest rookie-list success stories alongside childhood idol Brett Kirk.

When captain Callum Mills suffered an ACL injury last month in their semi-final win over Brisbane, it was only natural for the Swans to turn to Rampe.

Rampe would captain the Swans in what would be his final match, the club's preliminary final loss to Fremantle.

Dane Rampe reacts emotionally on the final siren of Sydney's first game following the Pullman Hotel incident. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

With nothing confirmed for his future besides a break from the AFL, Rampe said he leaves the club with confidence.

"I'm completely at peace with where the club sits," Rampe said.

"Does that mean that we're not going to be having robust conversations? Absolutely not.

"In fact, I hope to hear that they are having challenging conversations going forward, and that the media is reporting difficult conversations.

"That's a sign of a healthy club, a healthy culture, and I urge and implore the boys and the rest of the club to lean into that."

AAP

Tech.title: Apple Intelligence is finally coming to China with iOS 27.3
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple will launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3, the company announced on its Chinese newsroom website, as reported by MacRumors. The Apple Intelligence features will be available first in an iOS 27.3 beta that’s set to launch on November 4th, with a full iOS 27.3 release scheduled for December.

This launch doesn’t bring the new Siri AI to China. Instead, Apple is launching several of its earlier Apple Intelligence features like notification summaries, real-time translation, rewriting and proofreading tools, visual intelligence, and removing objects from photos. Apple also says it has worked with Ailbaba to add support for its Qwen chatbot in some experiences, which sounds similar to iOS’s integration with OpenAI’s ChatGPT that launched in 2024.

Apple Intelligence was approved in China in July, which signalled that the launch of the AI tools was getting near. Apple trained its own LLM specifically for China, Reuters reported in August.

Tech.title: Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Akai teased its new MPC Sample Key on Instagram earlier this week, and said it plans to open-source its software so the modding community can hack it to their hearts’ delight. While there’s no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set.

While the Sample Key shares many of the same controls as the MPC Sample — including the three context-sensitive encoders, a large main encoder — it seems designed for pitched sample playback, rather than chopping up drums. In fact, the “chop” button from the MPC Sample is missing entirely from the Sample Key.

The dedicated pitch and mod wheels are another clue there. But there are also buttons for changing the octave range of the 25-key keyboard, as well as ones labeled “chord” and “arp.” Presumably, those enable a chord playback mode and an arpeggiator. While using an arpeggiator to play back drum samples can be a fun way to create rhythms, it’s more commonly used for melodic and bass parts. And a chord mode would be basically useless for drums. Those options also appear to replace the chop function from the standard MPC Sample.

Previous Next



1 / 3

There also appears to be a dedicated looper that could be useful for live performance and layering sounds. And, instead of the Flex Beat effects from the original MPC Sample, there’s something called “Swarm.” Though what that is isn’t exactly clear at the moment.

Like the first entry in the Sample series, the Key has a built-in mic and speaker for all-in-one music production. While we haven’t gotten a glimpse at the back panel yet, the config options on the front suggest that, in addition to MIDI, the Sample Key will have CV outs for integrating with modular synths.

Correction October 30th: The MPC Sample Key is 25 keys, not 37.

Tech.title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
Tech.content:
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.

But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.

You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”

Tech.title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.

The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.

The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Meta communications head Andy Stone also signaled support for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.”

Microsoft says it will offer granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.

While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.”

Update, October 30th: Added a comment from Meta.

Tech.title: Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space:

Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨

Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this month.

“Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit,” Google says. “Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.”

Tech.title: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday, Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union.

It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with, which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also recently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.”

Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future.

Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT, and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards.

It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.”

Tech.title: The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
Tech.content:
is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The iPhone has more screens! The MacBook has a touchscreen! The HomeView does CarPlay apps! For the first time in a long time, Apple is in a period of unabashed gadget experimentation, and while the final results aren’t always perfect, it’s fun to watch the most successful product maker try some new things again. Even when, in this case, “trying” amounts to just slapping a touch panel on a lovely new MacBook Pro — just to see if you might use it.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate the merits of a touchscreen laptop, Nilay explains why he is absolutely positively going to buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and David asks, as always, could this have been an iPad?

After that, the hosts discuss Instagram’s foray into long-form content, and Adam Mosseri’s increasingly complicated relationship with AI content. Instagram is at once extraordinarily powerful and under serious threat, and Mosseri’s going to have a hard time making it all work. Finally, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, news about Anthropic’s IPO and Anduril’s laptops, and much more.

Tech.title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.

“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.

Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)

“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.” — Derek Mulvey

But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.

Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:

So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.

But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”

Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.

Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.

The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.

To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

Tech.title: Salesforce’s M&A spree continues with a reported $375M deal for defense tech startup Rune
Tech.content:
In Brief

Salesforce has agreed to acquire Rune Technologies, a startup that builds AI software to help the U.S. military predict supply needs and manage logistics from the field, for $375 million in cash and stock, Resilience Media reported.

The acquisition underscores Salesforce’s push into defense tech through Missionforce, its business unit serving national security and defense agencies. Since Missionforce launched last year, its business has grown 80% year over year, driven in part by a new 10-year, $5.6 billion contract with the U.S. Army, the company said in a blog post. By integrating Rune’s frontline logistics data, Missionforce will extend beyond back-office administrative planning to support battlefield operations.

Since its founding in 2024, Rune has raised a total of $30 million from investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures, and IQT, a CIA-backed non-profit venture firm formerly known as In-Q-Tel. The startup was last valued at $127 million when it raised a Series A led by Human Capital last year, according to PitchBook.

Salesforce has been on an acquisition spree this year. In addition to Rune, the CRM giant agreed to buy AI agent platform Fin (formerly Intercom) for $3.6 billion, bought Qualified for $1.2 billion, and signed an agreement to buy Listen Labs after the startup walked away from a $125 million Series C term sheet at a $1.5 billion valuation, as TechCrunch reported.

Tech.title: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant, is shutting down
Tech.content:
Ollie, a startup whose mission was to deliver an AI assistant that respected its users’ privacy, says that it will be shutting down in a week. Bill Lennon, the company’s co-founder and CEO, took to X on Friday to deliver the news, noting that the app will officially shut down on November 6.

“I’m really proud of what we accomplished,” Lennon said. “We built an incredible personal assistant with a small team, and learned a ton. I’m grateful to our amazing team, our users, our investors, and everyone who supported us on this journey.”

The text-based AI assistant market has exploded over the past year, as the increasingly powerful models that undergird such applications have made them significantly more useful for daily tasks.

Ollie, which discussed its $7.5 million seed round led from Khosla Ventures with TechCrunch in September, offered a subscription-based model. The assistant was focused on helping families stay connected and organized. The app connected to a user’s email and calendar, while also providing integrated functions to help with appointment bookings, meal planning, and bill payments. The company had also planned to eventually move into household budgeting.

Crucially, Ollie was one of the first mainstream apps that managed to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard that companies can attain via an independent audit. Unfortunately, user privacy has never been a hugely profitable aspect of the tech industry. If anything, many new digital assistants present unique privacy challenges for their users — as companies like Instinct have shown.

Ultimately, the pressures of the burgeoning AI industry had taken its toll on the company, Lennon said. “We got close, but ultimately couldn’t keep up,” he added. “With Muse, Instinct, and others entering the space, it became harder to stand out, grow, and raise the capital we needed to succeed.”

Ollie’s customers will receive instructions on how to export data and receive refunds in the coming days, Lennon added.

Tech.title: Intel’s stock crashes, knocking $12B from government’s stake
Tech.content:
Intel’s stock suffered one of its worst days ever on Friday, crashing around 28% after the chip giant reported a weaker-than-expected outlook for the fourth quarter.

This rout reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion, CNBC reports. The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. Nvidia, which also took a big stake in Intel in 2025, saw its stock drop a bit on Friday as well. Much of the tech industry — especially chipmakers — were caught in the sell-off.

Intel’s stock is still a profitable investment for the government so far (and for Nvidia), as it’s up more than 70% for the year, even if it’s dropped significantly from the sky-high prices it commanded over the summer.

The scare-off was caused when Intel warned to expect revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion in the fourth quarter when analysts were looking for around $17 billion.
